name: Acts
subtitle: A Witness Made of Scripture
howToRead: The church in Acts preaches Christ out of Israel’s own scriptures. Its great speeches are catenae in miniature — Peter at Pentecost reading the outpoured Spirit from Joel and the undecayed body from the Psalms, Stephen retelling the whole story of Israel until it indicts his judges, Paul in the Antioch synagogue threading Psalm 2, Isaiah, and Habakkuk into one argument, James settling the Gentile question on a verse of Amos. The narrative itself runs on scriptural rails — a chosen-then-rejected prophet, a people scattered and gathered, a word that breaks out to the nations — and it closes, fittingly, on Isaiah’s hardened ears. The chips beside each passage name the Scripture underneath it — solid for a formal quotation, dashed for an allusion, dotted for a fainter echo, ◇ for a figural pattern that borrows no words. A lighter chip and a trailing ? mark an echo that is faint or contested. Where the apostles follow the Greek of the Septuagint against the Hebrew, both readings are shown.

pericopes.text: The first book I wrote, Theophilus, concerned all that Jesus began both to do and to teach, until the day in which he was received up, after he had given commandment through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen. To these he also showed himself alive after he suffered, by many proofs, appearing to them over a period of forty days, and speaking about God’s Kingdom. Being assembled together with them, he commanded them, “Don’t depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which you heard from me. For John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit. I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day […]
echoes.note: The risen Jesus tells the apostles to wait for 'the promise of the Father' and the baptism 'in the Holy Spirit not many days from now.' Volume: no verbal quotation yet, but the conceptual content (an outpouring of the Spirit on God's people in the last days) maps directly onto Joel. Recurrence: decisive — Luke makes this same Joel text the explicit hermeneutical key at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-21), so the 'promise' here is programmatic foreshadowing. Thematic coherence: high; the whole opening frames the Spirit as eschatological gift. History of interpretation broadly reads the 'promise of the Father' as Joel's Spirit-pouring. Confidence high on Recurrence and Coherence even though the immediate Volume is thematic.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: The Spirit 'put within' God's people to enable obedience is the other great prophetic promise standing behind 'the promise of the Father.' Volume is low (no shared wording in translation), but Thematic Coherence is strong: Ezekiel's interiorized Spirit is the renewal-of-Israel hope that the apostles' question in v.6 presupposes. Recurrence modest. Honestly faint relative to Joel, hence echo/medium.

echoes.text: Moses entered into the midst of the cloud, and went up on the mountain; and Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
echoes.note: Jesus appears and teaches 'over a period of forty days.' Volume: only the numeral, so verbal borrowing is minimal — this is a figural/typological link, not a citation. Thematic coherence: forty-day periods of divine revelation and preparation recur with Moses on Sinai (Exod 24:18; 34:28), Israel's wilderness, and Elijah (1 Kgs 19:8); Luke evokes a charged interval of instruction before a covenantal threshold. Recurrence: Luke uses forty-day patterning elsewhere (Jesus' temptation, Luke 4:2). Marked figural because the correspondence is structural, not lexical.

pericopes.text: Therefore when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?” He said to them, “It isn’t for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set within his own authority. But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.”

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: 'You will be witnesses... to the uttermost parts of the earth' closely tracks the Servant's commission to be 'a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.' Volume: the phrase 'to the end(s) of the earth' is a distinctive LXX echo (heos eschatou tes ges). Recurrence: strong — Luke cites Isa 49:6 explicitly at Acts 13:47 and alludes again, making it a structural thesis statement for the book. Thematic coherence: very high; this verse programs Acts' whole geographic movement. A leading candidate in the history of interpretation for the key to Acts.

echoes.text: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me. I myself am Yahweh; and besides me there is no savior. I have declared, I have saved, and I have shown; and there was no strange god among you. Therefore you are my witnesses”, says Yahweh, “and I am God.
echoes.note: 'You will be witnesses to me' echoes the Lord's words to Israel, 'You are my witnesses... and my servant whom I have chosen.' Volume: the witness-language is distinctive and combined with election (the apostles 'whom he had chosen,' v.2). Recurrence: the witness motif saturates Acts. Thematic coherence: high; Israel's vocation to testify to the one God is transferred to the apostles. Overlaps with Isa 49:6 in the same Isaianic Servant matrix.

echoes.text: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding;
echoes.note: 'It isn't for you to know times or seasons (chronous e kairous) which the Father has set within his own authority' echoes Daniel's 'he changes times and seasons (kairous kai chronous)... he reveals deep and hidden things.' Volume: the paired words 'times and seasons' are a distinctive doublet shared with LXX Daniel. Thematic coherence: high; both texts locate the calendar of the kingdom in God's sovereign reserve. Recurrence: 'times and seasons' as a fixed pair recurs in Jewish apocalyptic. Solid mid-level link.

echoes.text: In that day I will raise up the tent of David who is fallen, and close up its breaches, and I will raise up its ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old; that they may possess the remnant of Edom, and all the nations who are called by my name,” says Yahweh who does this.
echoes.note: The apostles' question, 'are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?', sits atop the prophetic hope of the rebuilt 'booth of David' that the remnant and the nations might seek the Lord. Volume: no shared wording here. Recurrence: notable — Luke quotes Amos 9:11-12 at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:16-17) precisely to interpret how the restored Davidic kingdom includes the nations, which is exactly the tension between v.6 (Israel) and v.8 (the earth). Thematic coherence good; low confidence because the link is conceptual and back-referenced rather than verbal here.
echoes.lxxText: In that day I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and will rebuild the ruins of it, and will set up the parts thereof that have been broken down, and will build it up as in the ancient days: that the remnant of men, and all the Gentiles upon whom my name is called, may earnestly seek me, saith the Lord who does all these things.

pericopes.text: When he had said these things, as they were looking, he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight. While they were looking steadfastly into the sky as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white clothing, who also said, “You men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into the sky? This Jesus, who was received up from you into the sky will come back in the same way as you saw him going into the sky.”

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'A cloud received him out of their sight,' and the angels promise he 'will come back in the same way.' Volume: the cloud as the vehicle of the exalted Son of Man is the distinctive Danielic image (one 'coming with the clouds of heaven'). Luke reverses and reaffirms the trajectory — ascent now, return on clouds later. Recurrence: strong in Luke-Acts' Son-of-Man Christology (Luke 21:27; 22:69). Thematic coherence high; the cloud signals heavenly enthronement, the very kingship the disciples asked about in v.6.

echoes.text: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
echoes.note: Jesus 'was taken up' while the apostles 'looked steadfastly into the sky,' patterned on Elijah taken up to heaven as Elisha watched ('if you see me as I am taken from you...'). Volume: shared motif of a witnessed bodily assumption, the gaze of the successor(s), and the transfer of spirit/Spirit immediately afterward (Elisha's double portion ~ the apostles' Spirit-baptism). Recurrence: Luke deliberately uses Elijah-Elisha typology throughout (e.g., Luke 9:51, 9:61-62). Thematic coherence very high; the disciples' Spirit-empowerment in v.8 mirrors Elisha's inheritance. A staple of the history of interpretation.

echoes.text: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.
echoes.note: The ascension and promised return occur at/over the Mount of Olives (named in v.12), the very mountain on which 'the feet of the Lord' will stand on the eschatological day of his coming. Volume: low verbal overlap, but the geography is pointed and the angels' 'will come back in the same way' resonates with Zechariah's theophanic return to that mountain. Thematic coherence strong; recurrence modest. The setting makes this more than coincidental, hence echo/medium.

echoes.text: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.
echoes.note: Jesus' bodily removal to heaven faintly recalls Enoch, who 'walked with God, and he was not, for God took him' (LXX: 'God translated him'). Volume: low; only the shared motif of a righteous one taken without ordinary death. Recurrence: Enoch/assumption traditions were live in Second Temple Judaism. Coherence modest. Included as a faint, contested member of the 'assumption of the righteous' background alongside Elijah.

pericopes.text: Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. When they had come in, they went up into the upper room, where they were staying; that is Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas the son of James. All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer and supplication, along with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.

echoes.text: You shall measure outside of the city for the east side two thousand cubits, and for the south side two thousand cubits, and for the west side two thousand cubits, and for the north side two thousand cubits, the city being in the middle. This shall be the suburbs of their cities.
echoes.note: The distance from Olivet is 'a Sabbath day's journey,' a halakhic measure derived from the limits set around the Levitical cities and the camp (cf. the 2,000-cubit reckoning) and the Sabbath-rest command. Volume: the phrase reflects later legal interpretation rather than a quotation, but its scriptural root is the camp/city boundary measures. Thematic coherence modest. Faint, halakhic background note.

echoes.text: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.
echoes.note: The explicit naming of 'the mountain called Olivet' reinforces the eschatological resonance of the Mount of Olives as the place of the Lord's coming (Zech 14:4). Volume low (toponym only). Recurrence: Olivet frames both ascension and the Lukan passion. Coherence ties back to the return promised in v.11. Listed at low confidence as a topographic echo.

pericopes.text: In these days, Peter stood up in the midst of the disciples (and the number of names was about one hundred twenty), and said, “Brothers, it was necessary that this Scripture should be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke before by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who was guide to those who took Jesus. For he was numbered with us, and received his portion in this ministry. Now this man obtained a field with the reward for his wickedness, and falling headlong, his body burst open, and all his intestines gushed out. It became known to everyone who lived in Jerusalem that in their language that field was called ‘Akeldama,’ that is, ‘The field of blood.’ For it is written in the book of Psalms, ‘Let his habitation be made desolate. Let no one dwell therein;’ and, ‘Let another take his office.’

echoes.text: Let their habitation be desolate. Let no one dwell in their tents.
echoes.note: Explicitly introduced: 'it is written in the book of Psalms, Let his habitation be made desolate; let no one dwell therein.' Volume: a formal, formula-marked quotation with high verbal correspondence to LXX Ps 68:26 (genetheto he epaulis autou eremos). Recurrence: Psalm 69 is among the most-cited psalms in the NT and recurs in Luke's passion theology as a psalm of the righteous sufferer. Thematic coherence high; the betrayer's 'habitation' made desolate justifies vacating Judas' office. Textbook quotation.

echoes.text: Let his days be few. Let another take his office.
echoes.note: The second member of Peter's catena: 'Let another take his office (ten episkopen autou laboi heteros),' verbatim from LXX Ps 108:8. Volume: very high, a direct formula-marked citation. Thematic coherence: decisive — it supplies the warrant for electing a replacement apostle in vv.21-26. Recurrence: Psalm 109 is an imprecatory psalm against a treacherous adversary, read figurally of Judas. Unambiguous quotation.

echoes.text: “The Spirit of Yahweh spoke by me. His word was on my tongue.
echoes.note: Peter says 'the Holy Spirit spoke before by the mouth of David' the scripture about Judas. This inspiration formula echoes David's own claim, 'The Spirit of the Lord spoke by me, and his word was on my tongue.' Volume: shared the-Spirit-spoke-through-David formula. Thematic coherence high; it grounds the Davidic psalter as prophetic of Judas. Recurrence: Luke repeatedly attributes the Psalms to David's Spirit-inspired prophecy (e.g., Acts 2:30; 4:25).

echoes.text: I said to them, “If you think it best, give me my wages; and if not, keep them.” So they weighed for my wages thirty pieces of silver. Yahweh said to me, “Throw it to the potter, the handsome price that I was valued at by them!” I took the thirty pieces of silver, and threw them to the potter, in Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: Judas 'obtained a field with the reward for his wickedness,' and the place becomes 'the field of blood.' Volume: the field-bought-with-blood-money and the potter/field motif track Zechariah's thirty pieces of silver cast to the potter in the house of the Lord. Recurrence: Matthew makes the Zechariah link explicit; Luke's version is more allusive. Thematic coherence good — the betrayal price defiles a field. Mid-level because Luke's wording diverges from Zechariah's.

echoes.text: But the All-seeing Lord, the God of Israel, struck him with a fatal and invisible stroke; and as soon as he had ceased speaking this word, an incurable pain of the bowels seized him, and bitter torments of the inner parts; and that most justly, for he had tormented other men’s bowels with many and strange sufferings. But he in no wise ceased from his rude insolence; nay, still more was he filled with arrogancy, breathing fire in his passion against the […]
echoes.note: Judas 'falling headlong, his body burst open, and all his intestines gushed out' — a death-of-the-wicked topos closely matching the gruesome end of Antiochus IV, whose bowels were wracked and whose body rotted, a divine judgment on a persecutor. Volume: distinctive shared motif of the betrayer's body bursting/entrails as visible verdict. Thematic coherence high; deuterocanonical and permitted as a source. Recurrence: the 'horrible death of the persecutor' is a Hellenistic-Jewish topos (cf. Wisdom). Medium.

echoes.text: When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey, and arose, and went home, to his city, and set his house in order, and hanged himself; and he died, and was buried in the tomb of his father.
echoes.note: Judas as the counselor-turned-traitor of Jesus faintly recalls Ahithophel, David's trusted counselor who betrayed him and then died by his own hand. Volume: low (Luke reports a different mode of death than the Matthean hanging); the link is typological — the betrayer of the anointed king meets a self-inflicted, ignominious end. Recurrence: Ahithophel was widely read as a type of the traitor, and Psalm 69/109 imprecations were associated with such figures. Coherence good but verbal volume slight, hence echo/low.

pericopes.text: “Of the men therefore who have accompanied us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John, to the day that he was received up from us, of these one must become a witness with us of his resurrection.” They put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias. They prayed, and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all men, show which one of these two you have chosen to take part in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas fell away, that he might go to his own place.” They drew lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
echoes.note: The prayer addresses God as 'You, Lord, who know the hearts of all,' invoking the divine heart-knower who chooses leaders against human appearances — the very principle of Samuel's anointing of David ('the Lord looks on the heart'). Volume: the kardiognostes (heart-knower) idea is distinctive and Luke coins/repeats it (Acts 15:8). Thematic coherence high; God, not the lots alone, selects the apostle. Recurrence good.

echoes.text: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'They drew lots... and the lot fell on Matthias.' Volume: the procedure directly enacts the proverb, 'The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord' — the conceptual warrant for using lots to discern the divine choice. Thematic coherence very high; the casting of lots is framed (by the preceding prayer) as God's verdict, exactly Proverbs' theology of the lot. Recurrence: lot-casting for sacred appointment recurs across the OT (Lev 16:8; Josh 18:10; 1 Chr 24-26). Strong link.

echoes.text: Moses spoke to Yahweh, saying, “Let Yahweh, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.” Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Set him before Eleazar the priest, and before […]
echoes.note: After the leader's departure to heaven (Moses/Jesus), a successor is formally installed so the community is not 'as sheep without a shepherd' — Moses asks the Lord, 'who knows the spirits of all flesh,' to appoint a man, and Joshua is set in office. Volume: low verbal overlap, but note the striking parallel to v.24's heart/spirit-knower address. This is primarily a figural/structural correspondence: a divinely designated succession to preserve the leadership of the twelve. Thematic coherence high; the number-twelve restoration of Israel is at stake. Marked figural.

echoes.text: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: The qualification that the candidate 'accompanied us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us' echoes the idiom for leadership over Israel, 'who shall go out before them and come in before them' (of Joshua's commissioning). Volume: the 'go in and out' idiom is distinctive Septuagintal leadership language. Coherence reinforces the succession theme of the pericope. Low because the phrase is a common idiom (cf. Deut 31:2; 1 Sam 18:13).

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: The summary of Judas as one who 'received his portion in this ministry' yet 'fell away' (v.17, 25) faintly recalls the table-companion who betrays — 'my own familiar friend... who ate of my bread, has lifted up his heel against me.' Volume: low here (Luke does not quote it), but the betrayer-among-the-intimates frame coheres. Recurrence: this psalm is cited of Judas elsewhere in the gospel tradition. Faint, contested.

pericopes.text: Now when the day of Pentecost had come, they were all with one accord in one place. Suddenly there came from the sky a sound like the rushing of a mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak.

echoes.text: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled. Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the lower part of the mountain. Mount Sinai, all it, smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked […]
echoes.note: The Sinai theophany supplies the dominant template: a sound from heaven, fire descending on the assembly, and the whole 'house' shaken/filled echo the thunder, fire, and trembling mountain when YHWH descended in fire and the trumpet-sound grew loud (Exod 19:16-19). Volume is carried structurally (sound + fire + divine descent on the gathered people) more than by shared vocabulary. Recurrence is strong: Luke repeatedly frames the Spirit's coming as a new covenantal endowment. Thematic coherence is very high, since Pentecost (Weeks) was associated in Second Temple/rabbinic tradition with the Sinai law-giving, making Acts 2 a Spirit-Sinai counterpart. History of interpretation overwhelmingly reads Pentecost as a Sinai antitype.

echoes.text: The whole earth was of one language and of one speech. As they traveled east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they lived there. They said one to another, “Come, let’s make bricks, and burn them thoroughly.” They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar. They said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make ourselves a name, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole […]
echoes.note: Babel reversal: at Babel one language is confused and humanity scattered; at Pentecost the Spirit enables many tongues that gather scattered nations into mutual comprehension. Verbal volume is low/absent, but the structural correspondence (languages, scattering vs. ingathering) is a classic typological inversion. Thematic coherence is high given the immediately following nations-list (vv.9-11). Recurrence: Luke's universalizing program (gospel to all nations) reinforces the figure. Widely noted in history of interpretation as the undoing of Babel; the satisfaction of reading it this way is considerable.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: The outpouring of the Spirit enacted here is precisely what Peter will name as Joel's prophecy in vv.16-21; the narrative event (all filled with the Spirit, all speaking/prophesying) is the fulfillment Joel foretold of the Spirit poured 'on all flesh.' High thematic coherence and explicit recurrence within the same chapter. Volume in vv.1-4 is event-level rather than verbal, but the link is interpretively certain because Luke makes it explicit a few verses later.

echoes.text: Moses went out, and told the people Yahweh’s words; and he gathered seventy men of the elders of the people, and set them around the Tent. Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more. But two men remained in the camp. The name of one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the Spirit rested on […]
echoes.note: When the Spirit rests on the seventy elders they prophesy, and Moses wishes 'that all the LORD's people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them.' Acts 2 reads as the realization of that wish: the Spirit democratized onto the whole community, who immediately prophesy/speak. Moderate volume (shared motif of Spirit-induced prophecy distributed across many), strong thematic coherence, recurrence via Joel which itself develops the Numbers ideal.

echoes.text: He said, “Go out, and stand on the mountain before Yahweh.” Behold, Yahweh passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains, and broke in pieces the rocks before Yahweh; but Yahweh was not in the wind. After the wind an earthquake; but Yahweh was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake a fire passed; but Yahweh was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.
echoes.note: Elijah's Horeb theophany pairs wind and fire as accompaniments of divine presence, a constellation reused here (wind-like sound, fire-like tongues). Faint, carried by shared theophanic imagery rather than wording; contested because the Sinai/Exodus material is the more direct source and the elements function differently (there God is not in the wind/fire).

echoes.text: Then he said to me, Prophesy to the wind, prophesy, son of man, and tell the wind, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Come from the four winds, breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live. So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army. Then he said to me, Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel: behold, they say, Our bones are dried up, and our hope […]
echoes.note: The life-giving rûaḥ/breath/wind that comes and animates the people resonates with the wind-like sound that fills the house and empowers the disciples. Low verbal volume in the Greek, but the Spirit-as-wind giving new life is thematically coherent with the inauguration of the renewed community; contested as a deliberate echo.

pericopes.text: Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under the sky. When this sound was heard, the multitude came together, and were bewildered, because everyone heard them speaking in his own language. They were all amazed and marveled, saying to one another, “Behold, aren’t all these who speak Galileans? How do we hear, everyone in our own native language? Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and people from Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, the parts of Libya around Cyrene, visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians: we hear them speaking in our languages the mighty works of God!” They were all amazed, and were perplexed, saying one to another, “What does this mean?” Others, mocking, said, “They are filled with new wine.”

echoes.text: Now this is the history of the generations of the sons of Noah and of Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood. The sons of Japheth were: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The sons of Gomer were: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The sons of Javan were: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. Of these were the islands of the nations divided in their lands, everyone after his language, after their families, in […]
echoes.note: The roll-call of peoples 'from every nation under heaven' (Parthians, Medes, Elamites, etc., vv.9-11) functions as a New Testament Table of Nations, recalling the Genesis 10 enumeration of the descendants of Noah scattered across the earth. The motif of representative nations gathered echoes the primeval mapping of humanity; thematic coherence high, verbal overlap modest (proper-name catalogue form). Pairs with the Babel figure of vv.1-4.

echoes.text: This day will I begin to put the dread of you and the fear of you on the peoples who are under the whole sky, who shall hear the report of you, and shall tremble, and be in anguish because of you.”
echoes.note: The phrase 'peoples under the whole heaven' supplies the universalizing idiom behind 'every nation under heaven' (v.5). Faint, formulaic; contested as a specific source since the expression is common LXX phrasing.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day that the Lord will set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant that is left of his people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
echoes.note: Isaiah's eschatological ingathering of the dispersed of Israel/Judah from Egypt, Cush, Elam, Shinar, and the coastlands anticipates the gathering of diaspora Jews 'from every nation' to Jerusalem. The geographic spread of the returnees parallels the list of nations here. Low volume, plausible thematic coherence with a restoration-of-the-dispersed reading; contested.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: The crowd's marveling that each hears the disciples 'speaking in our own tongues the mighty works of God' realizes Joel's promised universal prophesying poured out on all flesh; the mockery of drunkenness (v.13) sets up Peter's Joel citation directly. Recurrence within the chapter is explicit; thematic coherence high.

pericopes.text: But Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice, and spoke out to them, “You men of Judea, and all you who dwell at Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen to my words. For these aren’t drunken, as you suppose, seeing it is only the third hour of the day. But this is what has been spoken through the prophet Joel: ‘It will be in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your young men will see visions. Your old men will dream dreams. Yes, and on my servants and on my handmaidens in those days, I will pour out my Spirit, and they will prophesy. I will show wonders in the sky above, and signs on the earth beneath; blood, and fire, and billows of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes. It will be, that whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.’

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit. I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day […]
echoes.note: Formal, formula-marked citation ('this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel,' v.16) reproducing Joel 2:28-32 (LXX 3:1-5) at high verbal volume: pouring out the Spirit on all flesh, sons/daughters prophesying, young men visions, old men dreams, servants and handmaids, wonders in heaven and signs on earth, blood/fire/smoke, sun to darkness and moon to blood before the great day of the Lord, and whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved. Luke's 'in the last days' adapts Joel's 'afterward.' The anchor quotation of the chapter; maximal on all three auditable tests.

echoes.text: Mount Sinai, all it, smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked greatly.
echoes.note: The 'smoke' (kapnos) among the apocalyptic signs (v.19) may resonate with the smoke of Sinai where 'the mountain was wholly in smoke' at the theophany, reinforcing the Sinai-Pentecost frame. Low volume and the wording is governed by Joel; contested.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: 'Before the great and notable day of the Lord' overlaps the Malachi expectation of the great and dreadful day of the LORD; the phrase is shared eschatological idiom that Joel and Malachi both carry. Faint and mediated through Joel; contested as an independent source.

pericopes.text: “Men of Israel, hear these words! Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God to you by mighty works and wonders and signs which God did by him in your midst, even as you yourselves know, him, being delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you have taken by the hand of lawless men, crucified and killed; whom God raised up, having freed him from the agony of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it. For David says concerning him, ‘I saw the Lord always before my face, For he is on my right hand, that I should not be moved. Therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced. Moreover my flesh also will dwell in hope; because you will not leave my soul in Hades, neither will you allow your Holy One to see decay. You made known to me the ways of life. You will make me full of gladness with your presence.’

echoes.text: I have set Yahweh always before me. Because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved. Therefore my heart is glad, and my tongue rejoices. My body shall also dwell in safety. For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption. You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more.
echoes.note: Formal citation introduced by 'David says concerning him' (v.25), reproducing Psalm 16:8-11 (LXX 15:8-11) at very high verbal volume: 'I saw the Lord always before me... at my right hand... my heart was glad, my tongue rejoiced, my flesh will dwell in hope, you will not abandon my soul to Hades nor let your Holy One see corruption; you made known to me the ways of life.' The corruption/incorruption clause is the load-bearing proof, expounded in vv.29-31. Maximal on all tests; recurrence reinforced by the same psalm in Acts 13.

echoes.text: The cords of death surrounded me. The floods of ungodliness made me afraid. The cords of Sheol were around me. The snares of death came on me. In my distress I called on Yahweh, and cried to my God. He heard my voice out of his temple. My cry before him came into his ears.
echoes.note: 'Freed him from the agony/pangs of death' (v.24) uses ōdines thanatou, the LXX rendering of the 'cords/pangs of death' surrounding the psalmist (Ps 18:4-5; 2 Sam 22:5-6), where God delivers from Sheol. Low-to-moderate verbal volume on the death-pangs phrase; thematic coherence with deliverance from death is strong, but the wording is a stock LXX idiom (also Ps 116:3), so contested.

pericopes.text: “Brothers, I may tell you freely of the patriarch David, that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Therefore, being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that of the fruit of his body, according to the flesh, he would raise up the Christ to sit on his throne, he foreseeing this spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that neither was his soul left in Hades, nor did his flesh see decay. This Jesus God raised up, to which we all are witnesses. Being therefore exalted by the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this, which you now see and hear. For David didn’t ascend into the heavens, but he says himself, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit by my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’ “Let all the house of Israel therefore know certainly that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.”

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: Formal citation introduced by 'he says himself' (v.34), reproducing Psalm 110:1 (LXX 109:1) at high verbal volume: 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.' Used to prove the exaltation/enthronement that David did not himself attain. Maximal on volume; recurrence is very high (most-cited OT verse in the NT) and thematic coherence with the resurrection-exaltation argument is exact.

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn to David in truth. He will not turn from it: “I will set the fruit of your body on your throne.
echoes.note: 'God had sworn with an oath to him that of the fruit of his body (loins)... he would set one on his throne' (v.30) is a near-verbatim echo of Psalm 132:11 LXX (God's sworn oath to David, 'of the fruit of your body I will set upon your throne'). High verbal volume in the oath-and-throne clause; thematic coherence with the Davidic-messianic argument is exact. Functions as an embedded citation alongside the Nathan oracle.

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
echoes.note: The Davidic covenant promise that God would raise up David's offspring and establish his kingdom/throne forever underlies 'God had sworn... that he would raise up the Christ to sit on his throne' (v.30). Strong thematic coherence and recurrence (the Nathan oracle is foundational to NT messianism); volume mediated through Ps 132. Paired with Ps 132:11 as the basis of David's prophetic foresight.

echoes.text: David slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David.
echoes.note: 'David both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day' (v.29) draws on the notice that David 'slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David' (1 Kgs 2:10), the historical premise of the argument that Psalm 16 cannot ultimately refer to David. Moderate verbal volume (death-and-burial formula), high thematic coherence as the hinge of Peter's exegesis.

echoes.text: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.
echoes.note: Peter re-cites the climactic line of Psalm 16 in vv.31 ('neither was his soul left in Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption') as the resolved exposition of the quotation given in vv.25-28. Direct re-quotation at high volume; recurrence within the pericope is the structural point of the argument.

pericopes.text: Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” Peter said to them, “Repent, and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is to you, and to your children, and to all who are far off, even as many as the Lord our God will call to himself.” With many other words he testified, and exhorted them, saying, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation!” Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls.

echoes.text: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.
echoes.note: 'The promise is to you and to your children and to all who are far off, as many as the Lord our God will call to himself' (v.39) picks up Joel's closing clause ('whoever calls on the name of the Lord... among the survivors whom the Lord calls'), already quoted in v.21. The 'as many as the Lord shall call' is a deliberate verbal echo of Joel's remnant 'whom the Lord calls.' Moderate volume, strong recurrence (re-using the just-cited oracle), high coherence.

echoes.text: I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him who is far off and to him who is near,” says Yahweh; “and I will heal them.”
echoes.note: 'To all who are far off' (tois eis makran, v.39) echoes Isaiah's 'Peace, peace, to the far and to the near' (Isa 57:19 LXX, 'those far off and those near'), an OT idiom for the inclusion of the distant/diaspora and, ultimately, the nations. Moderate verbal volume on the 'far off' phrase; thematic coherence with Acts' universal mission is high. Reused in NT reconciliation language elsewhere, supporting recurrence.

echoes.text: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.
echoes.note: 'Save yourselves from this crooked generation' (v.40) draws on the Song of Moses' indictment of Israel as 'a perverse and crooked generation' (Deut 32:5, skolias), the standard LXX phrase for covenant-faithless Israel. Moderate verbal volume (genea skolia), strong thematic coherence as a call to separate from the faithless generation.

echoes.text: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn.
echoes.note: Being 'cut to the heart' (katenygēsan, v.37) on recognizing the one they crucified resonates with Zechariah's promise that they will 'look on him whom they pierced' and mourn. Low verbal volume (different roots), but thematic coherence (contrition over the slain/pierced one) is suggestive; contested.
echoes.lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son.

pericopes.text: They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer. Fear came on every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles. All who believed were together, and had all things in common. They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need. Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God, and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.

echoes.text: However there shall be no poor with you (for Yahweh will surely bless you in the land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance to possess it) if only you diligently listen to Yahweh your God’s voice, to observe to do all this commandment which I command you this day.
echoes.note: The community 'had all things in common... and distributed to all, as any had need' (vv.44-45) realizes the Deuteronomic ideal that 'there shall be no poor among you' if Israel obeys, with goods shared so none lacks. Moderate volume via the 'need/no poor' motif; thematic coherence high, and Luke develops it again in Acts 4:34 ('there was not a needy person'), echoing Deut 15 directly, which supplies recurrence.

echoes.text: “‘You shall count from the next day after the Sabbath, from the day that you brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven Sabbaths shall be completed: even to the next day after the seventh Sabbath you shall number fifty days; and you shall offer a new meal offering to Yahweh. You shall bring out of your habitations two loaves of bread for a wave offering made of two tenth parts of an ephah of fine flour. They shall be baked with yeast, for first fruits […]
echoes.note: The whole chapter unfolds on the Feast of Weeks/Pentecost (Lev 23:15-21, fifty days from Passover, with firstfruits offered), and the harvest of 'about three thousand souls' added (v.41) reads as the firstfruits of the eschatological harvest gathered on that very feast. Low verbal volume; calendrical and firstfruits-harvest coherence is the basis; contested as deliberate allusion.

echoes.text: Then those who feared Yahweh spoke one with another; and Yahweh listened, and heard, and a book of memory was written before him, for those who feared Yahweh, and who honored his name.
echoes.note: The devout, fearing community joined in fellowship and praise, growing daily, faintly recalls the remnant who 'feared the LORD and spoke with one another,' written in the book of remembrance. Very faint, thematic-coherence-only; contested.

pericopes.text: Peter and John were going up into the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. A certain man who was lame from his mother’s womb was being carried, whom they laid daily at the door of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask gifts for the needy of those who entered into the temple. Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive gifts for the needy. Peter, fastening his eyes on him, with John, said, “Look at us.” He listened to them, expecting to receive something from them. But Peter said, “Silver and gold have I none, but what I have, that I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!” He took him by the right hand, and raised him up. Immediately his feet and his ankle bones received strength. Leaping up, he stood, and began to walk. He entered with them into the temple, walking, leaping, and praising God. All the people saw him walking and praising God. They recognized him, that it was he who used to sit begging for gifts for the needy at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. They were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.

echoes.text: Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: The healed man 'walking, leaping' (vv. 8-9) enacts Isaiah's eschatological promise 'then shall the lame man leap as a hart'; the verbal pairing of lameness and leaping is the signature image, and Luke uses the same scene to frame the apostolic age as the dawning restoration of Israel.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.
echoes.note: Same oracle of bodily restoration in the messianic age ('eyes of the blind opened'); the lame-man healing as a sign of the new era partakes of the wider Isa 35 catalogue even though only the lameness clause (v. 6) is verbally activated.

echoes.text: He raises up the poor out of the dust. Lifts up the needy from the ash heap;
echoes.note: 'He raiseth up the poor out of the dust' resonates faintly with the beggar at the gate being raised up; thematic coherence with God lifting the destitute, but no verbal borrowing.

pericopes.text: As the lame man who was healed held on to Peter and John, all the people ran together to them in the porch that is called Solomon’s, greatly wondering. When Peter saw it, he responded to the people, “You men of Israel, why do you marvel at this man? Why do you fasten your eyes on us, as though by our own power or godliness we had made him walk? The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Servant Jesus, whom you delivered up, and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had determined to release him. But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and killed the Prince of life, whom God raised from the dead, to which we are witnesses. By faith in his name, his name has made this man strong, whom you see and know. Yes, the faith which is through him has given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all.

echoes.text: Moreover he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look at God.
echoes.note: 'The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers' (v. 13) reproduces the patriarchal covenant formula of the burning bush, anchoring the resurrection proclamation in the God who self-identifies to Moses.

echoes.text: God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.
echoes.note: The expanded title 'the God of our fathers' as the LORD's memorial name reinforces the Exodus 3 self-disclosure; v. 15 supplies the 'God of your fathers... my name for ever' phrasing behind Peter's formula.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: 'has glorified his Servant (pais) Jesus' (v. 13) echoes the LXX of the fourth Servant Song, 'my servant... shall be exalted and glorified'; the combination of pais + glorification is a deliberate Servant identification.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.
echoes.note: The 'Righteous One' (v. 14) whom they denied draws on the suffering Servant who is called 'the righteous one, my servant' who justifies many; coheres with the pais/Servant frame of v. 13.

echoes.text: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.
echoes.note: 'the Holy One' (v. 14) recalls the Davidic 'you will not let your Holy One see corruption,' cited fully in Acts 2:27; the title clusters here with the resurrection claim 'God raised from the dead' (v. 15).

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'whom you delivered up' (v. 13) faintly mirrors the Servant who 'was delivered up' (paredothe) for the transgressors; the handing-over language belongs to the same Servant matrix.

pericopes.text: “Now, brothers, I know that you did this in ignorance, as did also your rulers. But the things which God announced by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he thus fulfilled. “Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out, so that there may come times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send Christ Jesus, who was ordained for you before, whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things, which God spoke long ago by the mouth of his holy prophets.

echoes.text: “‘When you shall err, and not observe all these commandments, which Yahweh has spoken to Moses, even all that Yahweh has commanded you by Moses, from the day that Yahweh gave commandment, and onward throughout your generations; then it shall be, if it was done unwittingly, without the knowledge of the congregation, that all the congregation shall offer one young bull for a burnt offering, for a pleasant aroma to Yahweh, with its meal offering, and its […]
echoes.note: 'you did this in ignorance' (v. 17) invokes the Torah distinction between unwitting sin (atonable) and high-handed sin; Peter casts the crucifixion as forgivable ignorance, opening the call to repentance.

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘If anyone sins unintentionally, in any of the things which Yahweh has commanded not to be done, and does any one of them:
echoes.note: The priestly category of sinning 'through ignorance' underlies Peter's exoneration in v. 17; thematic, no verbal quotation.

echoes.text: I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins.
echoes.note: 'that your sins may be blotted out' (v. 19) echoes the LORD's promise 'I am he that blotteth out thy transgressions'; the blotting-out image of divine forgiveness is distinctive.

echoes.text: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions.
echoes.note: 'blot out my transgressions' supplies the same penitential idiom behind v. 19; coheres with the call to repent, though Isa 43 is the closer match.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”
echoes.note: 'times of restoration (apokatastasis) of all things' (v. 21) draws on the Elijah-tradition of restoring/turning hearts before the day of the LORD; LXX Mal 3:23-24 uses apokatastesei, the verbal root behind Peter's eschatological 'restoration'.

echoes.text: I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the great locust, the grasshopper, and the caterpillar, my great army, which I sent among you.
echoes.note: Joel's promise of God restoring the years coheres with the 'times of refreshing... restoration of all things' (vv. 19-21); thematic restoration motif, no verbal link.

pericopes.text: For Moses indeed said to the fathers, ‘The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him in all things whatever he says to you. It will be, that every soul that will not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed from among the people.’ Yes, and all the prophets from Samuel and those who followed after, as many as have spoken, they also told of these days. You are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘In your seed will all the families of the earth be blessed.’ God, having raised up his servant, Jesus, sent him to you first, to bless you, in turning away everyone of you from your wickedness.”

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him. This is according to all that you desired of Yahweh your God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, “Let me not hear again the voice of Yahweh my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I not die.” Yahweh said to me, “They have well said that which they have spoken. I will raise them up a prophet from among their […]
echoes.note: vv. 22-23 quote the promise of 'a prophet like me from among your brethren... you shall listen to him,' applied to Jesus as the eschatological prophet-like-Moses; the most explicit OT citation in the sermon.

echoes.text: For whoever it is who shall not deny himself in that same day; shall be cut off from his people.
echoes.note: The penalty clause 'every soul that will not listen... shall be utterly destroyed from among the people' (v. 23) is not in Deut 18 but fused from Lev 23:29 ('cut off from his people'); a conflated citation, classic of the Acts speeches.

echoes.text: All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your seed, because you have obeyed my voice.”
echoes.note: 'In your seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed' (v. 25) cites the Abrahamic promise after the Aqedah, grounding the gospel's reach to all nations in the patriarchal covenant.

echoes.text: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”
echoes.note: The base form of the blessing-to-the-families promise; Peter's 'all the families of the earth' matches Gen 12:3 ('families') more closely than the 'nations' of Gen 22:18, so both stand behind the citation.

echoes.text: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you.
echoes.note: 'the covenant which God made with our fathers' (v. 25) recalls the everlasting covenant established with Abraham and his seed; supplies the covenantal frame for the quoted blessing.

echoes.text: “A Redeemer will come to Zion, and to those who turn from disobedience in Jacob,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'turning away every one of you from your wickedness' (v. 26) faintly echoes 'the Redeemer shall come... unto them that turn from transgression in Jacob'; thematic turning-from-sin, no firm verbal tie.

echoes.text: All Israel from Dan even to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established to be a prophet of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'all the prophets from Samuel' (v. 24) presupposes Samuel's establishment as the LORD's prophet to all Israel; an allusive nod to the prophetic line's inauguration rather than a quotation.

pericopes.text: As they spoke to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came to them, being upset because they taught the people and proclaimed in Jesus the resurrection from the dead. They laid hands on them, and put them in custody until the next day, for it was now evening. But many of those who heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to be about five thousand.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The apostles 'proclaimed in Jesus the resurrection from the dead'; the conceptual rooting of bodily resurrection in Israel's Scripture points most clearly to Daniel 12:2, the OT's clearest resurrection text and the locus the Sadducees (named here as objecting) famously denied. No verbal borrowing — thematic only — but Luke's framing of the Sadducee dispute presupposes this scriptural background.

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: A secondary OT resurrection text ('your dead shall live') that, with Daniel 12:2, supplies the scriptural matrix for the apostolic resurrection preaching the Sadducees here oppose. Faint, no lexical overlap; included for maximal coverage.

pericopes.text: In the morning, their rulers, elders, and scribes were gathered together in Jerusalem. Annas the high priest was there, with Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and as many as were relatives of the high priest. When they had stood them in the middle of them, they inquired, “By what power, or in what name, have you done this?” Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “You rulers of the people, and elders of Israel, if we are examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed, be it known to you all, and to all the people of Israel, that in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, in him does this man stand here before you whole. He is ‘the stone which was regarded as worthless by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner.’ There is salvation in none other, for neither is there any other name under heaven, that is given among men, by which we must be saved!”

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
echoes.note: Verse 11 directly quotes Ps 118:22 (LXX 117:22), 'the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner,' applied to the crucified-and-raised Jesus and turned polemically on 'you, the builders' (the rulers). High Volume (near-verbatim citation), high Recurrence (the rejected-stone testimonium pervades early Christian usage), and strong Thematic Coherence (rejection-then-vindication mirrors crucifixion-resurrection).

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: The 'stone' Christology in v.11 draws on the broader OT stone complex; Isa 28:16's precious cornerstone laid in Zion frequently fuses with Ps 118:22 in early Christian testimonia. No direct citation here, but the cornerstone vocabulary and foundation-of-salvation logic (leading into v.12) cohere with Isaiah's tested stone.

echoes.text: You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces. Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken in pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that no place was found for them: and the stone that struck the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.
echoes.note: Daniel's stone, cut without hands, that shatters the kingdoms and fills the earth, belongs to the same messianic stone-testimonia cluster; the contrast between human builders' rejection and God's exaltation of the stone resonates faintly with Daniel's God-given stone overturning earthly powers. Contested, no verbal link.

echoes.text: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me. “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.
echoes.note: Verse 12, 'there is salvation in none other... no other name... by which we must be saved,' echoes Isaiah's exclusivist monotheism of salvation: 'there is no other God besides me, a righteous God and a Savior; there is none besides me... be saved, all the ends of the earth.' The 'none other / no other' salvation formula maps onto Isaiah's 'none besides me.'

echoes.text: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.
echoes.note: Verse 12's stress that salvation comes only through 'the name' echoes Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5), 'everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved' — the same name-and-salvation linkage Peter cited at Pentecost (Acts 2:21), now narrowed to the name of Jesus. Thematic coherence is strong; the recurrence in Acts strengthens the link.

echoes.text: I myself am Yahweh; and besides me there is no savior.
echoes.note: 'I, even I, am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior' reinforces the exclusive-salvation claim of v.12. A faint reinforcing echo within the same Isaianic monotheism-of-salvation field as Isa 45:21-22; included for maximal coverage.

pericopes.text: Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus. Seeing the man who was healed standing with them, they could say nothing against it. But when they had commanded them to go aside out of the council, they conferred among themselves, saying, “What shall we do to these men? Because indeed a notable miracle has been done through them, as can be plainly seen by all who dwell in Jerusalem, and we can’t deny it. But so that this spreads no further among the people, let’s threaten them, that from now on they don’t speak to anyone in this name.” They called them, and commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus. But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves, for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.” When they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people; for everyone glorified God for that which was done. For the man on whom this miracle of healing was performed was more than forty years old.

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
echoes.note: The rulers' inability to deny the 'notable miracle' yet their determination to suppress it (vv.16-18) continues the irony of the just-quoted rejected stone (v.11): the builders go on rejecting despite the manifest vindication standing before them in the healed man. A narrative echo of the immediately preceding citation rather than a fresh source.

echoes.text: and lest you lift up your eyes to the sky, and when you see the sun and the moon and the stars, even all the army of the sky, you are drawn away and worship them, and serve them, which Yahweh your God has allotted to all the peoples under the whole sky.
echoes.note: Peter's principle in v.19, that obeying God rather than men must be judged 'in the sight of God,' resonates faintly with the Deuteronomic insistence on listening to God alone; the obey-God-not-men theme is biblical but here lacks any verbal anchor. Marked low and contested.

pericopes.text: Being let go, they came to their own company, and reported all that the chief priests and the elders had said to them. When they heard it, they lifted up their voice to God with one accord, and said, “O Lord, you are God, who made the heaven, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who by the mouth of your servant, David, said, ‘Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing? The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take council together, against the Lord, and against his Christ.’ “For truly, in this city against your holy servant, Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, were gathered together to do whatever your hand and your council foreordained to happen. Now, Lord, look at their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal; and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Servant Jesus.” When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness.

echoes.text: for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed the Sabbath day, and made it holy.
echoes.note: The prayer's address in v.24, 'you who made the heaven, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them,' is the fourfold creation formula of Exod 20:11 (the Sabbath commandment) almost verbatim in the LXX. High Volume on the formula; strong coherence as the appeal to the Creator-Sovereign grounds the appeal against earthly rulers that follows.

echoes.text: who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who keeps truth forever;
echoes.note: Psalm 146:6 (LXX 145:6), 'who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them,' is verbally as close as Exod 20:11 to v.24 and is a doxological-prayer use of the formula, making it an especially apt parallel for this corporate prayer. Strong Volume and coherence; offered alongside Exod 20:11.

echoes.text: You are Yahweh, even you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their army, the earth and all things that are on it, the seas and all that is in them, and you preserve them all. The army of heaven worships you.
echoes.note: Nehemiah's communal prayer, 'you have made heaven... the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them,' is another instance of the creation formula embedded in corporate prayer addressed to 'you, even you, are LORD alone' — closely matching this assembly's prayer opening 'O Lord, you are God.' Strong thematic fit; verbal overlap shared with the wider formula.

echoes.text: Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing? The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,
echoes.note: Verses 25-26 quote Psalm 2:1-2 verbatim (LXX), 'Why did the nations rage... the kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ,' explicitly attributed to David and then applied in vv.27-28 to Herod, Pilate, Gentiles and Israel arrayed against the anointed Jesus. Maximal Volume, high Recurrence (Ps 2 is a core messianic testimonium), high coherence.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: Verse 27's designation of Jesus as the one 'whom you anointed' presses the same Psalm 2 just cited, where the LORD's 'Christ/anointed' (v.2) is the begotten Son (v.7). The anointing language extends the Psalm 2 citation into the prayer's interpretation. Recurrence within the immediate context strengthens it.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
echoes.note: 'Your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed' (v.27) may also evoke Isa 61:1, 'the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me,' the Servant's Spirit-anointing for proclamation — coherent with the anointed-Servant motif but without verbal borrowing here. Low and contested.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: The repeated title 'your holy servant (pais) Jesus' (vv.27, 30) draws on the Isaianic Servant (Isa 52:13, 'behold, my servant'), the LXX pais being the term Acts applies to Jesus. Conceptual servant-Christology rather than citation; low confidence, contested.

echoes.text: “Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, who is enthroned among the cherubim, you are the God, even you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth. You have made heaven and earth.
echoes.note: Hezekiah's prayer ('O LORD... you are God... you have made heaven and earth,' Isa 37:16 / 2 Kgs 19:15) is a near-structural model for this prayer: address God as sole Creator, then lay enemies' threats before him and ask for deliverance and a vindicating sign (cf. v.29, 'look at their threats'). A formal/typological echo of the threatened-people's prayer-to-the-Creator pattern.

echoes.text: declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times things that are not yet done; saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure;
echoes.note: Verse 28, the rulers did only 'whatever your hand and your council foreordained to happen,' echoes Isaiah's God whose 'counsel shall stand' and who declares the end from the beginning (Isa 46:10). The pairing of God's sovereign 'counsel/will' overruling hostile human action coheres tightly with the prayer's theology.

echoes.text: I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.
echoes.note: The plea in v.30 that 'signs and wonders' be done evokes the fixed Exodus pairing of 'signs and wonders' worked by God's outstretched hand against Pharaoh (Exod 7:3 and throughout). Combined with 'stretch out your hand,' the language casts the apostolic mission in a new-Exodus, divine-deliverance key.

echoes.text: and Yahweh showed great and awesome signs and wonders on Egypt, on Pharaoh, and on all his house, before our eyes;
echoes.note: 'Signs and wonders' (v.30) is the recurrent Deuteronomic shorthand for the LORD's Exodus deliverance (Deut 6:22; cf. 26:8, 34:11). A reinforcing echo of the same Exodus-deliverance vocabulary; low and contested alongside Exod 7:3.

echoes.text: Mount Sinai, all it, smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked greatly.
echoes.note: Verse 31, 'the place was shaken where they were gathered,' echoes the Sinai theophany where the whole mountain trembled greatly at God's descent (Exod 19:18). The shaking as a sign of God's answering presence and the Spirit-filling that follows cohere with theophanic precedent.

echoes.text: The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke.
echoes.note: The shaking of 'the place' (the praying assembly) after the prayer also recalls Isa 6:4, where the thresholds/foundations of the temple shook at the divine voice amid the seraphic praise. A theophanic shaking echo; low and contested.

echoes.text: Tremble, you earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob,
echoes.note: Ps 114:7's call for the earth to 'tremble at the presence of the Lord' supplies the wider biblical motif of creation quaking before God; the shaken place in v.31 participates in this theophany-tremor field. Faint, no verbal link.

pericopes.text: The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul. Not one of them claimed that anything of the things which he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common. With great power, the apostles gave their testimony of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. Great grace was on them all. For neither was there among them any who lacked, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them, and brought the proceeds of the things that were sold, and laid them at the apostles’ feet, and distribution was made to each, according as anyone had need. Joses, who by the apostles was also called Barnabas (which is, being interpreted, Son of Encouragement), a Levite, a man of Cyprus by race, having a field, sold it, and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

echoes.text: However there shall be no poor with you (for Yahweh will surely bless you in the land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance to possess it)
echoes.note: Verse 34, 'neither was there among them any who lacked,' closely echoes Deut 15:4 LXX, 'there shall be no poor/needy among you,' the Deuteronomic ideal of the covenant community in which God's blessing eliminates poverty. Luke presents the Jerusalem community's common purse as the fulfillment of this Torah promise — strong thematic coherence and notable verbal overlap on 'no one lacked / no poor.'

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The believers being 'of one heart and soul' (v.32) faintly recalls the Shema's 'with all your heart and with all your soul' (Deut 6:5); here the heart-and-soul language describes communal unity rather than love of God. A lexical resonance only, low and contested.

echoes.text: and I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever, for their good, and of their children after them:
echoes.note: 'One heart and one soul' (v.32) may echo the new-covenant promise of Jer 32:39 (LXX 39:39), 'I will give them one heart and one way,' where God grants the restored people a unified heart. The Spirit-given unity of the believers coheres with this restoration promise. Low, contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Aaron, “You shall have no inheritance in their land, neither shall you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the children of Israel.
echoes.note: The closing note that Barnabas, 'a Levite' (v.36), sold his field and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet plays ironically against Num 18:20, where Levites were to have no landed inheritance because the LORD was their portion. Barnabas's divestment of a field embodies that Levitical landlessness in the new community. Typological/ironic, no verbal borrowing.

pericopes.text: But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira, his wife, sold a possession, and kept back part of the price, his wife also being aware of it, and brought a certain part, and laid it at the apostles’ feet. But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit, and to keep back part of the price of the land? While you kept it, didn’t it remain your own? After it was sold, wasn’t it in your power? How is it that you have conceived this thing in your heart? You haven’t lied to men, but to God.” Ananias, hearing these words, fell down and died. Great fear came on all who heard these things. The young men arose and wrapped him up, and they carried him out and buried him. About three hours later, his wife, not knowing what had happened, came in. Peter answered her, “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.” She said, “Yes, for so much.” But Peter asked her, “How is it that you have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.” She fell down immediately at his feet, and died. The young men came in and found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her by her husband. Great fear came on the whole assembly, and on all who heard these things.
