echoes.text: But the children of Israel committed a trespass in the devoted things; for Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. Therefore Yahweh’s anger burned against the children of Israel.
echoes.note: The Achan narrative is the controlling template. The verb 'kept back part' (nosphizomai, vv. 2-3) is the same rare term LXX Joshua 7:1 uses for Achan's appropriation of devoted spoil. As Israel's first sin after entering the land brings death into the new covenant community amid divine judgment, so Ananias' withholding brings death into the first days of the Spirit-filled church. Volume, thematic coherence, and recurrence (the lexical link) all converge; the typology is widely recognized.

echoes.text: When I saw among the plunder a beautiful Babylonian robe, two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold weighing fifty shekels, then I coveted them and took them. Behold, they are hidden in the ground in the middle of my tent, with the silver under it.”
echoes.note: Achan confesses he 'coveted' and 'hid' the silver and a portion of the spoil — the precise act of secret retention that Ananias and Sapphira repeat with the price of the land. The shared motif of concealed appropriation of what was set apart strengthens the figural reading.

echoes.text: Joshua said, “Why have you troubled us? Yahweh will trouble you this day.” All Israel stoned him with stones, and they burned them with fire and stoned them with stones.
echoes.note: Achan and his household are destroyed; the whole assembly witnesses the judgment. The death of a couple acting in concert and the spread of 'great fear' over the assembly (vv. 5, 11) mirror the corporate purgation of sin in the camp.

echoes.text: But Gehazi the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, “Behold, my master has spared this Naaman the Syrian, in not receiving at his hands that which he brought. As Yahweh lives, I will run after him, and take something from him.” So Gehazi followed after Naaman. When Naaman saw one running after him, he came down from the chariot to meet him, and said, “Is all well?” He said, “All is well. My master has sent me, saying, ‘Behold, even now two young men of […]
echoes.note: Gehazi secretly takes money Elisha had refused, lies about it, and is struck with judgment. The pattern — covetous secret acquisition of money in the holy sphere, a prophet who discerns the hidden deceit, and a curse falling immediately — closely parallels Peter's exposure of Ananias and Sapphira.

echoes.text: Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer, and put fire in it, and laid incense on it, and offered strange fire before Yahweh, which he had not commanded them. Fire came out from before Yahweh, and devoured them, and they died before Yahweh.
echoes.note: Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire at the inauguration of priestly worship and are struck dead on the spot, with the surrounding community charged to revere God's holiness. The sudden lethal judgment at the foundational moment of a new cultic order, producing awe, is typologically akin.

echoes.text: As he made an end of speaking all these words, the ground that was under them split apart. The earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households, all of Korah’s men, and all their goods. So they, and all that belonged to them went down alive into Sheol. The earth closed on them, and they perished from among the assembly.
echoes.note: Korah, Dathan, and Abiram are swallowed in sudden death for violating the divinely ordered community, instilling fear in all Israel. A faint analogue of immediate corporate-purgative judgment.

echoes.text: Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to number Israel.
echoes.note: 'Satan stood up against Israel and incited David' supplies the only clear OT instance of Satan inciting a sin within the covenant people; Peter's 'why has Satan filled your heart' (v. 3) draws on this conception of satanic instigation prompting an act against God.

echoes.text: when your fathers tempted me, tested me, and saw my work.
echoes.note: 'When your fathers tested me' frames Israel's wilderness rebellion as 'tempting' the LORD. Peter charges Sapphira with agreeing 'to tempt the Spirit of the Lord' (v. 9), language drawn from the wilderness testing tradition.

echoes.text: You shall not tempt Yahweh your God, as you tempted him in Massah.
echoes.note: 'You shall not test the LORD your God' is the legal locus of the prohibition Sapphira violates; reinforces the 'tempt the Spirit' motif.

echoes.text: Therefore the people quarreled with Moses, and said, “Give us water to drink.” Moses said to them, “Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test Yahweh?”
echoes.note: Massah, the paradigm of 'testing' the LORD at the waters; faint background to v. 9's 'tempt the Spirit of the Lord.'

echoes.text: Then he said to me, “This is the curse that goes out over the surface of the whole land; for everyone who steals shall be cut off according to it on the one side; and everyone who swears falsely shall be cut off according to it on the other side. I will cause it to go out,” says Yahweh of Armies, “and it will enter into the house of the thief, and into the house of him who swears falsely by my name; and it will remain in the midst of his house, and will […]
echoes.note: The flying scroll is a curse that 'enters the house' of the thief and the false swearer and consumes it; a faint thematic analogue to a deadly curse falling on a deceitful householding couple.

pericopes.text: By the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders were done among the people. They were all with one accord in Solomon’s porch. None of the rest dared to join them, however the people honored them. More believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women. They even carried out the sick into the streets, and laid them on cots and mattresses, so that as Peter came by, at the least his shadow might overshadow some of them. Multitudes also came together from the cities around Jerusalem, bringing sick people, and those who were tormented by unclean spirits: and they were all healed.

echoes.text: I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'Signs and wonders' (sēmeia kai terata, v. 12) is the fixed Septuagintal idiom for the LORD's mighty acts in Egypt. Its application to the apostles casts their ministry as a new exodus-scale display of divine power among the people.

echoes.text: and Yahweh showed great and awesome signs and wonders on Egypt, on Pharaoh, and on all his house, before our eyes;
echoes.note: 'The LORD showed signs and wonders, great and grievous, against Egypt' — a recurrent Deuteronomic formula behind Acts' summary that 'many signs and wonders were done among the people.'

echoes.text: He made the porch of pillars; its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth thirty cubits; and a porch before them; and pillars and a threshold before them.
echoes.note: Solomon's portico (stoa) gives the apostles' gathering place its name (v. 12); the Solomonic temple architecture grounds the new community in the continuity of Israel's sanctuary.

echoes.text: As they were burying a man, behold, they saw a band of raiders; and they threw the man into Elisha’s tomb. As soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.
echoes.note: Healing power transmitted through mere contact with Elisha's bones offers a precedent for healing mediated by Peter's passing shadow (v. 15) — power so abundant it operates at the margins of the prophet's person.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: The eschatological healing of all the afflicted — the sick made whole — stands behind the summary that the crowds 'were all healed' (v. 16) as a sign of the dawning age of restoration.

pericopes.text: But the high priest rose up, and all those who were with him (which is the sect of the Sadducees), and they were filled with jealousy, and laid hands on the apostles, and put them in public custody. But an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night, and brought them out, and said, “Go stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life.” When they heard this, they entered into the temple about daybreak, and taught. But the high priest came, and those who were with him, and called the council together, and all the senate of the children of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought. But the officers who came didn’t find them in the prison. They returned and reported, “We found the prison shut and locked, and the guards standing before the doors, but when we opened them, we found no one inside!” Now when the high priest, the captain of the temple, and the chief priests heard these words, they were very perplexed about them and what might become of this. One came and told them, “Behold, the men whom you put in prison are in the temple, standing and teaching the people.” Then the captain went with the officers, and brought them without violence, for they were afraid that the people might stone them.

echoes.text: “Stand in the gate of Yahweh’s house, and proclaim there this word, and say, ‘Hear Yahweh’s word, all you of Judah, who enter in at these gates to worship Yahweh.’”
echoes.note: 'Stand in the gate of the LORD's house and proclaim there this word' parallels the angel's commission, 'Go stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life' (v. 20). The prophetic charge to stand in the temple and declare the full message is the model.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh: Stand in the court of Yahweh’s house, and speak to all the cities of Judah, which come to worship in Yahweh’s house, all the words that I command you to speak to them; don’t diminish a word.
echoes.note: 'Stand in the court of the LORD's house and speak... all the words I command you; do not omit a word' — closely matches the angel's instruction to speak 'all the words of this life,' and the ensuing arrest-and-trial scene mirrors Jeremiah's temple trial.

echoes.text: who executes justice for the oppressed; who gives food to the hungry. Yahweh frees the prisoners.
echoes.note: 'The LORD sets the prisoners free' — the angelic jailbreak (vv. 19-23) enacts the psalm's portrait of God liberating the captive.

echoes.text: They struck the men who were at the door of the house with blindness, both small and great, so that they wearied themselves to find the door.
echoes.note: The angels at Sodom deliver and confound; the angel of the Lord opening sealed prison doors while guards remain unaware (vv. 19, 23) is a faint analogue of angelic deliverance amid baffled custodians.

pericopes.text: When they had brought them, they set them before the council. The high priest questioned them, saying, “Didn’t we strictly command you not to teach in this name? Behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and intend to bring this man’s blood on us.” But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed, hanging him on a tree. God exalted him with his right hand to be a Prince and a Savior, to give repentance to Israel, and remission of sins. We are His witnesses of these things; and so also is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.”

echoes.text: If a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree; his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall surely bury him the same day; for he who is hanged is accursed of God; that you don’t defile your land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance.
echoes.note: 'Hanging him on a tree' (v. 30) draws directly on the law that a man executed and hung 'on a tree' is under God's curse. Acts deliberately uses xylon ('tree/wood'), the LXX term, to characterize the crucifixion in the categories of this statute. High volume and clear verbal dependence.

echoes.text: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answered the king, Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter. If it happens, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace; and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods, nor worship the golden image which you have set up.
echoes.note: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse the king's command to disobey God, declaring they will serve God whatever the cost — the paradigm for 'We must obey God rather than men' (v. 29).

echoes.text: When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.
echoes.note: Daniel defies the royal decree to continue worshiping God, modeling principled obedience to God over human authority, the stance Peter articulates in v. 29.

echoes.text: God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.
echoes.note: 'The God of our fathers' (v. 30) is the self-designation revealed to Moses at the bush, anchoring the apostolic proclamation in the covenant identity of Israel's God.

echoes.text: The right hand of Yahweh is exalted! The right hand of Yahweh does valiantly!”
echoes.note: 'The right hand of the LORD is exalted' lies behind 'God exalted him with his right hand' (v. 31); Psalm 118 is a primary early-church resource for the vindication of the rejected one.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: The enthronement 'at the right hand' of God underwrites the exaltation of Jesus 'with his right hand' as Prince and Savior (v. 31), the dominant NT proof-text for the session.

echoes.text: Afterward Joshua struck them, put them to death, and hanged them on five trees. They were hanging on the trees until the evening.
echoes.note: The execution of enemy kings by hanging on trees illustrates the legal practice behind Deut 21 invoked in v. 30; a secondary witness to 'hanging on a tree.'

echoes.text: let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; and let him return to Yahweh, and he will have mercy on him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.
echoes.note: The call to return for abundant pardon stands faintly behind 'to give repentance to Israel and remission of sins' (v. 31).

pericopes.text: But they, when they heard this, were cut to the heart, and determined to kill them. But one stood up in the council, a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law, honored by all the people, and commanded to put the apostles out for a little while. He said to them, “You men of Israel, be careful concerning these men, what you are about to do. For before these days Theudas rose up, making himself out to be somebody; to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves: who was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were dispersed, and came to nothing. After this man, Judas of Galilee rose up in the days of the enrollment, and drew away some people after him. He also perished, and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered abroad. Now I tell you, withdraw from these men, and leave them alone. For if this counsel or this work is of men, it will be overthrown. But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it, and you would be found even to be fighting against God!” They agreed with him. Summoning the apostles, they beat them and commanded them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. They therefore departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus’ name. Every day, in the temple and at home, they never stopped teaching and preaching Jesus, the Christ.

echoes.text: There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel against the LORD' is the maxim underlying Gamaliel's principle: if the work is of God it cannot be overthrown, and resisting it is fighting against God (vv. 38-39).

echoes.text: Take counsel together, and it will be brought to nothing; speak the word, and it will not stand: for God is with us.”
echoes.note: 'Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us' directly parallels Gamaliel's 'if this counsel is of men it will be overthrown, but if of God you cannot overthrow it' (vv. 38-39).

echoes.text: Yahweh brings the counsel of the nations to nothing. He makes the thoughts of the peoples to be of no effect. The counsel of Yahweh stands fast forever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations.
echoes.note: 'The LORD brings the counsel of the nations to nothing... the counsel of the LORD stands forever' is the theological axis of Gamaliel's test distinguishing human schemes (which collapse, like Theudas and Judas, vv. 36-37) from God's enduring purpose.

echoes.text: but think not you that you shall be unpunished, having assayed to fight against God.
echoes.note: Of the persecuting king it is warned that he will not escape, 'for he has undertaken to fight against God' (theomachein) — the deuterocanonical source for Gamaliel's climactic 'you would be found even to be fighting against God' (v. 39).

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: The Servant 'despised and rejected' faintly informs the apostles 'rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name' (v. 41), participating in the pattern of the suffering righteous.

echoes.text: and when he was at the point to die with the stripes, he groaned aloud and said, To the Lord, that has the holy knowledge, it is manifest that, whereas I might have been delivered from death, I endure sore pains in my body by being scourged; but in soul I gladly suffer these things for my fear of him.
echoes.note: Eleazar endures scourging with joy for the sake of obedience; a faint background to the apostles rejoicing after being beaten (vv. 40-41).

pericopes.text: Now in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplying, a complaint arose from the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily service. The twelve summoned the multitude of the disciples and said, “It is not appropriate for us to forsake the word of God and serve tables. Therefore select from among you, brothers, seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business. But we will continue steadfastly in prayer and in the ministry of the word.” These words pleased the whole multitude. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch; whom they set before the apostles. When they had prayed, they laid their hands on them. The word of God increased and the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem exceedingly. A great company of the priests were obedient to the faith.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over them; and bring them to the Tent of Meeting, that they may stand there with you. I will come down and talk with you there. I will take of the Spirit which is on you, and will put it on them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, that you not bear it yourself alone.
echoes.note: The apostles, overwhelmed by the burden of the word plus table-service, delegate to appointed assistants who are 'full of the Spirit' — closely paralleling Moses, who cannot bear the people alone and has the LORD distribute his spirit upon seventy elders appointed to share the load. The structural logic (leader unwilling/unable to do all, helpers commissioned, Spirit operative) is the same. Thematic coherence high; volume moderate (no direct citation).

echoes.text: Moreover you shall provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens. Let them judge the people at all times. It shall be that every great matter they shall bring to you, but every small matter they shall judge themselves. So shall it be easier for you, and they shall share the load with you.
echoes.note: Jethro's counsel: Moses is to 'select capable men' of integrity and set them over the people to relieve him of a burden too heavy to carry alone, so he can attend to the weightier matters. Acts 6 mirrors the delegation pattern — 'select from among you... men of good report' set 'over this business' so the Twelve keep to prayer and the word. Recurs with the Numbers 11 motif of shared leadership.

echoes.text: Take wise men of understanding and well known according to your tribes, and I will make them heads over you.”
echoes.note: Moses: 'Choose wise, understanding, and reputable men from your tribes, and I will appoint them as your heads.' The triad wise / known-reputable / appointed maps tightly onto Acts 6:3 ('men of good report, full of wisdom, whom we may appoint'). The LXX vocabulary of selecting reputable, wise men gives real verbal volume here.

echoes.text: Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands on him. The children of Israel listened to him, and did as Yahweh commanded Moses.
echoes.note: Joshua was 'full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him,' and so was commissioned to lead. Acts 6 fuses the same two elements — men 'full of the Spirit and of wisdom' who are commissioned when the apostles 'laid their hands on them.' Strong thematic coherence and good verbal volume (spirit + wisdom + laying on of hands as ordination).

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and commission him in their sight. You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before Yahweh. At his word they shall go out, and at his […]
echoes.note: Moses commissions Joshua, 'a man in whom is the Spirit,' by laying his hand(s) on him before the assembly and the priest. The setting-apart-by-imposition-of-hands of a Spirit-filled man for office is the same ritual gesture used in Acts 6:6, reinforcing the Moses/Joshua succession typology behind the appointment of the seven.

echoes.text: You shall present the Levites before Yahweh. The children of Israel shall lay their hands on the Levites,
echoes.note: The Levites are set apart for the service of the tabernacle when the people 'lay their hands' on them. Since the seven are appointed precisely to 'serve tables' (a ministry of practical service), the Levitical consecration-by-handlaying for service may stand faintly behind the scene, but the verbal contact is thin and the Joshua-commissioning texts are the nearer parallel.

echoes.text: and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship,
echoes.note: Bezalel is 'filled with the Spirit of God, with wisdom' for the work of the sanctuary — the same pairing of Spirit and wisdom for a hands-on ministry of service that qualifies the seven (6:3, 6:5). Faint, but it belongs to a recurring OT pattern of Spirit+wisdom equipping for divinely assigned work.

echoes.text: The children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and grew exceedingly mighty; and the land was filled with them.
echoes.note: Israel 'was fruitful... and multiplied and grew exceedingly mighty.' Acts 6:7's growth refrain ('the word of God increased and the number of the disciples multiplied... exceedingly') deliberately reuses Septuagintal multiplication language, casting the church's expansion as a new Exodus-style flourishing of God's people. Recurrence is strong: this refrain runs through Acts.

echoes.text: God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
echoes.note: The creation mandate to 'be fruitful and multiply' is the headwater of the OT multiplication idiom that Acts 6:7 redeploys for the growing community. Diffuse rather than pointed; the proximate model is the Exodus growth language, but the Genesis blessing stands behind it.

echoes.text: He does execute justice for the fatherless and widow, and loves the foreigner, in giving him food and clothing.
echoes.note: The LORD 'executes justice for the orphan and the widow.' The presenting crisis of Acts 6 is widows being neglected in the daily distribution; the church's corrective embodies Torah's persistent demand that the covenant community secure justice for widows. Thematic, not verbal.

echoes.text: “You shall not take advantage of any widow or fatherless child. If you take advantage of them at all, and they cry at all to me, I will surely hear their cry; and my wrath will grow hot, and I will kill you with the sword; and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless.
echoes.note: 'You shall not afflict any widow' under threat of God's anger. The neglect of the Hellenist widows is exactly the failure Torah warns against, and the apostles' swift remedy reflects this covenantal obligation. Faint background to the social problem rather than a textual citation.

pericopes.text: Stephen, full of faith and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people. But some of those who were of the synagogue called “The Libertines”, and of the Cyrenians, of the Alexandrians, and of those of Cilicia and Asia arose, disputing with Stephen. They weren’t able to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke. Then they secretly induced men to say, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.” They stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes, and came against him and seized him, and brought him in to the council, and set up false witnesses who said, “This man never stops speaking blasphemous words against this holy place and the law. For we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place, and will change the customs which Moses delivered to us.” All who sat in the council, fastening their eyes on him, saw his face like it was the face of an angel.

echoes.text: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him. When Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come near him. Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the rulers of the congregation returned to him; and Moses spoke to them. […]
echoes.note: Stephen's face appears to the council 'like the face of an angel' — the most pointed Moses-typology in the chapter, recalling how Moses' face shone after speaking with God on Sinai so that the people were struck by its radiance. The irony is deliberate: those accusing Stephen of blaspheming Moses behold on him the very Mosaic glory. Strong thematic coherence; the heavenly luminosity motif gives it volume.

echoes.text: in all the signs and the wonders, which Yahweh sent him to do in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh, and to all his servants, and to all his land,
echoes.note: Moses is remembered for 'all the signs and wonders' the LORD sent him to do. Stephen, 'full of grace and power, performed great wonders and signs' (6:8), continuing the Moses-and-prophet pattern Acts assigns to its Spirit-filled witnesses. Recurs as a fixed Lukan idiom; coherent with the broader Moses framing of the trial.

echoes.text: I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'I will multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt' — the foundational Exodus pairing of 'signs and wonders' that Acts 6:8 reuses for Stephen's ministry. Together with Deut 34:11 it locates Stephen in the line of Mosaic authentication by mighty deeds.

echoes.text: The son of the Israelite woman blasphemed the Name, and cursed; and they brought him to Moses. His mother’s name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan. They put him in custody, until Yahweh’s will should be declared to them. Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Bring out of the camp him who cursed; and let all who heard him lay their hands on his head, and let all the congregation stone him. You shall speak to the children of Israel, […]
echoes.note: The law of the blasphemer: one who blasphemes the Name is brought before the assembly, witnesses are involved, and the offender is stoned outside the camp. Stephen is charged with 'blasphemous words' (6:11, 6:13) and will be stoned (ch. 7). Little verbal borrowing, but the legal-typological frame — blasphemy accusation issuing in stoning — is precisely this statute, which the trial scene self-consciously invokes.

echoes.text: “You shall not blaspheme God, nor curse a ruler of your people.
echoes.note: 'You shall not blaspheme God, nor curse a ruler of your people.' This is among the texts grounding the very category of the blasphemy charge leveled against Stephen ('blasphemous words against Moses and God,' 6:11). Background to the legal accusation rather than a quoted source.

echoes.text: Unrighteous witnesses rise up. They ask me about things that I don’t know about.
echoes.note: 'Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things I do not know.' The 'false witnesses' suborned against Stephen (6:13) reprise the lament-psalm motif of the righteous sufferer assailed by lying accusers. Thematic coherence strong within Luke's righteous-martyr portrait; verbal contact moderate.

echoes.text: Don’t deliver me over to the desire of my adversaries, for false witnesses have risen up against me, such as breathe out cruelty.
echoes.note: 'False witnesses have risen against me, and they breathe out violence.' Reinforces the same psalmic pattern as Ps 35:11 — the persecuted righteous one surrounded by perjurers — directly mirrored in the false witnesses set up against Stephen.

echoes.text: If an unrighteous witness rises up against any man to testify against him of wrongdoing, then both the men, between whom the controversy is, shall stand before Yahweh, before the priests and the judges who shall be in those days; and the judges shall make diligent inquisition: and, behold, if the witness is a false witness, and has testified falsely against his brother; then you shall do to him as he had thought to do to his brother. So you shall remove […]
echoes.note: Torah's procedure for the 'malicious witness' who testifies falsely against another. The deliberate suborning of 'false witnesses' (6:13) is an inversion of this very law — the council perverts the witness-procedure Deuteronomy designed to protect the innocent. Legal-thematic resonance.

echoes.text: “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.
echoes.note: The Decalogue's prohibition 'you shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.' The engineering of false testimony against Stephen is a flat violation of this command — diffuse background rather than a cited text, but part of the false-witness cluster.

echoes.text: then I will make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth. The priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in Yahweh’s house. When Jeremiah had made an end of speaking all that Yahweh had commanded him to speak to all the people, the priests and the prophets and all the people seized him, saying, “You shall surely die.” Why have you prophesied in Yahweh’s name, saying, This […]
echoes.note: Jeremiah prophesies that the LORD will make the temple 'like Shiloh' and the city a desolation; priests, prophets, and people seize him, demand his death, and put him on trial for speaking against 'this place.' Acts 6:13-14 charges Stephen with saying Jesus 'will destroy this place' — the prophet-on-trial-for-predicting-the-temple's-fall pattern is strikingly congruent. Little verbal borrowing, strong typological satisfaction.

echoes.text: therefore will I do to the house which is called by my name, in which you trust, and to the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.
echoes.note: 'I will do to the house that is called by my name... as I did to Shiloh' — Jeremiah's temple sermon announcing the sanctuary's destruction. The accusation that Stephen said Jesus 'will destroy this holy place' echoes this prophetic threat against the temple, situating Stephen among prophets who relativized the sanctuary's permanence.

pericopes.text: The high priest said, “Are these things so?” He said, “Brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and said to him, ‘Get out of your land, and from your relatives, and come into a land which I will show you.’ Then he came out of the land of the Chaldaeans, and lived in Haran. From there, when his father was dead, God moved him into this land, where you are now living. He gave him no inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on. He promised that he would give it to him for a possession, and to his seed after him, when he still had no child. God spoke in this way: that his seed would live as aliens in a strange land, and that they would be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years. ‘I will judge the nation to which they will be in bondage,’ said God, ‘and after that will they come out, and serve me in this place.’ He gave him the covenant of circumcision. So Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him the eighth day. Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob became the father of the twelve patriarchs.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s voice is on the waters. The God of glory thunders, even Yahweh on many waters.
echoes.note: Stephen opens by calling God 'the God of glory'; the phrase recalls the Psalter's thundering 'God of glory,' lending the divine epiphany to Abraham a cultic-theophanic register from the outset.

echoes.text: Now Yahweh said to Abram, “Get out of your country, and from your relatives, and from your father’s house, to the land that I will show you.
echoes.note: 'Get out of your land, and from your relatives, and come into a land which I will show you' reproduces the LXX call of Abram almost verbatim — the foundational migration command anchoring the whole speech's theme of God on the move, not bound to one place.

echoes.text: Terah took Abram his son, Lot the son of Haran, his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, his son Abram’s wife. They went from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan. They came to Haran and lived there.
echoes.note: The geography — Mesopotamia, the land of the Chaldeans, settling in Haran before reaching Canaan — tracks Terah's migration from Ur of the Chaldees to Haran exactly; Stephen knows the itinerary.

echoes.text: The days of Terah were two hundred five years. Terah died in Haran.
echoes.note: 'When his father was dead, God moved him into this land' presupposes Terah's death at Haran; Stephen harmonizes the chronology around the patriarch's burial there.

echoes.text: So Abram went, as Yahweh had spoken to him. Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed out of Haran. Abram took Sarai his wife, Lot his brother’s son, all their substance that they had gathered, and the souls whom they had gotten in Haran, and they went to go into the land of Canaan. Into the land of Canaan they came.
echoes.note: Abram's actual departure from Haran into Canaan, the land 'where you are now living,' fulfills the v.3 command and supplies the narrative motion of vv.4.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to Abram and said, “I will give this land to your seed.” He built an altar there to Yahweh, who appeared to him.
echoes.note: The promise to give the land 'to him for a possession, and to his seed after him' echoes the first land-grant oath at Shechem 'unto thy seed will I give this land.'

echoes.text: I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”
echoes.note: The land given 'for a possession' to Abraham and his seed reproduces the everlasting-possession formula of the covenant chapter, reinforcing that the gift was promissory, not yet realized.

echoes.text: Don’t contend with them; for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on; because I have given Mount Seir to Esau for a possession.
echoes.note: 'No inheritance... not so much as to set his foot on' echoes the idiom of 'not so much as a foot breadth' of land — Stephen sharpens the paradox that the promised land yielded Abraham not a single footstep of soil.

echoes.text: He said to Abram, “Know for sure that your seed will live as foreigners in a land that is not theirs, and will serve them. They will afflict them four hundred years.
echoes.note: 'His seed would live as aliens in a strange land, and they would be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years' is a near-verbatim citation of the covenant-of-the-pieces prophecy of the Egyptian sojourn.

echoes.text: I will also judge that nation, whom they will serve. Afterward they will come out with great wealth,
echoes.note: 'I will judge the nation to which they will be in bondage, and after that will they come out' continues the same Genesis 15 oracle of judgment on the enslaving nation and the exodus.

echoes.text: He said, “Certainly I will be with you. This will be the token to you, that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain.”
echoes.note: 'And serve me in this place' grafts the burning-bush promise ('ye shall serve God upon this mountain') onto the Genesis 15 prophecy, fusing the two great promises of worship after deliverance.

echoes.text: This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised.
echoes.note: 'He gave him the covenant of circumcision' directly invokes the Genesis 17 institution of circumcision as the sign of the covenant.

echoes.text: Abraham circumcised his son, Isaac, when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him.
echoes.note: Abraham 'circumcised him the eighth day' — Isaac circumcised at eight days old fulfills the eighth-day command and is narrated at Isaac's birth.

echoes.text: After that, his brother came out, and his hand had hold on Esau’s heel. He was named Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.
echoes.note: 'Isaac became the father of Jacob' compresses the generations of Genesis, naming the birth of Jacob to Isaac.

echoes.text: The sons of Leah: Reuben (Jacob’s firstborn), Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin. The sons of Bilhah (Rachel’s handmaid): Dan and Naphtali. The sons of Zilpah (Leah’s handmaid): Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob, who were born to him in Paddan Aram.
echoes.note: 'Jacob became the father of the twelve patriarchs' alludes to the roster of Jacob's twelve sons, the eponymous ancestors of the tribes.

pericopes.text: “The patriarchs, moved with jealousy against Joseph, sold him into Egypt. God was with him, and delivered him out of all his afflictions, and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He made him governor over Egypt and all his house. Now a famine came over all the land of Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction. Our fathers found no food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers the first time. On the second time Joseph was made known to his brothers, and Joseph’s race was revealed to Pharaoh. Joseph sent, and summoned Jacob, his father, and all his relatives, seventy-five souls. Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, himself and our fathers, and they were brought back to Shechem, and laid in the tomb that Abraham bought for a price in silver from the children of Hamor of Shechem.

echoes.text: His brothers envied him, but his father kept this saying in mind.
echoes.note: 'The patriarchs, moved with jealousy against Joseph' echoes 'his brethren envied him,' the seed of the betrayal — and a deliberate prototype of the present rejection of Jesus.

echoes.text: Midianites who were merchants passed by, and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. They brought Joseph into Egypt.
echoes.note: 'Sold him into Egypt' reproduces the brothers selling Joseph to the traders bound for Egypt.

echoes.text: Yahweh was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man. He was in the house of his master the Egyptian.
echoes.note: 'God was with him' echoes the refrain 'the LORD was with Joseph' that frames his Egyptian career.

echoes.text: The thing was good in the eyes of Pharaoh, and in the eyes of all his servants. Pharaoh said to his servants, “Can we find such a one as this, a man in whom is the Spirit of God?” Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Because God has shown you all of this, there is no one so discreet and wise as you. You shall be over my house, and according to your word will all my people be ruled. Only in the throne I will be greater than you.” Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Behold, I […]
echoes.note: Joseph given 'favor and wisdom before Pharaoh' and made 'governor over Egypt and all his house' summarizes Pharaoh's elevation of Joseph over all the land of Egypt.

echoes.text: He made him lord of his house, and ruler of all of his possessions;
echoes.note: Joseph made 'ruler of his house, and lord of all his substance' supplies the same poetic summary of his elevation that Stephen's 'governor over... all his house' tracks.

echoes.text: The seven years of famine began to come, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.
echoes.note: 'A famine came over all the land of Egypt and Canaan' echoes the onset of the seven years of dearth that reached every land.

echoes.text: The sons of Israel came to buy among those who came, for the famine was in the land of Canaan.
echoes.note: 'Our fathers found no food' reflects the famine 'in the land of Canaan' that drove Jacob's sons to seek grain.

echoes.text: Now Jacob saw that there was grain in Egypt, and Jacob said to his sons, “Why do you look at one another?” He said, “Behold, I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there, and buy for us from there, so that we may live, and not die.”
echoes.note: 'When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers the first time' reproduces Jacob's command to his sons to go down and buy corn in Egypt.

echoes.text: Then Joseph couldn’t control himself before all those who stood before him, and he cried, “Cause everyone to go out from me!” No one else stood with him, while Joseph made himself known to his brothers.
echoes.note: 'On the second time Joseph was made known to his brothers' echoes the great recognition scene, 'I am Joseph.'

echoes.text: The report of it was heard in Pharaoh’s house, saying, “Joseph’s brothers have come.” It pleased Pharaoh well, and his servants.
echoes.note: 'Joseph's race was revealed to Pharaoh' echoes the report that reached Pharaoh's house that Joseph's brethren had come.

echoes.text: Hurry, and go up to my father, and tell him, ‘This is what your son Joseph says, “God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me. Don’t wait. You shall dwell in the land of Goshen, and you will be near to me, you, your children, your children’s children, your flocks, your herds, and all that you have.
echoes.note: Joseph 'summoned Jacob, his father, and all his relatives' reproduces Joseph's message bidding his father come down to him in Egypt.

echoes.text: The sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, were two souls. All the souls of the house of Jacob, who came into Egypt, were seventy.
echoes.note: 'Seventy-five souls' follows the Septuagint total of Jacob's household (LXX adds Joseph's grandsons), distinguishing Stephen's source-text from the Hebrew 'seventy.'

echoes.text: Your fathers went down into Egypt with seventy persons; and now Yahweh your God has made you as the stars of the sky for multitude.
echoes.note: The numbering of the household that went down into Egypt (Hebrew 'threescore and ten') is the recurring census tradition Stephen draws on, here in its LXX seventy-five form.

echoes.text: Jacob rose up from Beersheba, and the sons of Israel carried Jacob, their father, their little ones, and their wives, in the wagons which Pharaoh had sent to carry him. They took their livestock, and their goods, which they had gotten in the land of Canaan, and came into Egypt—Jacob, and all his seed with him,
echoes.note: 'Jacob went down into Egypt' reproduces the migration of Jacob and all his seed into Egypt.

echoes.text: When Jacob made an end of charging his sons, he gathered up his feet into the bed, and yielded up the spirit, and was gathered to his people.
echoes.note: 'And he died' echoes Jacob yielding up the ghost and being gathered to his people.

echoes.text: Joseph died, as did all his brothers, and all that generation.
echoes.note: 'Himself and our fathers' died echoes 'Joseph died, and all his brethren, and all that generation,' marking the end of the patriarchal era.

echoes.text: Abraham listened to Ephron. Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver which he had named in the audience of the children of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, according to the current merchants’ standard. So the field of Ephron, which was in Machpelah, which was before Mamre, the field, the cave which was in it, and all the trees that were in the field, that were in all of its borders, were deeded
echoes.note: 'The tomb that Abraham bought for a price in silver' alludes to Abraham's purchase of the field of Machpelah for a burial place — though Stephen telescopes it with the Shechem plot.

echoes.text: He bought the parcel of ground where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for one hundred pieces of money.
echoes.note: The plot 'from the children of Hamor of Shechem' reproduces Jacob's purchase of a parcel at Shechem from the sons of Hamor — Stephen conflates the two patriarchal land purchases.

echoes.text: They buried the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, in Shechem, in the parcel of ground which Jacob bought of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred pieces of money. They became the inheritance of the children of Joseph.
echoes.note: 'Brought back to Shechem' echoes the burial of Joseph's bones in the parcel of ground at Shechem that Jacob bought from Hamor's sons — the source that explains Stephen's Shechem detail.

pericopes.text: “But as the time of the promise came close which God had sworn to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt, until there arose a different king, who didn’t know Joseph. The same took advantage of our race, and mistreated our fathers, and forced them to throw out their babies, so that they wouldn’t stay alive. At that time Moses was born, and was exceedingly handsome. He was nourished three months in his father’s house. When he was thrown out, Pharaoh’s daughter took him up, and reared him as her own son. Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. He was mighty in his words and works.

echoes.text: The children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and grew exceedingly mighty; and the land was filled with them.
echoes.note: 'The people grew and multiplied in Egypt' reproduces 'the children of Israel were fruitful... and multiplied,' the population explosion that triggers oppression.

echoes.text: He said to Abram, “Know for sure that your seed will live as foreigners in a land that is not theirs, and will serve them. They will afflict them four hundred years. I will also judge that nation, whom they will serve. Afterward they will come out with great wealth,
echoes.note: 'As the time of the promise came close which God had sworn to Abraham' loops back to the four-hundred-year covenant prophecy now reaching its term.

echoes.text: He increased his people greatly, and made them stronger than their adversaries.
echoes.note: 'He increased his people greatly' offers the poetic counterpart to Israel's multiplication in Egypt.

echoes.text: Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who didn’t know Joseph.
echoes.note: 'There arose a different king, who didn't know Joseph' is a near-verbatim rendering of 'there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph.'

echoes.text: Come, let us deal wisely with them, lest they multiply, and it happen that when any war breaks out, they also join themselves to our enemies, and fight against us, and escape out of the land.” Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with their burdens. They built storage cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Raamses.
echoes.note: 'Took advantage of our race, and mistreated our fathers' echoes Pharaoh's policy to 'deal wisely' and afflict Israel with burdens.

echoes.text: Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying, “You shall cast every son who is born into the river, and every daughter you shall save alive.”
echoes.note: 'Forced them to throw out their babies, so that they wouldn't stay alive' reproduces Pharaoh's edict to cast every newborn son into the river.

echoes.text: The woman conceived, and bore a son. When she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months.
echoes.note: Moses 'was exceedingly handsome... nourished three months in his father's house' closely follows 'she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months.'

echoes.text: When she could no longer hide him, she took a papyrus basket for him, and coated it with tar and with pitch. She put the child in it, and laid it in the reeds by the river’s bank.
echoes.note: 'When he was thrown out' alludes to the mother placing the infant in the ark among the reeds when she could no longer hide him.

echoes.text: Pharaoh’s daughter came down to bathe at the river. Her maidens walked along by the riverside. She saw the basket among the reeds, and sent her handmaid to get it.
echoes.note: 'Pharaoh's daughter took him up' reproduces the princess discovering and taking the child from the river.

echoes.text: The child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, and said, “Because I drew him out of the water.”
echoes.note: 'Reared him as her own son' echoes 'he became her son' when Moses was brought to Pharaoh's daughter.

echoes.text: Moses said to Yahweh, “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.”
echoes.note: 'Mighty in his words and works' stands in pointed tension with Moses' own self-description as 'slow of speech'; the haggadic praise of Moses' eloquence amplifies the biblical figure.

echoes.text: Solomon’s wisdom excelled the wisdom of all the children of the east, and all the wisdom of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'Instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians' presupposes the proverbial 'wisdom of Egypt' that Israel's later tradition both admired and relativized.

pericopes.text: But when he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. Seeing one of them suffer wrong, he defended him, and avenged him who was oppressed, striking the Egyptian. He supposed that his brothers understood that God, by his hand, was giving them deliverance; but they didn’t understand. “The day following, he appeared to them as they fought, and urged them to be at peace again, saying, ‘Sirs, you are brothers. Why do you wrong one another?’ But he who did his neighbor wrong pushed him away, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’ Moses fled at this saying, and became a stranger in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons.

echoes.text: In those days, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his brothers, and looked at their burdens. He saw an Egyptian striking a Hebrew, one of his brothers.
echoes.note: Moses, grown, going out 'to visit his brothers, the children of Israel,' reproduces 'Moses... went out unto his brethren, and looked on their burdens.'

echoes.text: He looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no one, he killed the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand.
echoes.note: Seeing the wrong and 'striking the Egyptian' reproduces Moses smiting the Egyptian and hiding him in the sand.

echoes.text: He went out the second day, and behold, two men of the Hebrews were fighting with each other. He said to him who did the wrong, “Why do you strike your fellow?”
echoes.note: 'The day following, he appeared to them as they fought' and urged peace reproduces Moses finding two Hebrews striving on the second day.

echoes.text: He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”
echoes.note: 'Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?' is a near-verbatim citation of the rebuffing Hebrew's words — the rejection-of-the-deliverer motif Stephen weaponizes.

echoes.text: Now when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and lived in the land of Midian, and he sat down by a well.
echoes.note: 'Moses fled at this saying, and became a stranger in the land of Midian' reproduces Moses fleeing Pharaoh and dwelling in Midian.

echoes.text: Moses was content to dwell with the man. He gave Moses Zipporah, his daughter. She bore a son, and he named him Gershom, for he said, “I have lived as a foreigner in a foreign land.”
echoes.note: Moses becoming 'the father of two sons' in Midian echoes his marriage to Zipporah and the birth of Gershom (the 'stranger in a strange land').

pericopes.text: “When forty years were fulfilled, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he wondered at the sight. As he came close to see, a voice of the Lord came to him, ‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’ Moses trembled, and dared not look. The Lord said to him, ‘Take your sandals off of your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground. I have surely seen the affliction of my people that is in Egypt, and have heard their groaning. I have come down to deliver them. Now come, I will send you into Egypt.’

echoes.text: Now Moses was keeping the flock of Jethro, his father-in-law, the priest of Midian, and he led the flock to the back of the wilderness, and came to God’s mountain, to Horeb. Yahweh’s angel appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed.
echoes.note: 'An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush' reproduces the angel of the LORD in the flame of fire out of the midst of the bush at Horeb.

echoes.text: Moses said, “I will turn aside now, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt.”
echoes.note: 'Moses... wondered at the sight. As he came close to see' echoes Moses turning aside to see the great sight of the unconsumed bush.

echoes.text: When Yahweh saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the midst of the bush, and said, “Moses! Moses!” He said, “Here I am.”
echoes.note: 'A voice of the Lord came to him' reproduces God calling to Moses out of the midst of the bush.

echoes.text: Moreover he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look at God.
echoes.note: 'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob' is a verbatim citation; 'Moses trembled, and dared not look' reproduces 'Moses hid his face.'

echoes.text: He said, “Don’t come close. Take your sandals off of your feet, for the place you are standing on is holy ground.”
echoes.note: 'Take your sandals off of your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground' is a near-verbatim citation — the holy-ground saying that anchors Stephen's argument that God is not confined to the temple.

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters, for I know their sorrows. I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians, and to bring them up out of that land to a good and large land, to a land flowing with milk and honey; to the place of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite.
echoes.note: 'I have surely seen the affliction of my people that is in Egypt, and have heard their groaning. I have come down to deliver them' closely follows the LORD's declaration that he has seen the affliction and come down to deliver.

echoes.text: Come now therefore, and I will send you to Pharaoh, that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt.”
echoes.note: 'Now come, I will send you into Egypt' reproduces 'Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh.'

echoes.text: God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.
echoes.note: 'Heard their groaning' echoes 'God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant,' tying the deliverance to the Abrahamic promise.

pericopes.text: “This Moses, whom they refused, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’—God has sent him as both a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. This man led them out, having worked wonders and signs in Egypt, in the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years. This is that Moses, who said to the children of Israel, ‘The Lord our God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me.’ This is he who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel that spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers, who received living oracles to give to us, to whom our fathers wouldn’t be obedient, but rejected him, and turned back in their hearts to Egypt, saying to Aaron, ‘Make us gods that will go before us, for as for this Moses, who led us out of the land of Egypt, we don’t know what has become of him.’ They made a calf in those days, and brought a sacrifice to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their hands. But God turned, and gave them up to serve the army of the sky, as it is written in the book of the prophets, ‘Did you offer to me slain animals and sacrifices forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? You took up the tabernacle of Moloch, the star of your god Rephan, the figures which you made to worship. I will carry you away beyond Babylon.’

echoes.text: He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”
echoes.note: 'Who made you a ruler and a judge?' is repeated from the Hebrew's taunt, now turned into the structural refrain of Israel rejecting the very deliverer God appoints.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s angel appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed.
echoes.note: Moses sent 'by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush' loops back to the angel in the burning bush as God's commissioning agent.

echoes.text: I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'Having worked wonders and signs in Egypt' echoes the LORD multiplying signs and wonders in the land of Egypt through Moses.

echoes.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all the night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.
echoes.note: Wonders 'in the Red Sea' alludes to the parting of the sea at the exodus.

echoes.text: Your children shall be wanderers in the wilderness forty years, and shall bear your prostitution, until your dead bodies are consumed in the wilderness.
echoes.note: 'In the wilderness for forty years' echoes the forty years of wandering decreed for the rebellious generation.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: 'The Lord our God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me' is a verbatim citation of the prophet-like-Moses promise — the christological hinge of the speech.

echoes.text: Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the lower part of the mountain.
echoes.note: 'In the assembly in the wilderness... on Mount Sinai' alludes to Israel gathered at the foot of Sinai when God spoke.

echoes.text: For it is no vain thing for you; because it is your life, and through this thing you shall prolong your days in the land, where you go over the Jordan to possess it.”
echoes.note: 'Living oracles' (logia zonta) echoes Moses' claim that the law 'is not a vain thing for you; because it is your life' — the Torah as the word of life.

echoes.text: Why does Yahweh bring us to this land, to fall by the sword? Our wives and our little ones will be captured or killed! Wouldn’t it be better for us to return into Egypt?” They said one to another, “Let us make a captain, and let us return into Egypt.”
echoes.note: Fathers who 'turned back in their hearts to Egypt' reproduces the wilderness murmuring, 'Let us make a captain, and let us return into Egypt.'

echoes.text: When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down from the mountain, the people gathered themselves together to Aaron, and said to him, “Come, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we don’t know what has become of him.”
echoes.note: 'Make us gods that will go before us, for as for this Moses... we don't know what has become of him' is a near-verbatim citation of the people's demand to Aaron.

echoes.text: He received what they handed him, and fashioned it with an engraving tool, and made it a molten calf; and they said, “These are your gods, Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt.” When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before it; and Aaron made a proclamation, and said, “Tomorrow shall be a feast to Yahweh.” They rose up early on the next day, and offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and to […]
echoes.note: 'They made a calf... and brought a sacrifice to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their hands' reproduces the golden-calf apostasy with its offerings and revelry.

echoes.text: They made a calf in Horeb, and worshiped a molten image. Thus they exchanged their glory for an image of a bull that eats grass.
echoes.note: 'Rejoiced in the works of their hands' echoes 'they made a calf in Horeb... and changed their glory into the similitude of an ox,' the Psalter's indictment of idolatry.

echoes.text: “Did you bring to me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness forty years, house of Israel?
echoes.note: 'Did you offer to me slain animals and sacrifices forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?' is a direct citation of Amos following the Septuagint.
echoes.lxxText: Have ye offered to me victims and sacrifices, O house of Israel, forty years in the wilderness?

echoes.text: You also carried the tent of your king and the shrine of your images, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves. Therefore will I cause you to go into captivity beyond Damascus,” says Yahweh, whose name is the God of Armies.
echoes.note: 'You took up the tabernacle of Moloch, the star of your god Rephan... I will carry you away beyond Babylon' cites Amos in its LXX form (Rephan for Hebrew Kiyyun; 'Babylon' for 'Damascus'), turning the exile threat against the temple establishment.

echoes.text: and lest you lift up your eyes to the sky, and when you see the sun and the moon and the stars, even all the army of the sky, you are drawn away and worship them, and serve them, which Yahweh your God has allotted to all the peoples under the whole sky.
echoes.note: God giving them up 'to serve the army of the sky' echoes the warning against worshipping the host of heaven — the sun, moon, and stars.

echoes.text: The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead the dough, to make cakes to the queen of the sky, and to pour out drink offerings to other gods, that they may provoke me to anger.
echoes.note: Sacrifice 'to the army of the sky' resonates with Jeremiah's denunciation of offerings to the queen of heaven and the host of heaven, the prophetic critique of false worship Stephen invokes.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not give any of your children to sacrifice to Molech; neither shall you profane the name of your God. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'The tabernacle of Moloch' resonates with the Levitical prohibition against passing one's seed through the fire to Molech.

pericopes.text: “Our fathers had the tabernacle of the testimony in the wilderness, even as he who spoke to Moses commanded him to make it according to the pattern that he had seen; which also our fathers, in their turn, brought in with Joshua when they entered into the possession of the nations, whom God drove out before the face of our fathers, to the days of David, who found favor in the sight of God, and asked to find a habitation for the God of Jacob. But Solomon built him a house. However, the Most High doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands, as the prophet says, ‘heaven is my throne, and the earth a footstool for my feet. What kind of house will you build me?’ says the Lord; ‘or what is the place of my rest? Didn’t my hand make all these things?’

echoes.text: See that you make them after their pattern, which has been shown to you on the mountain.
echoes.note: The tabernacle made 'according to the pattern that he had seen' cites the command to Moses to make all things after the pattern shown him in the mount.

echoes.text: but appoint the Levites over the Tabernacle of the Testimony, and over all its furnishings, and over all that belongs to it. They shall carry the tabernacle, and all its furnishings; and they shall take care of it, and shall encamp around it.
echoes.note: 'The tabernacle of the testimony' echoes the standard Pentateuchal designation 'tabernacle of the testimony' for the wilderness sanctuary.

echoes.text: When the people moved from their tents to pass over the Jordan, the priests who bore the ark of the covenant being before the people, and when those who bore the ark had come to the Jordan, and the feet of the priests who bore the ark had dipped in the edge of the water (for the Jordan overflows all its banks all the time of harvest), the waters which came down from above stood, and rose up in one heap, a great way off, at Adam, the city that is beside […]
echoes.note: 'Brought in with Joshua when they entered into the possession of the nations' alludes to Israel crossing Jordan under Joshua to take the land.

echoes.text: “For Yahweh has driven great and strong nations out from before you. But as for you, no man has stood before you to this day.
echoes.note: 'The nations, whom God drove out before the face of our fathers' echoes the conquest formula that the LORD drove out great nations before Israel.

echoes.text: When the king lived in his house, and Yahweh had given him rest from all his enemies all around, the king said to Nathan the prophet, “See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells within curtains.”
echoes.note: David 'asked to find a habitation for the God of Jacob' alludes to David's wish to build a house for the ark, the occasion of Nathan's oracle.

echoes.text: until I find out a place for Yahweh, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob.”
echoes.note: 'A habitation for the God of Jacob' closely follows the Psalmist's vow to 'find out a place... an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob.'

echoes.text: When David lived in his house, David said to Nathan the prophet, “Behold, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of the covenant of Yahweh is under curtains.”
echoes.note: David's desire to house the ark is also recounted in Chronicles, the parallel tradition behind Stephen's compressed summary.

echoes.text: In the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: 'But Solomon built him a house' reproduces Solomon's construction of the temple, the climax Stephen immediately relativizes.

echoes.text: But will God in very deed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house that I have built!
echoes.note: 'The Most High doesn't dwell in temples made with hands' echoes Solomon's own dedicatory confession, 'the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house?'

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: what kind of house will you build to me? and what place shall be my rest?
echoes.note: 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth a footstool for my feet. What kind of house will you build me?' is a verbatim citation of Isaiah's oracle against confining God to a temple.

echoes.text: For all these things has my hand made, and so all these things came to be,” says Yahweh: “but to this man will I look, even to him who is poor and of a contrite spirit, and who trembles at my word.
echoes.note: 'Didn't my hand make all these things?' continues the Isaiah 66 citation ('all those things hath mine hand made'), grounding the anti-temple argument in the Creator's transcendence.

pericopes.text: “You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit! As your fathers did, so you do. Which of the prophets didn’t your fathers persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, of whom you have now become betrayers and murderers. You received the law as it was ordained by angels, and didn’t keep it!”

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell the children of Israel, ‘You are a stiff-necked people. If I were to go up into your midst for one moment, I would consume you. Therefore now take off your jewelry from you, that I may know what to do to you.’”
echoes.note: 'You stiff-necked' applies God's own characterization of Israel ('thou art a stiffnecked people') to Stephen's hearers — the post-golden-calf indictment turned on the council.

echoes.text: Know therefore, that Yahweh your God doesn’t give you this good land to possess for your righteousness; for you are a stiff-necked people.
echoes.note: 'Stiff-necked' echoes the repeated Deuteronomic refrain 'thou art a stiffnecked people,' Moses' summary verdict on the wilderness generation.

echoes.text: I also walked contrary to them, and brought them into the land of their enemies; if then their uncircumcised heart is humbled, and they then accept the punishment of their iniquity;
echoes.note: 'Uncircumcised in heart' reproduces the Holiness Code's 'if then their uncircumcised hearts be humbled,' the metaphor of inner unfaithfulness.

echoes.text: To whom shall I speak and testify, that they may hear? Behold, their ear is uncircumcised, and they can’t listen. Behold, Yahweh’s word has become a reproach to them. They have no delight in it.
echoes.note: 'Uncircumcised in... ears' echoes Jeremiah's 'their ear is uncircumcised, and they cannot hearken' — deaf to the prophetic word.

echoes.text: But they rebelled, and grieved his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he himself fought against them.
echoes.note: 'You always resist the Holy Spirit' echoes 'they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit' — the rare OT 'Holy Spirit' language Stephen deploys against the present generation.

echoes.text: but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the wrath of Yahweh arose against his people, until there was no remedy.
echoes.note: 'Which of the prophets didn't your fathers persecute?' echoes the chronicler's verdict that they 'mocked the messengers of God... and misused his prophets,' the canonical summary of prophet-killing.

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: 'They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One' echoes Elijah's complaint that Israel 'slain thy prophets with the sword.'

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.
echoes.note: 'The Righteous One' (ho dikaios) typologically draws on the Servant whom God calls 'my righteous servant,' read as the suffering Messiah.

echoes.text: He said, “Yahweh came from Sinai, and rose from Seir to them. He shone from Mount Paran. He came from the ten thousands of holy ones. At his right hand was a fiery law for them.
echoes.note: 'You received the law as it was ordained by angels' draws on the LXX of Moses' blessing ('on his right hand... angels with him'), the tradition of angelic mediation of the Sinai law.

pericopes.text: Now when they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed at him with their teeth. But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God, and said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!” But they cried out with a loud voice, and stopped their ears, and rushed at him with one accord. They threw him out of the city, and stoned him. The witnesses placed their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. They stoned Stephen as he called out, saying, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!” He kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” When he had said this, he fell asleep.

echoes.text: As the appearance of the rainbow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of Yahweh’s glory. When I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard a voice of one that spoke.
echoes.note: Stephen 'saw the glory of God' in opened heaven echoes Ezekiel's vision of 'the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD,' the prophetic theophany pattern.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: Seeing 'Jesus standing on the right hand of God' draws on the enthronement oracle 'Sit thou at my right hand,' the supreme OT proof-text of exaltation — strikingly with Jesus standing rather than seated.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'The Son of Man standing at the right hand of God' fuses Daniel's vision of 'one like the Son of man' coming with the clouds with the right-hand enthronement.

echoes.text: The hand of the witnesses shall be first on him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.
echoes.note: 'The witnesses placed their garments' and the stoning reflect the Deuteronomic execution law that 'the hands of the witnesses shall be first upon him to put him to death.'

echoes.text: He who blasphemes Yahweh’s name, he shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall certainly stone him. The foreigner as well as the native-born, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death.
echoes.note: Stoning Stephen after the charge of blasphemy against the temple and God reflects the law that 'he that blasphemeth the name of the LORD... all the congregation shall certainly stone him.'

echoes.text: Into your hand I commend my spirit. You redeem me, Yahweh, God of truth.
echoes.note: 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!' reworks the Psalmist's 'into thine hand I commit my spirit,' the prayer of the dying righteous now addressed to Jesus.

pericopes.text: Saul was consenting to his death. A great persecution arose against the assembly which was in Jerusalem in that day. They were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles. Devout men buried Stephen, and lamented greatly over him. But Saul ravaged the assembly, entering into every house, and dragged both men and women off to prison.

echoes.text: They came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan, and there they lamented with a very great and severe lamentation. He mourned for his father seven days. When the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning in the floor of Atad, they said, “This is a grievous mourning by the Egyptians.” Therefore its name was called Abel Mizraim, which is beyond the Jordan.
echoes.note: The 'devout men' who 'lamented greatly' over Stephen recall the formulaic 'great and very sore lamentation' of the patriarchs over the dead (mourning for Jacob at the threshing floor of Atad). Volume rests on the doubled mourning vocabulary; thematic coherence is moderate (burial of a righteous man with public lament). The link is generic Septuagintal funerary idiom rather than a targeted citation.

echoes.text: So his servants took him out of the chariot, and put him in the second chariot that he had, and brought him to Jerusalem; and he died, and was buried in the tombs of his fathers. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah. Jeremiah lamented for Josiah: and all the singing men and singing women spoke of Josiah in their lamentations to this day; and they made them an ordinance in Israel: and behold, they are written in the lamentations.
echoes.note: Great public lamentation over a slain righteous one parallels the mourning over Josiah, where 'all Judah and Jerusalem mourned' and laments were established.
