Thematic coherence (a community grieving the death of a faithful figure) is present; verbal volume is faint. Plausibility is low since no distinctive wording is shared.

echoes.text: I will scatter you among the nations, and I will draw out the sword after you. Your land will be a desolation, and your cities shall be a waste.
echoes.note: The believers 'scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria' evokes the covenantal scattering language ('I will scatter you among the nations'), here ironically reversed so that dispersion becomes the engine of mission. The scattering motif recurs across Deuteronomy and the Prophets, lending thematic recurrence; but Luke gives it a salvific rather than punitive sense, weakening the direct correspondence.

pericopes.text: Therefore those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and proclaimed to them the Christ. The multitudes listened with one accord to the things that were spoken by Philip, when they heard and saw the signs which he did. For unclean spirits came out of many of those who had them. They came out, crying with a loud voice. Many who had been paralyzed and lame were healed. There was great joy in that city.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: Philip's healings—'many who had been paralyzed and lame were healed'—enact the eschatological restoration promised in Isaiah, where 'the lame man shall leap as a hart.' Volume is moderate (shared 'lame' healing imagery), recurrence is strong across Isaiah and Luke-Acts as a sign of the inbreaking kingdom, and thematic coherence is high: the signs authenticate the proclamation of the Christ. The link is conceptual rather than a quotation.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: Philip 'proclaimed' the Christ and the multitudes responded with 'great joy,' echoing the herald who publishes good tidings of peace and salvation. Thematic coherence (good news bringing joy to a city) is present; verbal volume is low and mediated through Luke's general euangelizo vocabulary.

echoes.text: The king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Avva, and from Hamath and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel; and they possessed Samaria, and lived in the cities of it. So it was, at the beginning of their dwelling there, that they didn’t fear Yahweh: therefore Yahweh sent lions among them, which killed some of them. Therefore they spoke to the king of Assyria, saying, “The […]
echoes.note: The evangelization of 'the city of Samaria' figurally reverses the region's origin as a syncretistic resettlement after the Assyrian exile, where transplanted peoples 'feared the LORD and served their own gods.' No verbal borrowing; the coherence is historical-typological—the place of compromised worship now receives the pure word with joy.

pericopes.text: But there was a certain man, Simon by name, who used to practice sorcery in the city, and amazed the people of Samaria, making himself out to be some great one, to whom they all listened, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is that great power of God.” They listened to him, because for a long time he had amazed them with his sorceries. But when they believed Philip preaching good news concerning the Kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Simon himself also believed. Being baptized, he continued with Philip. Seeing signs and great miracles occurring, he was amazed.

echoes.text: There shall not be found with you anyone who makes his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, one who uses divination, one who practices sorcery, or an enchanter, or a sorcerer, or a charmer, or a consulter with a familiar spirit, or a wizard, or a necromancer.
echoes.note: Simon's practice of 'sorcery' that 'amazed the people of Samaria' stands against the Torah's explicit ban on the diviner, soothsayer, enchanter, and sorcerer. Thematic coherence is strong (forbidden magic confronted by the true word of God), and the sorcery vocabulary recurs in the prophetic polemic; volume is conceptual rather than lexical.

echoes.text: but these two things shall come to you in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood; in their full measure shall they come on you, in the multitude of your sorceries, and the great abundance of your enchantments. For you have trusted in your wickedness; you have said, No one sees me; your wisdom and your knowledge, it has perverted you, and you have said in your heart, I am, and there is no one else besides me. Therefore evil will come on […]
echoes.note: Simon's long-standing 'sorceries' by which he held the people in thrall recall the impotent 'multitude of thy sorceries' and 'enchantments' of Babylon, which cannot save before the power of God. Recurrence of the sorcery-versus-God contrast is notable; verbal volume is faint and the correspondence is thematic.

echoes.text: Then Pharaoh also called for the wise men and the sorcerers. They also, the magicians of Egypt, did the same thing with their enchantments.
echoes.note: Simon, the magician overawed by genuine 'signs and great miracles,' loosely typifies Pharaoh's sorcerers whose arts are outmatched by the signs of God. Thematic coherence (true wonders eclipsing magic) is moderate; there is no shared wording, so the link is a faint figural resonance.

pericopes.text: Now when the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them, who, when they had come down, prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit; for as yet he had fallen on none of them. They had only been baptized in the name of Christ Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: The Samaritans' reception of the Holy Spirit through the apostles' prayer and laying on of hands extends the outpouring of the Spirit 'upon all flesh' programmatic for Acts. Recurrence within Luke-Acts (cited at Pentecost) is strong; here the volume is faint—no direct verbal contact—so the connection is a thematic continuation rather than a fresh allusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and commission him in their sight. You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before Yahweh. At his word they shall go out, and at his […]
echoes.note: The apostles 'laid their hands on them' and they received the Spirit, recalling the commissioning gesture by which Moses laid hands on Spirit-filled Joshua. Thematic coherence (laying on of hands conveying authority and Spirit) is moderate; the rite is widely attested in the Torah, so volume and distinctiveness are low.

pericopes.text: Now when Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, saying, “Give me also this power, that whomever I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.” But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart isn’t right before God. Repent therefore of this, your wickedness, and ask God if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity.” Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that none of the things which you have spoken happen to me.”

echoes.text: lest there should be among you man, woman, family, or tribe whose heart turns away this day from Yahweh our God, to go to serve the gods of those nations; lest there should be among you a root that produces bitter poison;
echoes.note: Peter's diagnosis that Simon is 'in the gall of bitterness' draws directly on the Deuteronomic warning against the apostate heart that is 'a root that beareth gall and wormwood.' Volume is high (the distinctive 'gall'/bitterness collocation), thematic coherence is exact (a covenant member whose heart turns from God), giving a strong verbal allusion.

echoes.text: “Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to release the bonds of wickedness, to undo the bands of the yoke, and to let the oppressed go free, and that you break every yoke?
echoes.note: Peter says Simon is in the 'bondage of iniquity'—literally a 'bond' or 'chain'—echoing Isaiah's call to 'loose the bands of wickedness' and undo every yoke. Volume is moderate (the bond-of-wickedness phrase), and thematic coherence is strong: sin as binding fetters from which one must repent. The correspondence is verbal-conceptual.

echoes.text: For their heart was not right with him, neither were they faithful in his covenant.
echoes.note: Peter's verdict that Simon's 'heart isn't right before God' resonates with the Psalm's indictment that Israel's 'heart was not right with him.' The 'heart not right' idiom is distinctive enough to register; recurrence of the motif across the Psalter is broad, lowering specificity. Volume is moderate, coherence high.

echoes.text: You shall rejoice before Yahweh your God, you, and your sons, your daughters, your male servants, your female servants, and the Levite who is within your gates, because he has no portion nor inheritance with you.
echoes.note: Simon has 'neither part nor lot in this matter,' echoing the inheritance language denying the outsider a 'part nor inheritance' among the covenant people. The 'part nor lot/inheritance' formula recurs widely (cf. the Levites' portion), giving thematic recurrence; here it pronounces exclusion for one whose heart is corrupt.

echoes.text: He has filled me with bitterness, he has sated me with wormwood.
echoes.note: The 'gall of bitterness' image may also draw on Lamentations' '(he) hath filled me with bitterness, he hath made me drunken with wormwood,' reinforcing the gall-and-wormwood pairing behind Peter's words. Listed as a secondary witness to the same idiom; verbal volume overlaps with the primary Deuteronomy allusion.

pericopes.text: They therefore, when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, and preached the Good News to many villages of the Samaritans. But an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, “Arise, and go toward the south to the way that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. This is a desert.” He arose and went; and behold, there was a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasure, who had come to Jerusalem to worship. He was returning and sitting in his chariot, and was reading the prophet Isaiah. The Spirit said to Philip, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot.” Philip ran to him, and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said, “Do you understand what you are reading?” He said, “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?” He begged Philip to come up and sit with him.

echoes.text: Neither let the foreigner, who has joined himself to Yahweh, speak, saying, “Yahweh will surely separate me from his people”; neither let the eunuch say, “Behold, I am a dry tree.” For thus says Yahweh, “To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, and choose the things that please me, and hold fast my covenant: to them I will give in my house and within my walls a memorial and a name better than of sons and of daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, […]
echoes.note: The Ethiopian 'eunuch' brought into the people of God figurally fulfills Isaiah's promise that the eunuch who keeps covenant will be given 'a name better than of sons and of daughters' within God's house. The correspondence is typological with strong thematic coherence (an excluded class welcomed); fittingly, the eunuch is reading the very scroll of Isaiah. Verbal volume is low, but the structural irony is pointed and the placement makes the allusion deliberate.

echoes.text: He who is emasculated by crushing or cutting shall not enter into Yahweh’s assembly.
echoes.note: The eunuch's prior exclusion is defined by the Torah's ruling that one 'wounded in the stones' shall not 'enter into the congregation of the LORD.' Luke's account quietly overturns this barrier; the coherence is high as the legal foil against which the eunuch's incorporation is read. No verbal borrowing, so the link is typological/figural.

echoes.text: Princes shall come out of Egypt. Ethiopia shall hurry to stretch out her hands to God.
echoes.note: An Ethiopian official coming to worship and returning home a believer answers the psalm's vision that 'Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God.' Thematic coherence is strong (Ethiopia turning to the true God) and the motif recurs in prophetic universalism; verbal volume is modest, making this a probable thematic allusion.

echoes.text: From beyond the rivers of Cush, my worshipers, even the daughter of my dispersed people, will bring my offering.
echoes.note: The eunuch as a worshiper coming 'from beyond the rivers of Ethiopia' to bring offering echoes Zephaniah's promise that 'from beyond the rivers of Ethiopia my suppliants... shall bring mine offering.' Recurrence with Psalm 68 strengthens the Ethiopia-to-Zion theme; volume is faint and the link is conceptual.

echoes.text: When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning Yahweh’s name, she came to prove him with hard questions. She came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels that bore spices, and very much gold, and precious stones; and when she had come to Solomon, she talked with him of all that was in her heart.
echoes.note: A high official of a southern queen ('Candace, queen of the Ethiopians,' steward of her treasure) journeying toward Jerusalem loosely recalls the Queen of Sheba's pilgrimage with her treasures to hear wisdom. Thematic coherence (foreign royalty seeking the God of Israel) is moderate; correspondence is associative, not verbal.

pericopes.text: Now the passage of the Scripture which he was reading was this, “He was led as a sheep to the slaughter. As a lamb before his shearer is silent, so he doesn’t open his mouth. In his humiliation, his judgment was taken away. Who will declare His generation? For his life is taken from the earth.” The eunuch answered Philip, “Who is the prophet talking about? About himself, or about someone else?” Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him Jesus.

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth. He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people?
echoes.note: The scroll the eunuch reads is quoted verbatim from the Septuagint of the Suffering Servant: 'He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; as a lamb before his shearer is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away...' Volume is maximal (sustained, explicit citation), and Philip's exposition makes the christological coherence the hinge of the pericope. This is the chapter's flagship quotation.

pericopes.text: As they went on the way, they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “Behold, here is water. What is keeping me from being baptized?” He commanded the chariot to stand still, and they both went down into the water, both Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the eunuch didn’t see him any more, for he went on his way rejoicing. But Philip was found at Azotus. Passing through, he preached the Good News to all the cities, until he came to Caesarea.

echoes.text: It will happen, as soon as I am gone from you, that the Spirit of Yahweh will carry you I don’t know where; and so when I come and tell Ahab, and he can’t find you, he will kill me. But I, your servant, have feared Yahweh from my youth.
echoes.note: After the baptism 'the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away,' echoing the Elijah tradition in which 'the Spirit of the LORD shall carry thee whither I know not.' Volume is strong on the distinctive 'Spirit of the LORD carrying off' a prophet, recurrence within the Elijah/Elisha cycle is notable, and thematic coherence (a Spirit-driven prophetic figure transported) is high.

echoes.text: They said to him, “See now, there are with your servants fifty strong men. Please let them go and seek your master. Perhaps the Spirit of Yahweh has taken him up, and put him on some mountain, or into some valley. He said, “You shall not send them.”
echoes.note: Philip's sudden removal also recalls the sons of the prophets' fear that 'the Spirit of the LORD hath taken up [Elijah], and cast him upon some mountain.' Reinforces the Elijah-typology behind Philip's translation; volume and coherence parallel the 1 Kings 18 link, the two together making the prophetic-rapture allusion firm.

echoes.text: Then the Spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me the voice of a great rushing, saying, Blessed be Yahweh’s glory from his place. I heard the noise of the wings of the living creatures as they touched one another, and the noise of the wheels beside them, even the noise of a great rushing. So the Spirit lifted me up, and took me away; and I went in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit; and the hand of Yahweh was strong on me.
echoes.note: The Spirit 'lifting up' and bearing away the prophet matches Ezekiel's experience that 'the Spirit took me up, and... carried me away.' Recurrence of Spirit-transport language across the prophets strengthens the motif; verbal volume here is moderate, the link best classed as a supporting echo to the Elijah allusions.

pericopes.text: But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest, and asked for letters from him to the synagogues of Damascus, that if he found any who were of the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. As he traveled, he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him. He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” He said, “Who are you, Lord?” The Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. Butrise up, and enter into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” The men who traveled with him stood speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one. Saul arose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened, he saw no one. They led him by the hand, and brought him into Damascus. He was without sight for three days, and neither ate nor drank.

echoes.text: I, Daniel, alone saw the vision; for the men who were with me didn’t see the vision; but a great quaking fell on them, and they fled to hide themselves. So I was left alone, and saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me; for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength. Yet heard I the voice of his words; and when I heard the voice of his words, then was I fallen into a deep sleep on my face, with my face […]
echoes.note: Daniel alone perceives the vision while the men with him do not see it but flee in terror; he then falls to the ground. Acts 9:7's companions 'stood speechless, hearing the sound but seeing no one' is the same selective-perception convention attached to an overwhelming theophany, with the seer prostrate. Volume and thematic coherence are strong; the divergence (companions hear vs. do not see) is exactly the kind of variation Luke replays in his retellings (cf. ch. 22, 26).

echoes.text: As the appearance of the rainbow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of Yahweh’s glory. When I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard a voice of one that spoke.
echoes.note: The appearance of the glory of the LORD as radiant brightness causes Ezekiel to fall on his face and hear a voice speaking. Saul's 'light from the sky,' falling to the earth, and a speaking voice replays the Kavod-theophany sequence. High thematic coherence with the prophetic call pattern; verbal volume is moderate (light/glory, fell, voice).

echoes.text: He said to me, Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you. The Spirit entered into me when he spoke to me, and set me on my feet; and I heard him who spoke to me. He said to me, Son of man, I send you to the children of Israel, to a nation of rebels who have rebelled against me. They and their fathers have transgressed against me even to this very day.
echoes.note: After Ezekiel falls, the voice commands 'Son of man, stand on your feet... I send you to the people.' Saul is told to 'rise up, and enter into the city,' the same fall-then-rise-and-go commissioning rhythm. Coherence with the immediately following sending to the nations is strong; verbal borrowing modest.

echoes.text: When Yahweh saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the midst of the bush, and said, “Moses! Moses!” He said, “Here I am.”
echoes.note: 'Moses, Moses' — the doubled-vocative call from a blazing divine manifestation, answered before commission. 'Saul, Saul' matches the convention. Recurrence is strong across the OT call type-scenes (Gen 22:11; 46:2; 1 Sam 3:10), which strengthens rather than dilutes the echo.

echoes.text: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!” The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was […]
echoes.note: The throne-vision call of Isaiah — overwhelmed prophet confronted by divine glory, then sent — is the archetype Luke draws Saul's commissioning into. Little verbal overlap, but the type-scene logic (theophany → unworthiness → sending) is the figural frame; coherence high, volume low.

echoes.text: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
echoes.note: Jeremiah is appointed 'a prophet to the nations' before birth; the Damascus call culminates (v.15) in Saul as the chosen vessel 'before the nations.' The conversion proper carries this only faintly; the nations-prophet resonance lands more in vv.10-19. Low volume here.

echoes.text: When the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on Abram. Now terror and great darkness fell on him.
echoes.note: A dread/darkness falls upon Abram at a covenant theophany; Saul is plunged into three days of darkness. Faint, contested — the motif of incapacitating darkness accompanying divine encounter, but no verbal contact.

pericopes.text: Now there was a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias!” He said, “Behold, it’s me, Lord.” The Lord said to him, “Arise, and go to the street which is called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judahfor one named Saul, a man of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying, and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias coming in, and laying his hands on him, that he might receive his sight.” But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem. Here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.” But the Lord said to him, “Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel. For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.” Ananias departed, and entered into the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me, that you may receive your sight, and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized. He took food and was strengthened. Saul stayed several days with the disciples who were at Damascus.

echoes.text: Yahweh called Samuel; and he said, “Here I am.” He ran to Eli, and said, “Here I am; for you called me.” He said, “I didn’t call; lie down again.” He went and lay down. Yahweh called yet again, “Samuel!” Samuel arose and went to Eli, and said, “Here I am; for you called me.” He answered, “I didn’t call, my son; lie down again.” Now Samuel didn’t yet know Yahweh, neither was Yahweh’s word yet revealed to him. Yahweh called Samuel again the third time. He […]
echoes.note: The LORD calls 'Ananias!' in a vision and he answers 'Behold, it's me, Lord' — the Samuel night-call type-scene, where the named summons is met with hinneni ('Here I am'). High coherence with the prophetic-vision call form; the responsive formula is the load-bearing parallel.

echoes.text: Listen, islands, to me; and listen, you peoples, from far: Yahweh has called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother has he made mention of my name: and he has made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand, he has hidden me: and he has made me a polished shaft; in his quiver has he kept me close: and he said to me, “You are my servant; Israel, in whom I will be glorified.” But I said, “I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength […]
echoes.note: The Servant is named from the womb to be 'a light to the nations,' and kings shall see (49:7). The Lord's word that Saul is 'my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel' fuses the Servant's mission to nations + kings + Israel. Strong thematic coherence; Luke is casting Saul in the Isaianic Servant role.

echoes.text: and took hold of his father. He rubbed the gall on his father’s eyes, saying, “Cheer up, my father.” When his eyes began to hurt, he rubbed them. Then the white films scaled away from the corners of his eyes; and he saw his son, and fell upon his neck.
echoes.note: Tobit's blindness is healed when the white films/scales peel from the corners of his eyes and he recovers his sight. 'Something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight' is strikingly close in image and vocabulary (the scaling-off of a film). Deuterocanonical; high volume on the distinctive scales-from-eyes motif.

echoes.text: Elisha prayed, and said, “Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.” Yahweh opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha. When they came down to him, Elisha prayed to Yahweh, and said, “Please strike this people with blindness.” He struck them with blindness according to the word of Elisha. Elisha said to them, “This is not the way, neither is this the city. Follow me, […]
echoes.note: Elisha prays and the LORD strikes the Aramean army with blindness, leads them into Damascus, then prays again that their eyes be opened and they see. Saul is struck blind, led by the hand into Damascus, and his eyes opened there. The Damascus setting plus blinding/opening-of-eyes makes this more than coincidental; medium for moderate verbal contact.

echoes.text: Then I said, “Ah, Lord Yahweh! Behold, I don’t know how to speak; for I am a child.” But Yahweh said to me, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for to whoever I shall send you, you shall go, and whatever I shall command you, you shall speak. Don’t be afraid because of them; for I am with you to deliver you,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Ananias's hesitant objection ('Lord, I have heard... how much evil he did') and the Lord's overriding 'Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel' replays the prophetic objection-and-reassurance pattern (Jer 1:6 'Ah, Lord'; cf. Exod 3:11; 4:1). Coherence high with the call form; verbal volume modest.

echoes.text: The word which came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, saying, Arise, and go down to the potter’s house, and there I will cause you to hear my words. Then I went down to the potter’s house, and behold, he was making a work on the wheels. When the vessel that he made of the clay was marred in the hand of the potter, he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it. Then Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, House of Israel, can’t I do with you as […]
echoes.note: The 'chosen vessel' image may draw on the potter-and-clay vessel that God refashions to his purpose. Faint and contested — Luke's skeuos eklogēs evokes the vessel-of-election idea but without verbal anchoring to the potter oracle specifically.

pericopes.text: Immediately in the synagogues he proclaimed the Christ, that he is the Son of God. All who heard him were amazed, and said, “Isn’t this he who in Jerusalem made havoc of those who called on this name? And he had come here intending to bring them bound before the chief priests!” But Saul increased more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived at Damascus, proving that this is the Christ. When many days were fulfilled, the Jews conspired together to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They watched the gates both day and night that they might kill him, but his disciples took him by night, and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket.

echoes.text: So Michal let David down through the window. He went, fled, and escaped.
echoes.note: Those plotting to kill watch the gates day and night, but Saul's disciples 'let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket' by night — exactly as Michal lets David down through a window so he can escape the men watching the house to kill him. The conjunction of murderous watch + nocturnal lowering-down escape is the strongest single parallel.

echoes.text: Then she let them down by a cord through the window; for her house was on the side of the wall, and she lived on the wall.
echoes.note: Rahab lets the spies down by a rope through her window because her house was built into the city wall. 'Let him down through the wall' matches the lowering-through-the-wall escape motif precisely; high volume on the wall + lowering imagery.

echoes.text: Deliver me from my enemies, my God. Set me on high from those who rise up against me. Deliver me from the workers of iniquity. Save me from the bloodthirsty men. For, behold, they lie in wait for my soul. The mighty gather themselves together against me, not for my disobedience, nor for my sin, Yahweh.
echoes.note: The psalm (titled to David's escape while enemies 'watched the house to kill him') pleads for deliverance from those who lie in wait. The 'watched the gates day and night to kill him' language resonates with the persecuted-righteous-one motif. Low volume, contested.

pericopes.text: When Saul had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him, and brought him to the apostles, and declared to them how he had seen the Lord on the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. He was with them entering into Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus. He spoke and disputed against the Hellenists, but they were seeking to kill him. When the brothers knew it, they brought him down to Caesarea, and sent him off to Tarsus. So the assemblies throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace, and were built up. They were multiplied, walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit.

echoes.text: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.
echoes.note: The summary that the churches were 'walking in the fear of the Lord' and were built up draws on the wisdom idiom of life ordered by the fear of the LORD. Diffuse stock biblical phrase; low volume, no single source.

pericopes.text: As Peter went throughout all those parts, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a certain man named Aeneas, who had been bedridden for eight years, because he was paralyzed. Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed!” Immediately he arose. All who lived at Lydda and in Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.

echoes.text: Now therefore thus says Yahweh, “You shall not come down from the bed where you have gone up, but shall surely die.”’” Elijah departed.
echoes.note: Peter's command to the bedridden Aeneas, 'Get up and make your bed,' reverses the prophetic word that one will not 'come down from the bed' to which he has gone up. Faint thematic inversion of the bed-of-affliction motif from the Elijah cycle; low and contested.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: The healing of the paralytic so that he immediately rises belongs to the prophetic vision of the lame leaping when God restores his people; 'all who lived at Lydda... turned to the Lord' fits the restoration-and-return frame. Low volume, no verbal borrowing.

pericopes.text: Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which when translated, means Dorcas. This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did. In those days, she fell sick, and died. When they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. As Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, imploring him not to delay in coming to them. Peter got up and went with them. When he had come, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood by him weeping, and showing the coats and garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them. Peter sent them all out, and knelt down and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up!” She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up. He gave her his hand, and raised her up. Calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. He stayed many days in Joppa with one Simon, a tanner.

echoes.text: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]
echoes.note: Elisha enters the room where the dead child lies, puts everyone out, prays, and the child opens her/his eyes. 'Peter sent them all out, and knelt down and prayed... he said, Tabitha, get up! She opened her eyes' matches the sequence point-for-point: privacy, prayer, command, the opening of the eyes. Highest-volume parallel in the pericope.

echoes.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]
echoes.note: Elijah raises the widow's son, who is laid in the upper room (loft) where the prophet prays; the result is faith ('now I know'). Tabitha is laid in an upper room, surrounded by widows, raised through Peter's prayer, and 'many believed.' Strong coherence: upper room + widow context + prayer + resurrection + resulting belief.

echoes.text: It fell on a day, that Elisha passed to Shunem, where there was a prominent woman; and she persuaded him to eat bread. So it was, that as often as he passed by, he turned in there to eat bread. She said to her husband, “See now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God, that passes by us continually. Please let us make a little room on the wall. Let us set for him there a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp stand. It shall be, when he comes to us, that he […]
echoes.note: Beyond the resuscitation itself, the Shunammite cycle frames the dead one laid in a prepared upper chamber and messengers sent urgently to fetch the man of God ('do not slacken your riding'); Joppa's disciples 'sent two men... imploring him not to delay.' The send-for-the-prophet-without-delay motif reinforces the Elisha typology.

pericopes.text: Now there was a certain man in Caesarea, Cornelius by name, a centurion of what was called the Italian Regiment, a devout man, and one who feared God with all his house, who gave gifts for the needy generously to the people, and always prayed to God. At about the ninth hour of the day, he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God coming to him, and saying to him, “Cornelius!” He, fastening his eyes on him, and being frightened, said, “What is it, Lord?” He said to him, “Your prayers and your gifts to the needy have gone up for a memorial before God. Now send men to Joppa, and get Simon, who is also called Peter. He lodges with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the seaside. When the angel who spoke to him had departed, Cornelius called two of his household servants and a devout soldier of those who waited on him continually. Having explained everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.

echoes.text: And now, when you prayed, and Sarah your daughter-in-law, I brought the memorial of your prayer before the Holy One. When you buried the dead, I was with you likewise.
echoes.note: Cornelius's prayers and alms 'have gone up for a memorial before God' closely matches Raphael's words that he presented Tobit's and Sarah's prayers as a memorial before the Holy One. Volume is strong (the technical idea of an angel presenting a God-fearer's prayers/alms as a 'memorial' before God) and the satisfaction is high, since Cornelius is precisely the pious almsgiver Tobit holds up as model.

echoes.text: He shall bring it to Aaron’s sons, the priests; and he shall take his handful of its fine flour, and of its oil, with all its frankincense; and the priest shall burn its memorial on the altar, an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to Yahweh.
echoes.note: The 'memorial' (azkarah) language — the portion of the offering that ascends as a pleasing memorial 'before the LORD' — supplies the cultic background for prayers and alms 'going up for a memorial before God,' reframing Cornelius's piety as an acceptable sacrifice. Thematic coherence is high; verbal volume moderate.

echoes.text: The offering of the righteous makes the altar fat; And the sweet savor thereof is before the Most High. The sacrifice of a righteous man is acceptable; And the memorial thereof shall not be forgotten. Glorify the Lord with a good eye, And stint not the first fruits of your hands. In every gift show a cheerful countenance, And dedicate your tithe with gladness.
echoes.note: Ben Sira teaches that the offering of the righteous and the gift of alms ascend and are remembered before the Most High; the same sapiential link between generous almsgiving and acceptance/memory before God informs the portrait of Cornelius. Plausible given the Septuagintal-Jewish piety setting.

echoes.text: Let my prayer be set before you like incense; the lifting up of my hands like the evening sacrifice.
echoes.note: Cornelius prays at the ninth hour (the hour of the evening sacrifice); the psalm's 'let my prayer be set forth as incense, the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice' frames prayer ascending at the sacrificial hour, coherent with prayers that 'have gone up' before God.

echoes.text: While I was speaking, and praying, and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my supplication before Yahweh my God for the holy mountain of my God; yes, while I was speaking in prayer, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me about the time of the evening offering.
echoes.note: Daniel prays and an angel (Gabriel) comes to him 'at the time of the evening offering'; Cornelius prays at the ninth hour and an angel of God appears. The pattern of angelic visitation at the hour of prayer/sacrifice is figurally echoed.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s angel called to him out of the sky, and said, “Abraham, Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.”
echoes.note: The angel addressing 'Cornelius!' and his fearful 'What is it, Lord?' faintly echoes the OT pattern of God/angel calling a name and the human responding (Abraham, Samuel). Low volume; offered maximally.

echoes.text: He has dispersed, he has given to the poor. His righteousness endures forever. His horn will be exalted with honor.
echoes.note: The God-fearer who 'has given to the poor' whose righteousness endures matches the devout, alms-giving, God-fearing Cornelius. Thematic only, no verbal borrowing.

pericopes.text: Now on the next day as they were on their journey, and got close to the city, Peter went up on the housetop to pray at about noon. He became hungry and desired to eat, but while they were preparing, he fell into a trance. He saw heaven opened and a certain container descending to him, like a great sheet let down by four corners on the earth, in which were all kinds of four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, reptiles, and birds of the sky. A voice came to him, “Rise, Peter, kill and eat!” But Peter said, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.” A voice came to him again the second time, “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.” This was done three times, and immediately the vessel was received up into heaven.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them, “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘These are the living things which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the animals, that you may eat. “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is […]
echoes.note: The sheet contains 'all kinds of four-footed animals, wild animals, reptiles, and birds' — exactly the taxonomic categories of Leviticus 11's clean/unclean legislation — and Peter's refusal ('common or unclean') invokes its core distinction. The command 'kill and eat' and the verdict 'what God has cleansed' directly engage and overturn this law. Volume, recurrence, and coherence all high.

echoes.text: You shall not eat any abominable thing. These are the animals which you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat, the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the chamois. Every animal that parts the hoof, and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, that may you eat. Nevertheless these you shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of those who have the hoof cloven: the camel, the hare, and the […]
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic restatement of the food laws (clean/unclean beasts, birds, swarming things; 'you shall not eat any abomination') is the parallel legislative source for Peter's scruple about eating the unclean. High coherence; included alongside Leviticus 11 as the second pillar of the dietary code.

echoes.text: Then I said, Ah Lord Yahweh! behold, my soul has not been polluted; for from my youth up even until now have I not eaten of that which dies of itself, or is torn of animals; neither came there abominable flesh into my mouth.
echoes.note: Peter's 'Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean' verbally mirrors Ezekiel's protest 'I have never defiled myself... neither has anything abominable/unclean come into my mouth.' Distinctive shared form (prophet's emphatic refusal of unclean food to a divine command). High volume.

echoes.text: Of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ship, to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female. Of the birds after their kind, of the livestock after their kind, of every creeping thing of the ground after its kind, two of every sort will come to you, to keep them alive.
echoes.note: The gathering of every kind of beast, creeping thing, and bird (the ark inventory by 'kinds') is faintly echoed in the sheet's comprehensive menagerie 'of the earth' descending from heaven. Figural, low volume.

echoes.text: God said, “Let the earth produce living creatures after their kind, livestock, creeping things, and animals of the earth after their kind”; and it was so. God made the animals of the earth after their kind, and the livestock after their kind, and everything that creeps on the ground after its kind. God saw that it was good. God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds […]
echoes.note: The creation categories — beasts, creeping things, birds — underlie the threefold listing in the vision; the divine pronouncement that all is now clean recalls the original 'very good' creation. Thematic/figural only.

pericopes.text: Now while Peter was very perplexed in himself what the vision which he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood before the gate, and called and asked whether Simon, who was also called Peter, was lodging there. While Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men seek you. But arise, get down, and go with them, doubting nothing; for I have sent them.” Peter went down to the men, and said, “Behold, I am he whom you seek. Why have you come?” They said, “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man and one who fears God, and well spoken of by all the nation of the Jews, was directed by a holy angel to invite you to his house, and to listen to what you say.” So he called them in and lodged them. On the next day Peter arose and went out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.

echoes.text: Then the Spirit entered into me, and set me on my feet; and he spoke with me, and said to me, Go, shut yourself inside your house.
echoes.note: The Spirit speaking to Peter and directing him to 'arise, get down, and go... for I have sent them' faintly parallels the prophetic pattern of the Spirit entering and commanding the prophet to go. Low volume; no distinctive wording.

pericopes.text: On the next day they entered into Caesarea. Cornelius was waiting for them, having called together his relatives and his near friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius met him, fell down at his feet, and worshiped him. But Peter raised him up, saying, “Stand up! I myself am also a man.” As he talked with him, he went in and found many gathered together. He said to them, “You yourselves know how it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation, but God has shown me that I shouldn’t call any man unholy or unclean. Therefore also I came without complaint when I was sent for. I ask therefore, why did you send for me?” Cornelius said, “Four days ago, I was fasting until this hour, and at the ninth hour, I prayed in my house, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing, and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer is heard, and your gifts to the needy are remembered in the sight of God. Send therefore to Joppa, and summon Simon, who is also called Peter. He lodges in the house of Simon a tanner, by the seaside. When he comes, he will speak to you.’ Therefore I sent to you at once, and it was good of you to come. Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God to hear all things that have been commanded you by God.”

echoes.text: I lifted up my eyes, and looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen, whose thighs were adorned with pure gold of Uphaz: his body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as flaming torches, and his arms and his feet like burnished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.
echoes.note: Cornelius recounts that during his fast at the ninth hour 'a man stood before me in bright clothing' — the angelophany described as a man in dazzling/bright garments matches Daniel's vision of a man clothed in shining apparel appearing during a period of fasting and prayer. Coherent verbal and situational overlap.

echoes.text: And they were both troubled, and fell upon their faces; for they were afraid. And he said to them, “Don’t be afraid. You will all have peace; but bless God forever. For I came not of any favor of my own, but by the will of your God. Therefore bless him forever. All these days I appeared to you. I didn’t eat or drink, but you all saw a vision. Now give God thanks, because I ascend to him that sent me. Write in a book all the things which have been done.” […]
echoes.note: Cornelius falls at Peter's feet to worship and Peter raises him: 'Stand up! I myself am also a man' — the refusal-of-veneration scene echoes Raphael's correction of Tobit and Tobias, redirecting worship from the messenger to God. Here transposed to a human apostle. Thematic coherence high.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them, “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘These are the living things which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the animals, that you may eat. “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is […]
echoes.note: Peter's 'it is unlawful for a Jew to associate with one of another nation, but God has shown me not to call any man unholy or unclean' transfers the clean/unclean categories of the dietary law (and its boundary-keeping function) to persons; recurrence of the Levitical theme from 10:9-16 within the chapter.

echoes.text: I set my face to the Lord God, to seek by prayer and petitions, with fasting and sackcloth and ashes.
echoes.note: Cornelius's 'I was fasting until this hour, and at the ninth hour I prayed' echoes Daniel's seeking God 'by prayer and supplications, with fasting' as the disposition that precedes angelic revelation. Faint.

pericopes.text: Peter opened his mouth and said, “Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism; but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him. The word which he sent to the children of Israel, preaching good news of peace by Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all— you yourselves know what happened, which was proclaimed throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached; even Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. We are witnesses of everything he did both in the country of the Jews, and in Jerusalem; whom they also killed, hanging him on a tree. God raised him up the third day, and gave him to be revealed, not to all the people, but to witnesses who were chosen before by God, to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that this is he who is appointed by God as the Judge of the living and the dead. All the prophets testify about him, that through his name everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins.”

echoes.text: For Yahweh your God, he is God of gods, and Lord of lords, the great God, the mighty, and the awesome, who doesn’t respect persons, nor takes reward.
echoes.note: 'God doesn't show favoritism' (ou prosopolemptes) directly restates the Deuteronomic confession that God 'regards not persons (does not lift the face) nor takes a bribe.' Distinctive theological formula; the basis for the whole Gentile-inclusion argument. High volume and coherence.

echoes.text: Now therefore let the fear of Yahweh be on you. Take heed and do it: for there is no iniquity with Yahweh our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of bribes.”
echoes.note: Jehoshaphat's charge that 'with the LORD our God there is no iniquity, nor respect of persons, nor taking of gifts' is a second locus of the 'no partiality' formula informing v34. Recurrence strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: 'Preaching good news of peace' (euangelizomenos eirenen) reproduces the herald who 'publishes peace, brings good tidings' on the mountains. The gospel-of-peace formula in v36 is drawn from this servant-song herald text. High volume.

echoes.text: I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him who is far off and to him who is near,” says Yahweh; “and I will heal them.”
echoes.note: 'Peace, peace, to him that is far off, and to him that is near' undergirds the proclamation of peace now extended to the far-off Gentiles in Cornelius's house; coherent with the chapter's inclusion theme.

echoes.text: Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace! Keep your feasts, Judah! Perform your vows, for the wicked one will no more pass through you. He is utterly cut off.
echoes.note: 'Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that brings good tidings, that publishes peace' is a parallel herald-of-peace text reinforcing the Isaianic background of v36.

echoes.text: He sends his word, and heals them, and delivers them from their graves.
echoes.note: 'The word which he sent to the children of Israel' faintly echoes 'he sent his word and healed them,' apt given the immediate reference to Jesus 'healing all who were oppressed.' Low volume.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
echoes.note: 'God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good' reflects 'the Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me' to bring good news and release. The Spirit-anointing summary of Jesus' ministry draws on this servant text. High coherence.

echoes.text: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.
echoes.note: 'My chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him' supports v38's portrait of the Spirit-endowed servant and v41's 'witnesses chosen before by God.' Thematic coherence high; verbal moderate.

echoes.text: If a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree; his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall surely bury him the same day; for he who is hanged is accursed of God; that you don’t defile your land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance.
echoes.note: 'Whom they also killed, hanging him on a tree' (kremasantes epi xylou) deliberately invokes the law that a man 'hanged on a tree' is accursed of God and must be taken down. The xylon language is the distinctive Deuteronomic marker. High volume.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'God raised him up the third day' resonates with 'on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him.' A recurrent NT third-day intertext; figural/typological with moderate verbal touch.

echoes.text: Be it far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked. May that be far from you. Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?”
echoes.note: Jesus 'appointed by God as the Judge of the living and the dead' echoes the title 'Judge of all the earth.' Thematic.

echoes.text: Let them sing before Yahweh, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity.
echoes.note: 'He comes to judge the earth... the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity' undergirds the designation of the risen one as eschatological Judge in v42.

echoes.text: and they shall teach no more every man his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, Know Yahweh; for they shall all know me, from their least to their greatest, says Yahweh: for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin will I remember no more.
echoes.note: 'Everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins' to which 'all the prophets testify' echoes the new-covenant promise 'I will forgive their iniquity, and remember their sin no more,' the prophetic witness to forgiveness Peter invokes. Coherent.

echoes.text: The inhabitant won’t say, “I am sick.” The people who dwell therein will be forgiven their iniquity.
echoes.note: 'The people that dwell therein shall be forgiven their iniquity' is among the prophetic texts of forgiveness that 'all the prophets testify' to in v43. Faint, offered maximally.

pericopes.text: While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all those who heard the word. They of the circumcision who believed were amazed, as many as came with Peter, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the Gentiles. For they heard them speaking in other languages and magnifying God. Then Peter answered, “Can anyone forbid these people from being baptized with water? They have received the Holy Spirit just like us.” He commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay some days.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: 'The gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the Gentiles' fulfills 'I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh' — the same Joel oracle already cited at Pentecost (recurrence within Acts), now extended to 'all flesh' inclusive of Gentiles. High coherence; the pouring-out language is distinctive.

echoes.text: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring:
echoes.note: 'I will pour my Spirit upon your seed' provides a parallel outpouring-of-the-Spirit promise reinforcing the Joel intertext behind v45. Moderate verbal overlap.

echoes.text: neither will I hide my face any more from them; for I have poured out my Spirit on the house of Israel, says the Lord Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'I have poured out my Spirit upon the house of Israel' is a further prophetic pour-out text in the background of the Spirit falling on the hearers. Faint.

echoes.text: Until the Spirit is poured on us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is considered a forest.
echoes.note: 'Until the Spirit be poured upon us from on high' contributes to the prophetic expectation of the Spirit's outpouring realized here on the Gentiles.

echoes.text: The whole earth was of one language and of one speech. As they traveled east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they lived there. They said one to another, “Come, let’s make bricks, and burn them thoroughly.” They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar. They said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make ourselves a name, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole […]
echoes.note: The Gentiles 'speaking in other languages and magnifying God' figurally reverses Babel's scattering of tongues, with diverse speech now uniting in praise. Typological, no verbal borrowing.

pericopes.text: Now the apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles had also received the word of God. When Peter had come up to Jerusalem, those who were of the circumcision contended with him, saying, “You went in to uncircumcised men, and ate with them!” But Peter began, and explained to them in order, saying, “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: a certain container descending, like it was a great sheet let down from heaven by four corners. It came as far as me. When I had looked intently at it, I considered, and saw the four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, creeping things, and birds of the sky. I also heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter, kill and eat!’ But I said, ‘Not so, Lord, for nothing unholy or unclean has ever entered into my mouth.’ But a voice answered me the second time out of heaven, ‘What God has cleansed, don’t you call unclean.’ This was done three times, and all were drawn up again into heaven. Behold, immediately three men stood before the house where I was, having been sent from Caesarea to me. The Spirit told me to go with them, without discriminating. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered into the man’s house. He told us how he had seen the angel standing in his house, and saying to him, ‘Send to Joppa, and get Simon, who is called Peter, who will speak to you words by which you will be saved, you and all your house.’ As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them, even as on us at the beginning. I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.’ If then God gave to them the same gift as us, when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I, that I could withstand God?” When they heard these things, they held their peace, and glorified God, saying, “Then God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life!”

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them, “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘These are the living things which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the animals, that you may eat. “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is […]
echoes.note: The vision's core conflict — a divine command to 'kill and eat' four-footed animals, creeping things, and birds, and Peter's refusal because 'nothing unholy or unclean has ever entered into my mouth' — directly engages the Levitical taxonomy of clean and unclean creatures. Volume is high (the whole pericope turns on these dietary categories); recurrence is strong (the sister account in Acts 10 and the parallel here); thematic coherence is high. The narrative reads the Levitical food law figurally, the abolition of the clean/unclean boundary dramatizing the inclusion of Gentiles.

echoes.text: You shall not eat any abominable thing. These are the animals which you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat, the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the chamois. Every animal that parts the hoof, and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, that may you eat. Nevertheless these you shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of those who have the hoof cloven: the camel, the hare, and the […]
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic restatement of the clean/unclean animal law stands behind Peter's scruple alongside Leviticus 11. Lower volume than Leviticus (no distinctive verbal pickup unique to Deuteronomy), but the same legal substrate the vision overturns.

echoes.text: Then I said, Ah Lord Yahweh! behold, my soul has not been polluted; for from my youth up even until now have I not eaten of that which dies of itself, or is torn of animals; neither came there abominable flesh into my mouth.
echoes.note: Peter's protest, 'Not so, Lord, for nothing unholy or unclean has ever entered into my mouth,' closely echoes Ezekiel's own protest at the command to eat defiling food: 'I have not eaten of that which dies of itself... neither came there abominable flesh into my mouth.' The verbal and situational parallel (prophet objecting to a divine eating-command on grounds of lifelong purity) is striking; this is a strong allusion, perhaps the model for Peter's words.

echoes.text: Of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ship, to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female. Of the birds after their kind, of the livestock after their kind, of every creeping thing of the ground after its kind, two of every sort will come to you, to keep them alive.
echoes.note: The vision's catalogue — 'four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, creeping things, and birds of the sky' — recalls the ordered creaturely classes gathered to the ark (beasts after their kind, creeping things, fowl). The taxonomic phrasing echoes the Genesis flood inventory of all flesh; thematic coherence is moderate (universal scope of living kinds), volume modest.

echoes.text: God said, “Let the earth produce living creatures after their kind, livestock, creeping things, and animals of the earth after their kind”; and it was so. God made the animals of the earth after their kind, and the livestock after their kind, and everything that creeps on the ground after its kind. God saw that it was good. God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds […]
echoes.note: The triad of earth-beasts, creeping things, and birds also recalls the creation account's enumeration of the living creatures over which humanity is given dominion. A faint echo: the categories are generic and shared with the flood narrative, so attribution to Genesis 1 specifically is weak.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: Peter's report that 'the Holy Spirit fell on them, even as on us at the beginning' frames Gentile Spirit-reception by the same Joel oracle invoked at Pentecost ('I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh'). The 'all flesh' universality of Joel undergirds the argument that the same gift is now given to Gentiles; medium volume, high thematic coherence with the chapter's inclusion theme.

echoes.text: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you. I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: The pairing of cleansing ('What God has cleansed, don't you call unclean') with the gift of the Spirit recalls Ezekiel's promise to sprinkle clean water and put a new Spirit within the people. A figural resonance — purification and Spirit-bestowal joined — rather than a verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: Neither let the foreigner, who has joined himself to Yahweh, speak, saying, “Yahweh will surely separate me from his people”; neither let the eunuch say, “Behold, I am a dry tree.” For thus says Yahweh, “To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, and choose the things that please me, and hold fast my covenant: to them I will give in my house and within my walls a memorial and a name better than of sons and of daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, […]
echoes.note: Jerusalem's verdict that 'God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life' coheres with Isaiah's vision of foreigners joined to the LORD and gathered to his house. A thematic echo of Gentile incorporation; no verbal link, so confidence is low.

pericopes.text: They therefore who were scattered abroad by the oppression that arose about Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except to Jews only. But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who, when they had come to Antioch, spoke to the Hellenists, preaching the Lord Jesus. The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord.

echoes.text: For on the first day of the first month began he to go up from Babylon; and on the first day of the fifth month came he to Jerusalem, according to the good hand of his God on him.
echoes.note: 'The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed' takes up the recurrent Hebrew idiom of the LORD's hand being upon a person for blessing and success, prominent in Ezra ('the good hand of his God upon him'). Recurrence of this idiom across the OT is high (Ezra 7:6, 7:28, 8:18); thematic coherence (divine empowerment of mission) is strong; volume moderate.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on Elijah; and he tucked his cloak into his belt and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.
echoes.note: 'The hand of the LORD was on Elijah' is another instance of the same idiom of divine enablement. A faint echo contributing to the recurrence of the 'hand of the Lord' motif rather than a specific source.

pericopes.text: The report concerning them came to the ears of the assembly which was in Jerusalem. They sent out Barnabas to go as far as Antioch, who, when he had come, and had seen the grace of God, was glad. He exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they should remain near to the Lord. For he was a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith, and many people were added to the Lord. Barnabas went out to Tarsus to look for Saul. When he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they were gathered together with the assembly, and taught many people. The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.

echoes.text: You shall fear Yahweh your God; you shall serve him; and you shall cling to him, and you shall swear by his name.
echoes.note: Barnabas's exhortation 'that with purpose of heart they should remain near to (cleave to) the Lord' echoes the Deuteronomic and Joshuanic charge to 'cleave unto the LORD your God' with the whole heart. Thematic coherence high (covenant loyalty of heart); verbal resonance on cleaving/holding fast; moderate volume.

echoes.text: Only take diligent heed to do the commandment and the law which Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded you, to love Yahweh your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, to hold fast to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.”
echoes.note: Joshua's farewell command to love the LORD, walk in his ways, and 'cleave unto him' with all the heart and soul stands behind the same 'purpose of heart... remain near to the Lord' exhortation. Reinforces the recurrence of the OT cleaving-to-the-Lord formula.

echoes.text: You shall leave your name for a curse to my chosen; and the Lord Yahweh will kill you; and he will call his servants by another name:
echoes.note: 'The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch' may faintly resonate with Isaiah's promise that the LORD's servants 'shall be called by another name.' A contested, low-volume figural echo of the giving of a new name to God's people; no verbal borrowing.

pericopes.text: Now in these days, prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them named Agabus stood up, and indicated by the Spirit that there should be a great famine all over the world, which also happened in the days of Claudius. As any of the disciples had plenty, each determined to send relief to the brothers who lived in Judea; which they also did, sending it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.

echoes.text: The seven years of plenty, that were in the land of Egypt, came to an end. The seven years of famine began to come, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread. When all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread, and Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do.” The famine was over all the surface of the earth. Joseph opened all the store […]
echoes.note: Agabus's Spirit-given prediction of 'a great famine all over the world' and the disciples' decision to lay up relief beforehand follows the Joseph pattern: a famine 'over all the face of the earth,' foreknown by divine revelation, met by provident gathering and distribution of food. Thematic coherence is high (prophetic foreknowledge of famine answered by organized relief); the typological link of foresight-then-provision is the strongest of several prophet-and-famine resonances.

echoes.text: Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the foreigners of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.”
echoes.note: Agabus standing up to declare a coming famine follows the prophet-announces-famine type set by Elijah, who declares the drought and dearth before Ahab. Recurrence of the motif (prophet foretelling famine) is its main support; no verbal borrowing, so figural/echo rather than quotation.

echoes.text: Now Elisha had spoken to the woman, whose son he had restored to life, saying, “Arise, and go, you and your household, and stay for a while wherever you can; for Yahweh has called for a famine. It shall also come on the land seven years.”
echoes.note: Elisha's announcement of a coming famine 'upon the land seven years' is a further instance of the OT prophet-and-famine pattern that Agabus's prophecy continues. A low-volume contributor to recurrence.

echoes.text: Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life. For these two years the famine has been in the land, and there are yet five years, in which there will be neither plowing nor harvest. God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant in the earth, and to save you alive by a great deliverance. So now it wasn’t you who sent me here, but God, and he has made me a father to Pharaoh, lord […]
echoes.note: The sending of relief 'to the brothers who lived in Judea' by the hands of Barnabas and Saul faintly recalls Joseph's provision of food and life-preservation for his brothers during the famine. A figural echo of famine relief sent to one's brethren; modest thematic coherence, no verbal link.

pericopes.text: Now about that time, King Herod stretched out his hands to oppress some of the assembly. He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword. When he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter also. This was during the days of unleavened bread. When he had arrested him, he put him in prison, and delivered him to four squads of four soldiers each to guard him, intending to bring him out to the people after the Passover. Peter therefore was kept in the prison, but constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him.

echoes.text: This day shall be to you for a memorial, and you shall keep it a feast to Yahweh: throughout your generations you shall keep it a feast by an ordinance forever. “‘Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; even the first day you shall put away yeast out of your houses, for whoever eats leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel. In the first day there shall be to you a holy convocation, and in the […]
echoes.note: Luke explicitly times the arrest 'during the days of unleavened bread' and intends to bring Peter out 'after the Passover,' anchoring the whole episode in the Exodus 12 festival calendar. The verbal marker (azuma / pascha) is direct, and the placement is deliberate: the coming deliverance of Peter is staged against the festival commemorating Israel's deliverance.

echoes.text: Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who didn’t know Joseph. He said to his people, “Behold, the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we. Come, let us deal wisely with them, lest they multiply, and it happen that when any war breaks out, they also join themselves to our enemies, and fight against us, and escape out of the land.” Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with their burdens. They built storage cities […]
echoes.note: A hostile king 'stretching out his hand' against God's people, killing them, and seeking to suppress the growing community recalls Pharaoh's campaign against Israel. The figural pairing (tyrant vs. people on the eve of Passover) is reinforced by the chapter's later 'grew and multiplied' (cf. Exod 1:7). Thematic coherence is strong though verbal volume is low.

echoes.text: Your hand will find out all of your enemies. Your right hand will find out those who hate you.
echoes.note: 'Your hand will find out all your enemies' — the idiom of the royal hand reaching out to seize. Faint lexical resonance with 'stretched out his hands'; offered as a contested possibility for the persecuting-hand motif.

pericopes.text: The same night when Herod was about to bring him out, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains. Guards in front of the door kept the prison. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side, and woke him up, saying, “Stand up quickly!” His chains fell off from his hands. The angel said to him, “Get dressed and put on your sandals.” He did so. He said to him, “Put on your cloak, and follow me.” And he went out and followed him. He didn’t know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he saw a vision. When they were past the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate that leads into the city, which opened to them by itself. They went out, and went down one street, and immediately the angel departed from him. When Peter had come to himself, he said, “Now I truly know that the Lord has sent out his angel and delivered me out of the hand of Herod, and from everything the Jewish people were expecting.”
