echoes.text: This is how you shall eat it: with your belt on your waist, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste: it is Yahweh’s Passover.
echoes.note: The angel's commands — 'Get dressed and put on your sandals... Put on your cloak' — closely mirror the Passover instruction to eat 'with your waist girded, your sandals on your feet,' ready to depart in haste. Given the explicit Passover setting (12:3-4), the verbal volume and thematic coherence make this the keystone allusion: Peter's release is a re-enacted exodus.

echoes.text: Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron, because they rebelled against the words of God, and condemned the counsel of the Most High. Therefore he brought down their heart with labor. They fell down, and there was no one to help. Then they cried to Yahweh in their trouble, and he saved them out of their distresses. He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke away their chains. Let them […]
echoes.note: 'Such as sat in darkness... bound in affliction and iron... he brought them out of darkness, and broke their chains in pieces. He has broken the gates of bronze, and cut the bars of iron asunder.' Striking convergence with the dark cell, the chains falling off, and the iron gate opening. High thematic coherence and notable volume for the prison-deliverance imagery.

echoes.text: My God has sent his angel, and has shut the lions’ mouths, and they have not hurt me; because as before him innocence was found in me; and also before you, O king, have I done no hurt.
echoes.note: 'My God has sent his angel, and has shut the lions' mouths' parallels Peter's confession, 'the Lord has sent out his angel and delivered me.' Both feature a righteous man condemned by a king, divinely rescued by an angel overnight, with near-identical 'God sent his angel' formula. Recurrence of the angelic-deliverance type is strong.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s angel encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.
echoes.note: 'The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.' The pairing of 'angel of the Lord' with 'delivers' matches Peter's two-fold language exactly in theme. Moderate volume, high coherence with the rescue motif.

echoes.text: He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!” He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again. Yahweh’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.”
echoes.note: An angel rouses the sleeping prophet Elijah by touch — 'he touched him, and said, Arise' — paralleling the angel who 'struck Peter on the side, and woke him up, saying, Stand up quickly.' Shared scene-grammar of angelic touch-and-rouse; verbal volume modest.

echoes.text: Moses told his father-in-law all that Yahweh had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel’s sake, all the hardships that had come on them on the way, and how Yahweh delivered them. Jethro rejoiced for all the goodness which Yahweh had done to Israel, in that he had delivered them out of the hand of the Egyptians. Jethro said, “Blessed be Yahweh, who has delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians, and out of the hand of Pharaoh; who has […]
echoes.note: Jethro blesses the LORD who 'delivered you out of the hand of Pharaoh... out of the hand of the Egyptians.' Peter's 'delivered me out of the hand of Herod' reuses the classic exodus 'out of the hand of [the king]' deliverance idiom, reinforcing the Passover framing.

echoes.text: who executes justice for the oppressed; who gives food to the hungry. Yahweh frees the prisoners. Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind. Yahweh raises up those who are bowed down. Yahweh loves the righteous.
echoes.note: 'The LORD looses the prisoners... opens the eyes of the blind.' Part of the cluster of psalmic prisoner-release imagery (with Ps 107, 116) reinforcing the recurrence test for divine liberation of the bound.

echoes.text: Yahweh, truly I am your servant. I am your servant, the son of your handmaid. You have freed me from my chains.
echoes.note: 'You have loosed my bonds.' Faint echo within the prisoner-release cluster; low volume, offered maximally.

echoes.text: Yahweh went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them on their way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light, that they might go by day and by night:
echoes.note: The pillar of fire that 'gave them light' to go by night faintly anticipates the 'light shone in the cell' guiding Peter's nighttime departure — a light-by-night deliverance motif keyed to the exodus.

echoes.text: But when he was already present there with his guards near the treasury, the Soverign of spirits and of all authority caused a great apparition, so that all that had presumed to come in with him, stricken with dismay at the power of God, fainted and were sore afraid. For there was seen by them a horse with a terrible rider upon him, and adorned with beautiful trappings, and he rushed fiercely and struck at Heliodorus with his forefeet, and it seemed that […]
echoes.note: Angelic intervention against an intruder in the temple treasury exemplifies the deuterocanonical angelic-rescue/judgment type that frames Acts 12 as a whole; faint, offered for recurrence.

pericopes.text: Thinking about that, he came to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was called Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying. When Peter knocked at the door of the gate, a maid named Rhoda came to answer. When she recognized Peter’s voice, she didn’t open the gate for joy, but ran in, and reported that Peter was standing in front of the gate. They said to her, “You are crazy!” But she insisted that it was so. They said, “It is his angel.” But Peter continued knocking. When they had opened, they saw him, and were amazed. But he, beckoning to them with his hand to be silent, declared to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. He said, “Tell these things to James, and to the brothers.” Then he departed, and went to another place.

echoes.text: He went to seek a man, and found Raphael who was an angel; and he didn’t know it. He said to him, “Can I go with you to Rages of Media? Do you know those places well?” The angel said to him, “I will go with you. I know the way well. I have lodged with our brother Gabael.” Tobias said to him, “Wait for me, and I will tell my father.” He said to him, “Go, and don’t wait. And he went in and said to his father, “Behold, I have found someone who will go with […]
echoes.note: The community's reaction 'It is his angel' presupposes a Second-Temple guardian-angel belief whose narrative roots include Raphael accompanying Tobias. No verbal borrowing, but a conceptual background echo for the angel-as-double notion.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]
echoes.note: The motif of disbelief and laughter/incredulity at an unexpected, joyful announcement (Sarah at the door of the tent) faintly mirrors the gathered believers calling Rhoda 'crazy' and refusing to credit the good news. Very faint; offered maximally.

pericopes.text: Now as soon as it was day, there was no small stir among the soldiers about what had become of Peter. When Herod had sought for him, and didn’t find him, he examined the guards, and commanded that they should be put to death. He went down from Judea to Caesarea, and stayed there.

echoes.text: The king commanded, and they brought those men who had accused Daniel, and they cast them into the den of lions, them, their children, and their wives; and the lions mauled them, and broke all their bones in pieces, before they came to the bottom of the den.
echoes.note: The reversal whereby those who guarded/accused the rescued righteous man are themselves put to death parallels Darius casting Daniel's accusers to the lions after his deliverance. The guards executed in Herod's place reflect the same ironic-substitution pattern.

echoes.text: The waters returned, and covered the chariots and the horsemen, even all Pharaoh’s army that went in after them into the sea. There remained not so much as one of them.
echoes.note: After the Passover/exodus deliverance, the pursuing soldiers perish; the death of Herod's squads following Peter's escape faintly continues the exodus typology (deliverance of the people, destruction of the captor's forces).

pericopes.text: Now Herod was very angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came with one accord to him, and, having made Blastus, the king’s personal aide, their friend, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food. On an appointed day, Herod dressed himself in royal clothing, sat on the throne, and gave a speech to them. The people shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and died.

echoes.text: But the All-seeing Lord, the God of Israel, struck him with a fatal and invisible stroke; and as soon as he had ceased speaking this word, an incurable pain of the bowels seized him, and bitter torments of the inner parts; and that most justly, for he had tormented other men’s bowels with many and strange sufferings. But he in no wise ceased from his rude insolence; nay, still more was he filled with arrogancy, breathing fire in his passion against the […]
echoes.note: The death of the proud persecutor Antiochus Epiphanes — struck by God, his body breeding worms, rotting while still alive, finally acknowledging he is mortal not divine — is the closest model for Herod 'eaten by worms' for failing to 'give God the glory.' Shared distinctive elements (proud king, worm-affliction, divine smiting, refusal/recognition of mortality) give high volume and coherence.

echoes.text: Son of man, tell the prince of Tyre, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Because your heart is lifted up, and you have said, I am a god, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas; yet you are man, and not God, though you set your heart as the heart of God— behold, you are wiser than Daniel; there is no secret that is hidden from you; by your wisdom and by your understanding you have gotten yourself riches, and have gotten gold and silver into your […]
echoes.note: Set precisely against Tyre and Sidon, this oracle condemns the prince of Tyre who said 'I am a god, I sit in the seat of God,' declaring he is a man and not a god, struck dead by judgment. The crowd's 'voice of a god, and not of a man!' and Herod's instant death make this a pointed, geographically apt allusion (Tyre/Sidon supply context, 12:20).

echoes.text: The king spoke and said, Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty? While the word was in the king’s mouth, a voice came from the sky, saying, “O king Nebuchadnezzar, to you it is spoken: The kingdom has departed from you. You shall be driven from men; and your dwelling shall be with the animals of the field. You shall be made to eat grass as oxen. Seven times shall […]
echoes.note: Nebuchadnezzar's self-glorifying speech ('Is not this great Babylon, which I have built...') is immediately answered by a voice from heaven and divine humbling. The pattern of a king's prideful public oration met by sudden God-sent affliction for failing to honor God strongly parallels Herod's throne speech and stroke.

echoes.text: But when his heart was lifted up, and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him: and he was driven from the sons of men, and his heart was made like the animals’, and his dwelling was with the wild donkeys; he was fed with grass like oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of the sky; until he knew that the Most High God rules in the kingdom of men, and that he sets up over it […]
echoes.note: Belshazzar is condemned because he 'lifted up himself' and did not glorify 'the God in whose hand your breath is.' The explicit charge against Herod — 'he didn't give God the glory' — matches Daniel's indictment of the king who withholds glory from God.

echoes.text: Your pomp is brought down to Sheol, with the sound of your stringed instruments. Maggots are spread out under you, and worms cover you.
echoes.note: The taunt over the fallen king of Babylon: 'the maggot is spread under you, and worms cover you.' The worm-judgment on a king who exalted himself 'above the stars of God' resonates with Herod's worm-eaten death for usurping divine honors.

echoes.text: “Woe to the nations who rise up against my race! The Lord Almighty will take vengeance on them in the day of judgement, to put fire and worms in their flesh; and they will weep and feel their pain forever.”
echoes.note: 'The Lord Almighty will take vengeance on them in the day of judgment; he will send fire and worms into their flesh.' Deuterocanonical worm-and-fire judgment language for the enemies of God supports the recurrence of the worm-death motif as divine punishment.

echoes.text: “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images.
echoes.note: 'I am the LORD... my glory I will not give to another.' Undergirds the explicit rationale 'he didn't give God the glory'; God's jealousy for his glory is the principle Herod violates by accepting acclamation as a god.

echoes.text: Why is earth and ashes proud? Because in his life he has cast away his bowels. It is a long disease; the physician mocketh: And he is a king today, and tomorrow he will die. For when a man is dead, He will inherit creeping things, and beasts, and worms. It is the beginning of pride when a man departs from the Lord; And his heart is departed from him that made him. For the beginning of pride is sin; And he that keeps it will pour forth abomination. For […]
echoes.note: 'Why is earth and ashes proud?'... God 'casts down the thrones of rulers, and sets up the meek' and afflicts the proud — a wisdom meditation on the downfall of arrogant kings that thematically frames Herod's enthroned pride and sudden fall.

echoes.text: My servants shall bring them down from Lebanon to the sea. I will make them into rafts to go by sea to the place that you shall appoint me, and will cause them to be broken up there, and you shall receive them. You shall accomplish my desire, in giving food for my household.” So Hiram gave Solomon timber of cedar and timber of fir according to all his desire. Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand measures of wheat for food to his household, and twenty […]
echoes.note: Tyre's dependence on Israelite/royal grain supply (Hiram's people fed from Solomon's stores) supplies the background to 'their country depended on the king's country for food' (12:20). A historical-cultural echo rather than a textual citation.

echoes.text: And he that but now supposed himself to have the waves of the sea at his bidding, so vainglorious was he beyond the condition of a man, and that thought to weigh the heights of the mountains in a balance, was now brought to the ground and carried in a litter, showing to all that the power was manifestly God’s; so that out of the body of the impious man worms swarmed, and while he was still living in anguish and pains, his flesh fell off, and by reason of […]
echoes.note: Specifically: Antiochus 'thought he could command the waves of the sea... and weigh the high mountains in a balance' yet 'worms swarmed out of his body' and his flesh decayed. The juxtaposition of god-like presumption with worm-infested collapse is the sharpest single parallel to Herod's fate and may be cited distinctly within the 2 Macc 9 unit.

pericopes.text: But the word of God grew and multiplied. Barnabas and Saul returned to Jerusalem, when they had fulfilled their service, also taking with them John who was called Mark.

echoes.text: The children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and grew exceedingly mighty; and the land was filled with them.
echoes.note: 'The children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied' — set immediately after Pharaoh's failed oppression, exactly as 'the word of God grew and multiplied' caps Herod's failed persecution. The exodus-typology of Acts 12 makes this growth-after-tyrant verbal echo deliberate.

echoes.text: God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
echoes.note: The creation mandate 'be fruitful and multiply' supplies the underlying 'grow and multiply' diction that Luke applies to the word of God, personifying it as a living, increasing entity.

echoes.text: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
echoes.note: God's word that goes forth and does not return empty but accomplishes and prospers undergirds the notion of the 'word of God' itself growing and multiplying as an active force; thematic rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: Now in the assembly that was at Antioch there were some prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.” Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.

echoes.text: You shall present the Levites before Yahweh. The children of Israel shall lay their hands on the Levites,
echoes.note: The laying on of hands to set apart Barnabas and Saul for service echoes the Levitical rite where Israel lays hands on the Levites to consecrate them for the Lord's work. Verbal overlap is slight (a shared gesture rather than wording), but the thematic coherence of commissioning for sacred service is strong. Plausibility high given Luke's pervasive use of Pentateuchal cultic practice.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and commission him in their sight. You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before Yahweh. At his word they shall go out, and at his […]
echoes.note: Moses lays hands on Joshua to commission him for a divinely appointed task before the assembly, the closest narrative analogue to commissioning two leaders by hand-laying after the Spirit designates them. Recurrence of the hand-laying-for-mission motif strengthens the link, though no verbal citation.

echoes.text: When I had gone up onto the mountain to receive the stone tablets, even the tablets of the covenant which Yahweh made with you, then I stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water.
echoes.note: Fasting as preparation for receiving divine direction recalls Moses' wilderness fasting before God. Faint, generic; included for maximal coverage.

pericopes.text: So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia. From there they sailed to Cyprus. When they were at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. They had also John as their attendant. When they had gone through the island to Paphos, they found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Bar Jesus, who was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of understanding. This man summoned Barnabas and Saul, and sought to hear the word of God. But Elymas the sorcerer (for so is his name by interpretation) withstood them, seeking to turn aside the proconsul from the faith. But Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, fastened his eyes on him, and said, “Full of all deceit and all cunning, you son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, will you not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord? Now, behold, the hand of the Lord is on you, and you will be blind, not seeing the sun for a season!” Immediately a mist and darkness fell on him. He went around seeking someone to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord.

echoes.text: There shall not be found with you anyone who makes his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, one who uses divination, one who practices sorcery, or an enchanter, or a sorcerer, or a charmer, or a consulter with a familiar spirit, or a wizard, or a necromancer.
echoes.note: Elymas the magos/false prophet embodies precisely the sorcery and divination Deuteronomy forbids in Israel; Luke frames the confrontation as the true word of God against the prohibited mantic arts. Thematic coherence high, verbal overlap conceptual rather than lexical.

echoes.text: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul. […]
echoes.note: The 'false prophet' (pseudoprophetes) who seeks to turn the proconsul aside from the faith answers to the Deuteronomic false prophet who tries to seduce Israel away from the Lord; the verb 'turn aside' resonates with Deut 13's leading astray.

echoes.text: Who is wise, that he may understand these things? Who is prudent, that he may know them? For the ways of Yahweh are right, and the righteous walk in them; But the rebellious stumble in them.
echoes.note: Paul's charge of 'perverting the straight ways of the Lord' inverts Hosea's closing maxim that 'the ways of the LORD are right (straight)' and the righteous walk in them while transgressors stumble. The straight-ways imagery is a recognizable prophetic idiom; volume moderate.

echoes.text: He who walks blamelessly walks surely, but he who perverts his ways will be found out.
echoes.note: 'He who perverts his ways will be found out' supplies the wisdom background for condemning one who makes crooked the straight paths of the Lord. Faint, idiomatic.

echoes.text: They struck the men who were at the door of the house with blindness, both small and great, so that they wearied themselves to find the door.
echoes.note: Elymas struck with mist and darkness, groping for someone to lead him, closely parallels the men of Sodom struck with blindness so they could not find the door, a divine judgment-blinding. Strong narrative recurrence with 2 Kings 6 below.

echoes.text: When they came down to him, Elisha prayed to Yahweh, and said, “Please strike this people with blindness.” He struck them with blindness according to the word of Elisha.
echoes.note: Elisha prays and the Aramean army is struck blind by the prophet's word, the OT type for a man of God blinding an enemy of the Lord's purpose; the prophet-induced judicial blindness is the operative pattern behind Paul's act.

echoes.text: Yahweh will strike you with madness, with blindness, and with astonishment of heart. You will grope at noonday, as the blind gropes in darkness, and you shall not prosper in your ways. You will only be oppressed and robbed always, and there will be no one to save you.
echoes.note: The covenant curse of blindness, groping at noonday as the blind grope in darkness, supplies the language of Elymas groping for a guide. Thematic coherence with judgment-blinding; verbal echo of groping.

echoes.text: behold, the hand of Yahweh is on your livestock which are in the field, on the horses, on the donkeys, on the camels, on the herds, and on the flocks with a very grievous pestilence.
echoes.note: 'The hand of the Lord is upon you' echoes the recurring Exodus formula of the LORD's hand falling in judgment (e.g., upon Pharaoh's livestock and Egypt). A stock OT idiom for divine striking; volume low.

echoes.text: But the hand of Yahweh was heavy on them of Ashdod, and he destroyed them, and struck them with tumors, even Ashdod and its borders.
echoes.note: 'The hand of the LORD was heavy' upon the Philistines is another instance of the judgment-hand idiom behind 'the hand of the Lord is on you.' Generic, included for breadth.

pericopes.text: Now Paul and his company set sail from Paphos, and came to Perga in Pamphylia. John departed from them and returned to Jerusalem. But they, passing on from Perga, came to Antioch of Pisidia. They went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and sat down. After the reading of the law and the prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of exhortation for the people, speak.” Paul stood up, and beckoning with his hand said, “Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen.

echoes.text: All the people gathered themselves together as one man into the broad place that was before the water gate; and they spoke to Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses, which Yahweh had commanded to Israel. Ezra the priest brought the law before the assembly, both men and women, and all who could hear with understanding, on the first day of the seventh month. He read therein before the broad place that was before the water gate from early […]
echoes.note: The synagogue pattern of reading the Law and the Prophets followed by exhortation reflects the post-exilic public reading of the Law with exposition; Luke's scene presupposes this liturgical inheritance. Background rather than citation.

echoes.text: Hear my teaching, my people. Turn your ears to the words of my mouth.
echoes.note: Paul's opening summons, 'Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen,' echoes the Asaphite call to the people to give ear, the conventional opening of a historical recital (as the sermon then becomes). Faint formulaic resonance.

pericopes.text: The God of this people chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they stayed as aliens in the land of Egypt, and with an uplifted arm, he led them out of it. For a period of about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. When he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land for an inheritance, for about four hundred fifty years. After these things he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet. Afterward they asked for a king, and God gave to them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. When he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, to whom he also testified, ‘I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’

echoes.text: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth. Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, […]
echoes.note: 'The God of this people Israel chose our fathers' restates Deuteronomy's foundational election theology, that the LORD set his love on and chose the patriarchs and their seed. Strong thematic coherence and clear conceptual borrowing opening the historical resume.

echoes.text: Only Yahweh had a delight in your fathers to love them, and he chose their seed after them, even you above all peoples, as at this day.
echoes.note: 'The LORD set his affection on your fathers to love them and chose their descendants' is a near-synonymous parallel to the election of the fathers; reinforces the choosing language. Recurrence strengthens the Deuteronomic source pool.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh, for by a strong hand he shall let them go, and by a strong hand he shall drive them out of his land.”
echoes.note: Deliverance from Egypt 'with a strong hand' undergirds Paul's 'with uplifted arm he led them out.' The Exodus deliverance formula is unmistakable here.

echoes.text: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:
echoes.note: 'I will redeem you with an outstretched arm' supplies the exact 'uplifted/high arm' (brachion hypselos) by which God led Israel out of Egypt. High-volume verbal borrowing of a fixed Exodus formula.

echoes.text: Or has God tried to go and take a nation for himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs, by wonders, by war, by a mighty hand, by an outstretched arm, and by great terrors, according to all that Yahweh your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?
echoes.note: God's taking a nation out of Egypt 'by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and great terrors' is the canonical Deuteronomic exodus formula behind 'with uplifted arm he led them out.' Reinforces Exod 6:6.

echoes.text: The children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and grew exceedingly mighty; and the land was filled with them.
echoes.note: 'He made the people great (exalted them) during their stay in Egypt' echoes the multiplication of Israel in Egypt, who grew exceedingly numerous. Conceptual; the LXX verb differs.

echoes.text: Israel also came into Egypt. Jacob lived in the land of Ham. He increased his people greatly, and made them stronger than their adversaries.
echoes.note: Israel sojourning in Egypt where 'the LORD made his people very fruitful, and made them stronger than their foes' closely matches 'exalted the people during their stay as aliens in Egypt.' This psalm is itself a historical recital paralleling Paul's, raising recurrence.

echoes.text: The children of Israel ate the manna forty years, until they came to an inhabited land. They ate the manna until they came to the borders of the land of Canaan.
echoes.note: 'The forty years in the wilderness' draws on the canonical forty-year wandering during which Israel ate manna. Stock chronological datum but verbally precise.

echoes.text: Your children shall be wanderers in the wilderness forty years, and shall bear your prostitution, until your dead bodies are consumed in the wilderness. After the number of the days in which you spied out the land, even forty days, for every day a year, you will bear your iniquities, even forty years, and you will know my alienation.’
echoes.note: The forty years in the wilderness as the span of God's bearing with a rebellious generation supplies both the number and the note of divine forbearance ('he put up with them'). Strong thematic coherence.

echoes.text: and in the wilderness, where you have seen how that Yahweh your God bore you, as a man does bear his son, in all the way that you went, until you came to this place.”
echoes.note: 'The LORD your God carried (bore) you as a father carries his son' lies behind the well-attested variant 'he bore/nursed them' for forty years; even in the 'put up with them' reading, Deut 1:31's wilderness-forbearance is the matrix. Textual-critical note: etropophoresen vs etrophophoresen.

echoes.text: Forty long years I was grieved with that generation, and said, “It is a people that errs in their heart. They have not known my ways.”
echoes.note: 'For forty years I loathed that generation' supplies the forty-years-plus-divine-toleration motif behind God 'putting up with them' in the wilderness. Recurrence with Numbers 14.

echoes.text: When Yahweh your God brings you into the land where you go to possess it, and casts out many nations before you, the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, seven nations greater and mightier than you;
echoes.note: 'When he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan' directly quotes the Deuteronomic catalogue of the 'seven nations greater and mightier than you' the LORD casts out before Israel. Distinctive numeral 'seven nations' is verbatim.

echoes.text: “‘You went over the Jordan, and came to Jericho. The men of Jericho fought against you, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite; and I delivered them into your hand.
echoes.note: Joshua's recital of the nations of Canaan delivered into Israel's hand and the land given as inheritance parallels Paul's compression; Josh 24 is itself a covenant historical resume, raising recurrence.

echoes.text: These are the inheritances which the children of Israel took in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest, Joshua the son of Nun, and the heads of the fathers’ houses of the tribes of the children of Israel, distributed to them, by the lot of their inheritance, as Yahweh commanded by Moses, for the nine tribes, and for the half-tribe.
echoes.note: 'He gave them their land for an inheritance' restates the apportioning of Canaan as inheritance by lot. Thematic coherence high; standard conquest language.

echoes.text: Behold, I have set the land before you. Go in and possess the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give to them and to their seed after them.’”
echoes.note: The land sworn to the fathers given for possession underlies 'he gave them their land for an inheritance.' Generic land-gift formula.

echoes.text: He also drove out the nations before them, allotted them for an inheritance by line, and made the tribes of Israel to dwell in their tents.
echoes.note: 'He drove out nations before them and apportioned them for an inheritance' compresses conquest-plus-inheritance exactly as Paul does, within another historical psalm. Recurrence reinforces.

echoes.text: Yahweh raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them.
echoes.note: 'After that he gave them judges' directly summarizes the book of Judges' refrain that the LORD raised up judges to deliver Israel. Clear thematic and verbal correspondence.

echoes.text: All Israel from Dan even to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established to be a prophet of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'until Samuel the prophet' fixes the transition point at Samuel, recognized from Dan to Beersheba as a prophet of the LORD, the last of the judges. Distinctive named figure.

echoes.text: and they said to him, “Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.”
echoes.note: 'Then they asked for a king' directly recalls Israel's demand to Samuel, 'appoint a king to judge us like all the nations.' Strong verbal and narrative correspondence.

echoes.text: Now therefore see the king whom you have chosen, and whom you have asked for: and behold, Yahweh has set a king over you.
echoes.note: 'Here is the king you have chosen, for whom you asked' reinforces the request-for-a-king motif. Recurrence within the same Samuel narrative.

echoes.text: He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by their families; and the family of the Matrites was taken; and Saul the son of Kish was taken: but when they sought him, he could not be found.
echoes.note: Saul son of Kish 'of the tribe of Benjamin' is drawn from the selection-by-lot narrative naming Saul of the tribe of Benjamin and the family of Kish. Distinctive named details.

echoes.text: Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Becorath, the son of Aphiah, the son of a Benjamite, a mighty man of valor. He had a son, whose name was Saul, an impressive young man; and there was not among the children of Israel a better person than he. From his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people.
echoes.note: The introduction of Kish the Benjamite and his son Saul, a choice young man, supplies the 'Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin.' Reinforces 10:21.

echoes.text: For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as idolatry and teraphim. Because you have rejected Yahweh’s word, he has also rejected you from being king.”
echoes.note: 'When he had removed him' alludes to the LORD's rejection of Saul as king ('you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has rejected you from being king'). Thematic coherence high.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Samuel, “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite; for I have provided a king for myself among his sons.”
echoes.note: God's word to Samuel, 'I have rejected Saul... I have provided for myself a king,' bridges the removal of Saul and the raising up of David. Reinforces the removal-then-David sequence.

echoes.text: He sent, and brought him in. Now he was ruddy, and withal of a beautiful face, and goodly to look on. Yahweh said, “Arise, anoint him; for this is he.” Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brothers: and the Spirit of Yahweh came mightily on David from that day forward. So Samuel rose up, and went to Ramah.
echoes.note: 'He raised up David to be their king' draws on the anointing of David at Bethlehem, whom the LORD designates and Samuel anoints. Distinctive narrative behind the David accession.

echoes.text: But now your kingdom shall not continue. Yahweh has sought for himself a man after his own heart, and Yahweh has appointed him to be prince over his people, because you have not kept that which Yahweh commanded you.”
echoes.note: 'A man after my own heart, who will do all my will' quotes Samuel's verdict to Saul that the LORD has sought out 'a man after his own heart' to be ruler. The 'man after my heart' phrase is verbatim; this is the controlling source of the composite citation.

echoes.text: I have found David, my servant. I have anointed him with my holy oil,
echoes.note: 'I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him' supplies the opening clause 'I have found David,' fused with 1 Sam 13:14 into Paul's composite testimony. Verbal borrowing of 'I have found David.'

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
echoes.note: 'The LORD looks on the heart' undergirds the 'man after my heart' verdict, reinforcing the heart-language of David's election. Conceptual support for the composite quotation.

echoes.text: Who says of Cyrus, ‘He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure,’ even saying of Jerusalem, ‘She will be built;’ and of the temple, ‘Your foundation will be laid.’”
echoes.note: 'who will do all my will/pleasure' resembles the LORD's word that Cyrus 'shall fulfill all my purpose'; some see the third clause of Paul's composite drawn from this anointed-agent idiom. Faint and contested.

pericopes.text: From this man’s seed, God has brought salvation to Israel according to his promise, before his coming, when John had first preached the baptism of repentance to Israel. As John was fulfilling his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. But behold, one comes after me the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom.
echoes.note: 'From this man's seed God has brought salvation to Israel according to his promise' rests on the Davidic covenant promise that God will raise up David's seed after him and establish his kingdom. The promise-to-David seed theology is the backbone of the verse.

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn to David in truth. He will not turn from it: “I will set the fruit of your body on your throne.
echoes.note: 'The LORD swore to David... one of the fruit of your body I will set on your throne' supplies the sworn promise of a descendant, reinforcing the seed-of-David savior. Recurrence with 2 Sam 7.

echoes.text: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.
echoes.note: The shoot from the stump of Jesse, a messianic seed of David, contributes to the seed-of-David savior expectation. Conceptual messianic background.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: John's preparatory preaching before the Coming One echoes the messenger sent ahead to prepare the way of the Lord. Faint; the forerunner motif is operative.

echoes.text: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God.
echoes.note: John's preparatory role and self-effacement before the one who comes after resonate with the wilderness voice preparing the way of the LORD. Background to the Baptist tradition rather than a citation here.

pericopes.text: Brothers, children of the stock of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, the word of this salvation is sent out to you. For those who dwell in Jerusalem, and their rulers, because they didn’t know him, nor the voices of the prophets which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. Though they found no cause for death, they still asked Pilate to have him killed. When they had fulfilled all things that were written about him, they took him down from the tree, and laid him in a tomb. But God raised him from the dead, and he was seen for many days by those who came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses to the people.

echoes.text: you seed of Abraham, his servant, you children of Jacob, his chosen ones.
echoes.note: Address to 'children of the stock of Abraham' echoes the covenant designation 'offspring of Abraham his servant,' situating the hearers within the elect line. Idiomatic.

echoes.text: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you.
echoes.note: 'Children of the stock of Abraham' rests on the covenant with Abraham and his seed; the word of salvation comes first to the covenant heirs. Generic covenant background.

echoes.text: They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.
echoes.note: That they 'found no cause for death' yet had him killed and 'laid in a tomb' resonates with the Servant who had done no violence yet was assigned a grave; the innocence-then-burial pattern is the Servant Song's. Thematic coherence medium-high.

echoes.text: If a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree; his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall surely bury him the same day; for he who is hanged is accursed of God; that you don’t defile your land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance.
echoes.note: 'They took him down from the tree' draws on the law that a man hanged on a tree must be taken down the same day, a text Luke and Paul repeatedly attach to the crucifixion. Distinctive 'tree' (xylon) language and the taking-down detail.

echoes.text: For dogs have surrounded me. A company of evildoers have enclosed me. They have pierced my hands and feet. I can count all of my bones. They look and stare at me. They divide my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing.
echoes.note: The condemnation and execution of the innocent one with the connivance of rulers faintly recalls the lament psalm of the suffering righteous appropriated for the passion. Contested, low volume here.

pericopes.text: We bring you good news of the promise made to the fathers, that God has fulfilled the same to us, their children, in that he raised up Jesus. As it is also written in the second psalm, ‘You are my Son. Today I have become your father.’ “Concerning that he raised him up from the dead, now no more to return to corruption, he has spoken thus: ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’ Therefore he says also in another psalm, ‘You will not allow your Holy One to see decay.’ For David, after he had in his own generation served the counsel of God, fell asleep, and was laid with his fathers, and saw decay. But he whom God raised up saw no decay.

echoes.text: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”
echoes.note: 'The promise made to the fathers' includes the Abrahamic blessing-to-the-nations promise now declared fulfilled. Background to the promise theology of the verse.

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;
echoes.note: The 'promise made to the fathers' that God has fulfilled by raising Jesus centers on the Davidic covenant, especially 'I will be his father and he shall be my son,' which dovetails with the Ps 2 citation. Reinforces the father-son sonship theme.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you' is quoted verbatim as the second-psalm proof that God raised up Jesus. Explicit formula citation ('as it is written in the second psalm'); maximal volume.

echoes.text: Turn your ear, and come to me; hear, and your soul shall live: and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David.
echoes.note: 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings/mercies of David' (ta hosia Dauid ta pista) is quoted to prove the resurrection-incorruption, linking the everlasting covenant mercies promised to David to the risen Christ. Explicit LXX citation.

echoes.text: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.
echoes.note: 'You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption/decay' is quoted ('in another psalm') as the climactic resurrection proof-text, then argued to apply to Jesus and not David. Verbatim LXX quotation; the linchpin of the resurrection argument.

echoes.text: David slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David.
echoes.note: 'David... fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw decay' draws on the notice that David slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, grounding Paul's argument that David did see corruption. Distinctive 'slept with his fathers' idiom.

echoes.text: “I have made a covenant with my chosen one, I have sworn to David, my servant, ‘I will establish your seed forever, and build up your throne to all generations.’” Selah.
echoes.note: The sworn covenant with David ('I will establish your seed forever') reinforces the 'sure mercies of David' applied to the imperishable risen one. Recurrence with Isa 55:3 covenant language.

pericopes.text: Be it known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man is proclaimed to you remission of sins, and by him everyone who believes is justified from all things, from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses. Beware therefore, lest that come on you which is spoken in the prophets: ‘Behold, you scoffers, and wonder, and perish; for I work a work in your days, a work which you will in no way believe, if one declares it to you.’”

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.
echoes.note: 'Everyone who believes is justified' faintly recalls the Servant who 'shall make many to be accounted righteous,' the OT seed of justification language. Conceptual, contested.

echoes.text: “Look among the nations, watch, and wonder marvelously; for I am working a work in your days, which you will not believe though it is told you.
echoes.note: 'Behold, you scoffers, and wonder, and perish; for I work a work in your days, a work you will not believe though one declares it' is quoted verbatim (LXX, 'scoffers/despisers') as the prophetic warning closing the sermon. Explicit citation, maximal volume.
echoes.lxxText: Behold, ye despisers, and look, and wonder marvelously, and vanish: for I work a work in your days, which ye will in no wise believe, though a man declare it to you.

pericopes.text: So when the Jews went out of the synagogue, the Gentiles begged that these words might be preached to them the next Sabbath. Now when the synagogue broke up, many of the Jews and of the devout proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas; who, speaking to them, urged them to continue in the grace of God. The next Sabbath almost the whole city was gathered together to hear the word of God. But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with jealousy, and contradicted the things which were spoken by Paul, and blasphemed. Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, and said, “It was necessary that God’s word should be spoken to you first. Since indeed you thrust it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. For so has the Lord commanded us, saying, ‘I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth.’” As the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of God. As many as were appointed to eternal life believed. The Lord’s word was spread abroad throughout all the region. But the Jews stirred up the devout and prominent women and the chief men of the city, and stirred up a persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and threw them out of their borders. But they shook off the dust of their feet against them, and came to Iconium. The disciples were filled with joy with the Holy Spirit.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: 'I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth' is quoted verbatim (LXX) as the Lord's commission justifying the turn to the Gentiles. Explicit Servant-Song citation; maximal volume.

echoes.text: “I, Yahweh, have called you in righteousness, and will hold your hand, and will keep you, and make you a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations;
echoes.note: 'A light for the Gentiles' also stands in the first Servant Song ('I will give you... for a light to the nations'), reinforcing the light-to-the-nations commission Paul cites. Recurrence with Isa 49:6.

echoes.text: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.
echoes.note: The Jews 'filled with jealousy' contradicting the word, leading to the turn toward the Gentiles, faintly enacts the Song of Moses' principle that God provokes Israel to jealousy by a non-people, a motif Paul develops elsewhere. Contested here.

echoes.text: Also I shook out my lap, and said, “So may God shake out every man from his house, and from his labor, that doesn’t perform this promise; even thus be he shaken out, and emptied.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh. The people did according to this promise.
echoes.note: Shaking off the dust of the feet against the city as a sign-act of rejection has loose kinship with prophetic shaking-out gestures of repudiation (Nehemiah shaking out his lap against covenant-breakers). Very faint; the gesture is more dominical instruction than OT citation.

pericopes.text: In Iconium, they entered together into the synagogue of the Jews, and so spoke that a great multitude both of Jews and of Greeks believed. But the disbelieving Jews stirred up and embittered the souls of the Gentiles against the brothers. Therefore they stayed there a long time, speaking boldly in the Lord, who testified to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands. But the multitude of the city was divided. Part sided with the Jews, and part with the apostles. When some of both the Gentiles and the Jews, with their rulers, made a violent attempt to mistreat and stone them, they became aware of it, and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra, Derbe, and the surrounding region. There they preached the Good News.

echoes.text: and Yahweh showed great and awesome signs and wonders on Egypt, on Pharaoh, and on all his house, before our eyes;
echoes.note: The Lord 'testified to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands' (v3). The pair 'signs and wonders' (sēmeia kai terata) is the fixed Septuagintal idiom for the Exodus deliverance, where the Lord 'showed signs and wonders' against Egypt. Thematic Coherence is strong (divine attestation of the messenger); Volume rests on the set two-word phrase. Plausibility high: Luke saturates Acts with Exodus-shaped signs-and-wonders language.

echoes.text: in all the signs and the wonders, which Yahweh sent him to do in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh, and to all his servants, and to all his land,
echoes.note: Reinforces the 'signs and wonders' idiom by tying it specifically to a commissioned human agent (Moses 'whom the Lord sent to do all the signs and wonders'), paralleling miracles done 'by their hands.' Recurrence within the Pentateuch supports the topos; Volume is faint on its own. Contested as a distinct source rather than part of the broader Exodus signs-and-wonders cluster.

echoes.text: “Bring out of the camp him who cursed; and let all who heard him lay their hands on his head, and let all the congregation stone him.
echoes.note: The plot to 'mistreat and stone them' (v5) presupposes the Torah's mode of execution by stoning, carried out by the community and its rulers. Volume low (no verbal borrowing), but the legal practice underlies the narrative threat. Contested: the link is conceptual to the institution of stoning rather than to this verse specifically.

pericopes.text: At Lystra a certain man sat, impotent in his feet, a cripple from his mother’s womb, who never had walked. He was listening to Paul speaking, who, fastening eyes on him, and seeing that he had faith to be made whole, said with a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet!” He leaped up and walked. When the multitude saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voice, saying in the language of Lycaonia, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” They called Barnabas “Jupiter”, and Paul “Mercury”, because he was the chief speaker. The priest of Jupiter, whose temple was in front of their city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates, and would have made a sacrifice along with the multitudes.

echoes.text: Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: The man 'a cripple from his mother's womb, who never had walked' is healed and 'leaped up and walked' (vv8-10). Isaiah's eschatological promise, 'then shall the lame man leap (halletai) as a hart,' supplies the rare verb and the lame-restored motif. Volume high (distinctive 'leap' for a healed lame man); Thematic Coherence strong (the dawning age of restoration enacted among the nations); Recurrence good (Isa 35 is a programmatic restoration text echoed across Luke-Acts).

echoes.text: He said to me, Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you.
echoes.note: Paul's command 'Stand upright on your feet!' (v10) echoes the prophetic summons 'Son of man, stand upon your feet, and I will speak with you.' Volume rests on the shared imperative to stand on the feet; Thematic Coherence moderate (a word of power that raises a prostrate/incapable person). Contested whether Luke intends a prophetic-call resonance or merely a healing command.

echoes.text: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they don’t speak. They have eyes, but they don’t see. They have ears, but they don’t hear. They have noses, but they don’t smell. They have hands, but they don’t feel. They have feet, but they don’t walk, neither do they speak through their throat. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.
echoes.note: The crowd cries 'The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men' and the priest of Zeus prepares oxen and garlands (vv11-13). The psalm's mockery of idols 'the work of men's hands' frames the scene's irony: the living agents of God are taken for the lifeless gods of the nations. Volume nil (no verbal contact); the link is typological-thematic, exposing pagan idolatry. Contested as an intended echo.

pericopes.text: But when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of it, they tore their clothes, and sprang into the multitude, crying out, “Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made the sky and the earth and the sea, and all that is in them; who in the generations gone by allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. Yet he didn’t leave himself without witness, in that he did good and gave you rains from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.” Even saying these things, they hardly stopped the multitudes from making a sacrifice to them.

echoes.text: for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed the Sabbath day, and made it holy.
echoes.note: The summons to turn to 'the living God, who made the sky and the earth and the sea, and all that is in them' (v15) reproduces the Sabbath-commandment formula 'the Lord made the heaven and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them.' Volume very high (the full four-membered creation list verbatim); Thematic Coherence strong (Creator vs. the 'vain things' of idolatry). The clearest scriptural backbone of the Lystra speech.

echoes.text: who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who keeps truth forever;
echoes.note: Parallel source for v15: the Lord 'who made the heaven and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them,' here explicitly tied to the 'living' God who keeps faith and provides. Volume very high (same creation catalogue); Thematic Coherence strong (God as faithful provider, matching v17's rains and food). Likely conflated with Exod 20:11 in the speech's monotheistic appeal.

echoes.text: You are Yahweh, even you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their army, the earth and all things that are on it, the seas and all that is in them, and you preserve them all. The army of heaven worships you.
echoes.note: Ezra's prayer, 'You are the Lord alone; you have made heaven... the earth... the seas, and all that is in them, and you preserve them all,' is the great post-exilic monotheistic confession built on the same creation list and joined to providential preservation, both present in vv15-17. Volume moderate (creation catalogue plus preservation); Recurrence supports the formula's currency in Second Temple worship.

echoes.text: The sea is his, and he made it. His hands formed the dry land.
echoes.note: 'The sea is his, for he made it, and his hands formed the dry land' undergirds v15's pairing of sea and earth as the Creator's work and stands behind the call to worship the true God rather than idols. Volume moderate; Thematic Coherence high (creation as ground for worship, against false gods).

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth' is the headwater of the heaven-and-earth creation language deployed in v15. Volume moderate (foundational phrasing) but diffuse, since the speech follows the fuller Exod/Ps liturgical lists rather than Genesis directly. Recurrence very high across Scripture.

echoes.text: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.
echoes.note: The exhortation to 'turn from these vain things' (mataia, v15) draws on the prophetic-Pentateuchal label for idols as 'vanities' that 'provoked me with their vanities/no-gods.' Volume moderate (mataia is the LXX term for idols); Thematic Coherence strong (idols as empty nothings opposed to the living God). Contested only as to which idol-vanity text is primary.

echoes.text: Are there any among the vanities of the nations that can cause rain? or can the sky give showers? Aren’t you he, Yahweh our God? therefore we will wait for you; for you have made all these things.
echoes.note: 'Are there any among the vanities (idols) of the nations that can cause rain? ... it is you, O Lord our God,' directly ties the 'vain things' of v15 to the rain-giving of v17: the nations' idols cannot give rain, but the living God does. Volume moderate but precise (vanities + rain), making this an unusually apt double-link. Thematic Coherence very high.

echoes.text: Those who regard lying vanities forsake their own mercy.
echoes.note: 'Those who regard vain idols (mataia) forsake their own mercy' adds Recurrence to the 'vain things' (v15) idol-vocabulary in a Gentile setting (Nineveh/sailors), apt to a speech to pagans. Volume faint (single shared term). Contested as a discrete source within the broad idol-vanity cluster.

echoes.text: For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as we have, and lived?
echoes.note: 'The living God' (v15) is a fixed OT epithet distinguishing the true God from idols; Deut 5:26 ('the voice of the living God') is a Pentateuchal anchor. Volume moderate (set title); Thematic Coherence high (living God vs. dead idols, the speech's thesis). Recurrence very high across the OT.

echoes.text: So I let them go after the stubbornness of their hearts, that they might walk in their own counsels.
echoes.note: 'who in the generations gone by allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways' (v16) echoes God giving Israel 'up to their own hearts' lusts, and they walked in their own counsels.' Volume moderate (the idiom of being let to walk in one's own ways); Thematic Coherence strong (divine forbearance/handing-over of the nations). Contested between this and the Deut 32 nations-allotment tradition.

echoes.text: that I will give the rain of your land in its season, the former rain and the latter rain, that you may gather in your grain, your new wine, and your oil.
echoes.note: 'he... gave you rains from the sky and fruitful seasons' (v17) reflects the covenant promise 'I will give the rain of your land in its season, the early and the latter rain, that you may gather in your grain.' Volume high (rain given in due season → harvest); Thematic Coherence strong (God's good gifts as witness). A core text for the natural-revelation argument.

echoes.text: then I will give you your rains in their season, and the land shall yield its increase, and the trees of the field shall yield their fruit.
echoes.note: 'I will give you rain in its season, and the land shall yield its produce' parallels the rains and 'fruitful seasons' of v17. Volume moderate; Recurrence reinforces the Pentateuchal rain-blessing topos alongside Deut 11:14.

echoes.text: Neither do they say in their heart, ‘Let us now fear Yahweh our God, who gives rain, both the former and the latter, in its season; who preserves to us the appointed weeks of the harvest.’
echoes.note: 'Let us fear the Lord our God, who gives rain, both the early and the latter, in its season, who keeps for us the appointed weeks of the harvest' is the closest prophetic parallel to v17's rains and 'fruitful seasons.' Volume high (rain in season + fixed harvest seasons); Thematic Coherence strong (creation's seasons as a witness summoning to fear/turn to God).

echoes.text: You visit the earth, and water it. You greatly enrich it. The river of God is full of water. You provide them grain, for so you have ordained it. You drench its furrows. You level its ridges. You soften it with showers. You bless it with a crop. You crown the year with your bounty. Your carts overflow with abundance. The wilderness grasslands overflow. The hills are clothed with gladness. The pastures are covered with flocks. The valleys also are clothed […]
echoes.note: The psalm of God visiting the earth with rain, enriching it, crowning the year with bounty so the valleys 'shout for joy,' matches v17's rains, fruitful seasons, and resulting 'food and gladness.' Volume moderate (rain → fertility → joy sequence); Thematic Coherence high (providence evoking gladness).

echoes.text: who covers the sky with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth, who makes grass grow on the mountains.
echoes.note: 'who covers the heaven with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth, who makes grass to grow on the mountains' echoes v17's rains-from-heaven-producing-food. Volume moderate; Recurrence supports the providence-praise tradition.

echoes.text: He causes the grass to grow for the livestock, and plants for man to cultivate, that he may produce food out of the earth: wine that makes glad the heart of man, oil to make his face to shine, and bread that strengthens man’s heart.
echoes.note: God brings forth food from the earth and 'wine that gladdens the heart of man... and bread that strengthens man's heart' closely matches v17's 'filling our hearts with food and gladness.' Volume moderate-to-high (food + gladness of heart); Thematic Coherence strong (creation's provision as joy-giving witness).

echoes.text: You have put gladness in my heart, more than when their grain and their new wine are increased.
echoes.note: 'You have put gladness in my heart, more than in the time their grain and wine increased' overlaps v17's 'filling our hearts with... gladness' linked to harvest abundance. Volume faint (gladness in the heart + grain/wine); contested as distinct from Ps 104.

echoes.text: who gives rain on the earth, and sends waters on the fields;
echoes.note: 'who gives rain on the earth, and sends water on the fields' adds Recurrence to the rain-as-divine-gift motif of v17. Volume faint (general statement); contested as an intended source.

pericopes.text: But some Jews from Antioch and Iconium came there, and having persuaded the multitudes, they stoned Paul, and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. But as the disciples stood around him, he rose up, and entered into the city. On the next day he went out with Barnabas to Derbe.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “The man shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall stone him with stones outside of the camp.” All the congregation brought him outside of the camp, and stoned him to death with stones, as Yahweh commanded Moses.
echoes.note: Paul is stoned and 'dragged out of the city' (v19), reflecting the Torah practice of taking the condemned 'outside the camp' to be stoned. Volume moderate (stoning + expulsion from the community space); Thematic Coherence moderate (Paul suffers the prophet's/martyr's fate at the city's edge). Contested between this and Lev 24.

echoes.text: They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: The stoning of Paul, left for dead yet rising (vv19-20), stands in the typological line of God's messengers stoned for their witness, exemplified by Zechariah son of Jehoiada, stoned 'in the court of the house of the Lord.' Volume nil verbally; the link is the figural pattern of the persecuted prophet. Plausibility good given Luke's persecuted-witness theme; contested as an intended allusion.

echoes.text: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but Yahweh delivers him out of them all.
echoes.note: 'Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord delivers him out of them all' fits Paul's stoning and immediate rising (vv19-20), anticipating the explicit 'many afflictions' of v22. Volume faint; contested as a deliberate echo here rather than a general providence motif.

pericopes.text: When they had preached the Good News to that city, and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, confirming the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that through many afflictions we must enter into the Kingdom of God. When they had appointed elders for them in every assembly, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they had believed. They passed through Pisidia, and came to Pamphylia. When they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia. From there they sailed to Antioch, from where they had been committed to the grace of God for the work which they had fulfilled. When they had arrived, and had gathered the assembly together, they reported all the things that God had done with them, and that he had opened a door of faith to the nations. They stayed there with the disciples for a long time.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over them; and bring them to the Tent of Meeting, that they may stand there with you. I will come down and talk with you there. I will take of the Spirit which is on you, and will put it on them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, that you not bear it yourself alone.
echoes.note: 'When they had appointed elders for them in every assembly' (v23) reflects the foundational appointment of elders to share leadership of God's people, where Moses gathers seventy elders to bear the burden with him. Volume moderate (institution of elders for the community); Thematic Coherence strong (ordered leadership over the people of God). Contested between this and the Exod 18 model.

echoes.text: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but Yahweh delivers him out of them all.
echoes.note: 'through many afflictions we must enter into the Kingdom of God' (v22) restates the wisdom that 'many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord delivers him out of them all.' Volume moderate (the phrase 'many afflictions'); Thematic Coherence strong (suffering as the path of the faithful toward deliverance).

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: God 'had opened a door of faith to the nations' (v27) realizes the Servant's mandate to be 'a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth,' a programmatic Gentile-mission text in Luke-Acts (cf. Acts 13:47). Volume nil here (no verbal contact in v27); the link is the figural fulfillment of the nations' inclusion. Contested as an echo within this verse specifically.

pericopes.text: Some men came down from Judea and taught the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised after the custom of Moses, you can’t be saved.” Therefore when Paul and Barnabas had no small discord and discussion with them, they appointed Paul and Barnabas, and some others of them, to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question. They, being sent on their way by the assembly, passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, declaring the conversion of the Gentiles. They caused great joy to all the brothers. When they had come to Jerusalem, they were received by the assembly and the apostles and the elders, and they reported all things that God had done with them. But some of the sect of the Pharisees who believed rose up, saying, “It is necessary to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses.”

echoes.text: This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you. He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your seed. He who is born in your […]
echoes.note: The Judean teachers demand circumcision 'after the custom of Moses' as necessary for salvation; the underlying institution is the Abrahamic covenant of circumcision, the sign required of every male, where the uncircumcised is 'cut off.' The whole dispute presupposes this text as the charter of the boundary marker. Verbal coherence ('circumcised') and thematic centrality are strong.

echoes.text: In the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.
echoes.note: The Mosaic codification of circumcision (eighth-day) is what 'the custom of Moses' (v.1) most directly names, distinguishing the demand here from the merely Abrahamic command; supports the phrase 'keep the law of Moses' (v.5).

echoes.text: When a stranger shall live as a foreigner with you, and will keep the Passover to Yahweh, let all his males be circumcised, and then let him come near and keep it; and he shall be as one who is born in the land: but no uncircumcised person shall eat of it.
echoes.note: The Torah's own rule that a foreigner must be circumcised before sharing in the Passover/community is the legal logic the circumcision party extends to Gentile believers — only the circumcised may belong. Faint, conceptual.

pericopes.text: The apostles and the elders were gathered together to see about this matter. When there had been much discussion, Peter rose up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that a good while ago God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the nations should hear the word of the Good News, and believe. God, who knows the heart, testified about them, giving them the Holy Spirit, just like he did to us. He made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith. Now therefore why do you tempt God, that you should put a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.”

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
echoes.note: Peter calls God the one 'who knows the heart' (kardiognostes, v.8) who 'made no distinction... cleansing their hearts.' This recalls the LORD who, unlike man looking on outward appearance, 'looks on the heart' — here applied to overturning the outward circumcision marker in favor of inward purity. Strong thematic coherence.

echoes.text: then hear in heaven, your dwelling place, and forgive, and do, and render to every man according to all his ways, whose heart you know; (for you, even you only, know the hearts of all the children of men;)
echoes.note: Solomon's prayer addresses God who alone 'knows the hearts of all the children of men'; a recurrent OT divine epithet standing behind Peter's heart-knowing God who reads Gentile faith. Recurrence test supports the motif.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I the LORD search the heart' — part of the same cluster of heart-searching texts informing v.8's claim that God testified about the Gentiles by reading their hearts.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.
echoes.note: God 'cleansing their hearts by faith' (v.9) echoes the promise that the LORD will circumcise the heart — interiorized, divinely-wrought purity displacing the external rite at issue in the chapter. Thematically potent for the circumcision debate.

echoes.text: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you. I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: Heart-cleansing language (v.9) coheres with the promise to sprinkle clean water, give a new heart, and put the Spirit within — note v.8's gift of the Spirit alongside the cleansing. The Spirit + cleansed heart pairing is striking.

echoes.text: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked.
echoes.note: 'Circumcise the foreskin of your heart' reinforces the inward-circumcision motif behind 'cleansing their hearts' (v.9). Faint, overlaps with Deut 30:6.

echoes.text: It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.
echoes.note: Peter's 'yoke... which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear' (v.10) uses yoke-as-burden imagery; OT yoke metaphor (e.g., the good of bearing the yoke) lies in the background, though Peter inverts it as an unbearable load. Figural/contested.

pericopes.text: All the multitude kept silence, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul reporting what signs and wonders God had done among the nations through them. After they were silent, James answered, “Brothers, listen to me. Simeon has reported how God first visited the nations, to take out of them a people for his name.
