This agrees with the words of the prophets. As it is written, ‘After these things I will return. I will again build the tabernacle of David, which has fallen. I will again build its ruins. I will set it up, That the rest of men may seek after the Lord; all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who does all these things. All of God’s works are known to him from eternity.’ “Therefore my judgment is that we don’t trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God, but that we write to them that they abstain from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood. For Moses from generations of old has in every city those who preach him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath.”

echoes.text: In that day I will raise up the tent of David who is fallen, and close up its breaches, and I will raise up its ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old; that they may possess the remnant of Edom, and all the nations who are called by my name,” says Yahweh who does this.
echoes.note: James's formal scriptural proof (vv.16-17): 'I will... build the tabernacle of David which has fallen... that the rest of men may seek after the Lord, all the Gentiles who are called by my name.' This follows the Septuagint against the Hebrew: MT 'that they may possess the remnant of Edom' becomes LXX 'that the rest of mankind may seek' (Heb. yireshu 'possess' read as yidreshu 'seek'; 'Edom' read as 'adam, mankind) — the very reading that makes Gentile inclusion the prophetic point. Highest volume and decisive function in the argument.
echoes.lxxText: In that day I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and will rebuild the ruins of it, and will set up the parts thereof that have been broken down, and will build it up as in the ancient days: that the remnant of men, and all the Gentiles upon whom my name is called, may earnestly seek me, saith the Lord who does all these things.

echoes.text: It shall happen, after that I have plucked them up, I will return and have compassion on them; and I will bring them again, every man to his heritage, and every man to his land.
echoes.note: The opening of the citation, 'After these things I will return' (v.16), is not in Amos; it most closely matches 'I will return and have compassion on them,' suggesting James has conflated Amos with Jeremiah's restoration promise. A genuine secondary source spliced into the quotation.

echoes.text: Afterward the children of Israel shall return, and seek Yahweh their God, and David their king, and shall come with trembling to Yahweh and to his blessings in the last days.
echoes.note: 'Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God and David their king' shares the post-restoration 'seek the Lord' + Davidic motif underlying vv.16-17. Possible contributor to the catena's 'after these things... seek the Lord.' Contested.

echoes.text: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God, and Yahweh has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.
echoes.note: James says God 'first visited the nations, to take out of them a people for his name' (v.14). The phrase 'a people for his name/possession' reuses the election formula by which Israel was 'a people for his own possession' — now extended to Gentiles. Strong thematic reuse of covenant election language.

echoes.text: Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice, and keep my covenant, then you shall be my own possession from among all peoples; for all the earth is mine;
echoes.note: 'A people for his name' (v.14) echoes the Sinai promise that Israel would be God's 'treasured possession out of all peoples' — the foundational election text now applied to the nations. Recurrence with Deut 7:6 / 14:2.

echoes.text: Many nations shall join themselves to Yahweh in that day, and shall be my people; and I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that Yahweh of Armies has sent me to you.
echoes.note: 'Many nations shall join themselves to the LORD in that day and shall be my people' anticipates God taking a people from the Gentiles (v.14); part of the prophetic stream James invokes ('the words of the prophets,' v.15). Faint.

echoes.text: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me.
echoes.note: The closing tag, 'known to him from eternity / who declared these things of old' (vv.17b-18), resembles Isaiah's 'Who has declared this from of old?' — supplying the 'long-known to God' coloring appended to the Amos citation. Contested wording.

echoes.text: “You shall say to them, ‘Any man there is of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice, and doesn’t bring it to the door of the Tent of Meeting, to sacrifice it to Yahweh; that man shall be cut off from his people.
echoes.note: James's first prohibition, 'the pollution of idols' (v.20), corresponds to the resident-alien (ger) law forbidding sacrifices offered apart from the LORD — i.e., meat from idol-worship. The four-item decree as a whole derives from the laws binding on the stranger sojourning in Israel (Lev 17-18). High coherence; foundational to the decree.

echoes.text: “‘Any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who eats any kind of blood, I will set my face against that soul who eats blood, and will cut him off from among his people. For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life. Therefore I have said to the children of Israel, “No person […]
echoes.note: The prohibition of 'blood' (v.20) directly reuses the repeated Levitical ban applying to both Israelite and the resident alien: 'no one of you shall eat blood.' Explicitly extended to the ger, which is why it grounds rules for Gentile believers.

echoes.text: “‘Whatever man there is of the children of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who takes in hunting any animal or bird that may be eaten; he shall pour out its blood, and cover it with dust. For as to the life of all flesh, its blood is with its life: therefore I said to the children of Israel, “You shall not eat the blood of any kind of flesh; for the life of all flesh is its blood. Whoever eats it shall be cut off.” “‘Every […]
echoes.note: 'What is strangled' (v.20) reflects the requirement to drain the blood of any animal caught/killed — flesh with blood in it (a strangled animal) is forbidden, again binding on the sojourner. The 'strangled'/blood pairing in the decree mirrors this law.

echoes.text: “‘None of you shall approach anyone who are his close relatives, to uncover their nakedness: I am Yahweh. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father, nor the nakedness of your mother: she is your mother. You shall not uncover her nakedness. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife. It is your father’s nakedness. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, the daughter of your father, or the daughter of your mother, […]
echoes.note: 'Sexual immorality' (porneia, v.20) corresponds to the forbidden-unions catalogue of Lev 18, which v.26 expressly imposes on 'the stranger that sojourns among you.' The decree's fourth item completes the set of Holiness-Code rules for resident aliens.

echoes.text: But flesh with its life, that is, its blood, you shall not eat.
echoes.note: The blood prohibition (v.20) also rests on the Noahic command given to all humanity — 'flesh with its life, its blood, you shall not eat' — which suits Gentiles since it precedes and exceeds Israel's law. Often paired with Lev 17 as the rationale for a universally-binding minimum.

echoes.text: “‘Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, a holy convocation; you shall do no kind of work. It is a Sabbath to Yahweh in all your dwellings.
echoes.note: 'Moses... read in the synagogues every Sabbath' (v.21) presupposes the Sabbath institution as the appointed day of holy convocation. Faint, institutional background to the verse.

pericopes.text: Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole assembly, to choose men out of their company, and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, chief men among the brothers. They wrote these things by their hand: “The apostles, the elders, and the brothers, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: greetings. Because we have heard that some who went out from us have troubled you with words, unsettling your souls, saying, ‘You must be circumcised and keep the law,’ to whom we gave no commandment; it seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose out men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We have sent therefore Judas and Silas, who themselves will also tell you the same things by word of mouth. For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality, from which if you keep yourselves, it will be well with you. Farewell.”

echoes.text: “You shall say to them, ‘Any man there is of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice, and doesn’t bring it to the door of the Tent of Meeting, to sacrifice it to Yahweh; that man shall be cut off from his people.
echoes.note: The written decree restates the prohibitions: 'things sacrificed to idols' (v.29) reuses the Levitical ban on sacrifices offered outside the LORD's worship, binding on the resident alien. Repetition of the v.20 list.

echoes.text: “‘Any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who eats any kind of blood, I will set my face against that soul who eats blood, and will cut him off from among his people. For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life. Therefore I have said to the children of Israel, “No person […]
echoes.note: 'Blood' (v.29) again reflects the Holiness Code's repeated prohibition extended to the sojourner.

echoes.text: “‘Whatever man there is of the children of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who takes in hunting any animal or bird that may be eaten; he shall pour out its blood, and cover it with dust. For as to the life of all flesh, its blood is with its life: therefore I said to the children of Israel, “You shall not eat the blood of any kind of flesh; for the life of all flesh is its blood. Whoever eats it shall be cut off.” “‘Every […]
echoes.note: 'Things strangled' (v.29) reflects the requirement to drain blood from killed animals; flesh retaining blood is forbidden to Israelite and stranger alike.

echoes.text: “‘None of you shall approach anyone who are his close relatives, to uncover their nakedness: I am Yahweh. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father, nor the nakedness of your mother: she is your mother. You shall not uncover her nakedness. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife. It is your father’s nakedness. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, the daughter of your father, or the daughter of your mother, […]
echoes.note: 'Sexual immorality' (v.29) corresponds to the forbidden unions of Lev 18, imposed on the resident alien (v.26). The letter's four items reproduce the ger-laws of Lev 17-18.

echoes.text: But flesh with its life, that is, its blood, you shall not eat.
echoes.note: The blood abstention (v.29) coheres with the universal Noahic command against eating flesh with its blood, the natural basis for a rule binding on Gentiles.

pericopes.text: So, when they were sent off, they came to Antioch. Having gathered the multitude together, they delivered the letter. When they had read it, they rejoiced over the encouragement. Judas and Silas, also being prophets themselves, encouraged the brothers with many words, and strengthened them. After they had spent some time there, they were sent back with greetings from the brothers to the apostles. But Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.

After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.” Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also. But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work. Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him, and sailed away to Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas, and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God. He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.

He came to Derbe and Lystra: and behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewess who believed; but his father was a Greek. The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium gave a good testimony about him. Paul wanted to have him go out with him, and he took and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those parts; for they all knew that his father was a Greek. As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered the decrees to them to keep which had been ordained by the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem. So the assemblies were strengthened in the faith, and increased in number daily.

echoes.text: God said to Abraham, “As for you, you will keep my covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations. This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you. He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he […]
echoes.note: Paul circumcises Timothy 'because of the Jews.' The act invokes the Abrahamic covenant of circumcision as the enduring sign of belonging to the covenant people; Luke presents it as missionary accommodation rather than salvific necessity, but the gesture is unintelligible apart from this foundational statute.

echoes.text: When a stranger shall live as a foreigner with you, and will keep the Passover to Yahweh, let all his males be circumcised, and then let him come near and keep it; and he shall be as one who is born in the land: but no uncircumcised person shall eat of it.
echoes.note: The Passover rule that an uncircumcised man may not partake, while the circumcised foreigner becomes 'as one born in the land,' frames Timothy (son of a Jewess, Greek father) as a borderline figure regularized by circumcision so he can move freely among Jews. Thematic resonance; no verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: You shall teach them the statutes and the laws, and shall show them the way in which they must walk, and the work that they must do.
echoes.note: Delivering 'the decrees... to keep' which the apostles and elders ordained echoes the Mosaic pattern of transmitting statutes and ordinances for the people to keep; the apostolic council functions as a new authoritative legislature. Structural/lexical resonance (statutes delivered to be kept).

echoes.text: The children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and grew exceedingly mighty; and the land was filled with them.
echoes.note: 'The assemblies... increased in number daily' recalls the Septuagintal language of Israel multiplying and increasing greatly in Egypt (cf. Genesis 1:28); a recurring Lukan growth-formula casting the church as the multiplying covenant people.

pericopes.text: When they had gone through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit didn’t allow them. Passing by Mysia, they came down to Troas. A vision appeared to Paul in the night. There was a man of Macedonia standing, begging him, and saying, “Come over into Macedonia and help us.” When he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that the Lord had called us to preach the Good News to them.

echoes.text: God spoke to Israel in the visions of the night, and said, “Jacob, Jacob!” He said, “Here I am.” He said, “I am God, the God of your father. Don’t be afraid to go down into Egypt, for there I will make of you a great nation. I will go down with you into Egypt. I will also surely bring you up again. Joseph will close your eyes.”
echoes.note: God speaks to Israel/Jacob 'in visions of the night,' directing his movement to a new land ('I will go down with thee') with assurance of divine purpose. The Macedonian vision in the night that redirects Paul's journey across into Europe shares the genre (night vision) and function (divine redirection of geography) closely.

echoes.text: Yahweh went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them on their way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light, that they might go by day and by night:
echoes.note: The Spirit twice forbidding and not allowing the missionaries' chosen routes, then steering them, echoes the pillar of cloud and fire guiding Israel's route step by step; divine micromanagement of the missionary itinerary as a new wilderness leading. Thematic only.

echoes.text: After these things Yahweh’s word came to Abram in a vision, saying, “Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.”
echoes.note: 'A vision appeared to Paul in the night' uses the stock revelatory idiom of the word/vision of the LORD coming in the night; Abram's night vision is the paradigm of God commissioning through nocturnal revelation. Generic verbal resonance.

echoes.text: Then was the secret revealed to Daniel in a vision of the night. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven.
echoes.note: Mystery 'revealed in a night vision' as the medium of divine disclosure; faint Septuagintal parallel for night-vision revelation that resolves a course of action.

pericopes.text: Setting sail therefore from Troas, we made a straight course to Samothrace, and the day following to Neapolis; and from there to Philippi, which is a city of Macedonia, the foremost of the district, a Roman colony. We were staying some days in this city. On the Sabbath day we went outside of the city by a riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down, and spoke to the women who had come together. A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worshiped God, heard us; whose heart the Lord opened to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul. When she and her household were baptized, she begged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and stay.” So she persuaded us.

echoes.text: She makes for herself carpets of tapestry. Her clothing is fine linen and purple.
echoes.note: Lydia, a 'seller of purple' whose household and hospitality she manages, evokes the capable woman of Proverbs 31 whose clothing is purple and who trades in fine cloth; a wealthy, industrious, God-honoring matron. Suggestive characterization, no quotation.

echoes.text: blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen, goats’ hair,
echoes.note: Purple as the prized textile of the tabernacle offerings; Lydia's trade in purple carries an aura of dignity and devoted craft. Lexical (purple) only.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.
echoes.note: 'The Lord opened her heart to listen' is the divine-initiative idiom of the LORD circumcising/opening the heart so that Israel will hear and obey; conversion is portrayed as God's sovereign opening of the heart, the inward counterpart to covenant circumcision. Thematic coherence strong.

echoes.text: Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.
echoes.note: 'Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things' as the prayer-paradigm for God enabling perception of his word; Lydia's opened heart to attend to Paul's words is its narrative fulfillment. Conceptual parallel.

pericopes.text: As we were going to prayer, a certain girl having a spirit of divination met us, who brought her masters much gain by fortune telling. Following Paul and us, she cried out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to us a way of salvation!” She was doing this for many days. But Paul, becoming greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!” It came out that very hour. But when her masters saw that the hope of their gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas, and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. When they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, “These men, being Jews, are agitating our city, and advocate customs which it is not lawful for us to accept or to observe, being Romans.” The multitude rose up together against them, and the magistrates tore their clothes off of them, and commanded them to be beaten with rods. When they had laid many stripes on them, they threw them into prison, charging the jailer to keep them safely, who, having received such a command, threw them into the inner prison, and secured their feet in the stocks.

echoes.text: There shall not be found with you anyone who makes his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, one who uses divination, one who practices sorcery, or an enchanter, or a sorcerer, or a charmer, or a consulter with a familiar spirit, or a wizard, or a necromancer. For whoever does these things is an abomination to Yahweh. Because of these abominations, Yahweh your God drives them out from before you.
echoes.note: The slave girl has a 'spirit of divination' (Greek: a python spirit) and earns money by fortune-telling. The Mosaic legislation expressly bans divination, soothsaying, and consulting spirits as abominations among the nations Israel dispossesses; Paul's exorcism enacts the abolition of precisely this pagan practice. Strong thematic and conceptual coherence with the core prohibition.

echoes.text: “‘Don’t turn to those who are mediums, nor to the wizards. Don’t seek them out, to be defiled by them. I am Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: 'Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards.' The girl's mantic spirit is the very category Israel is forbidden to consult; Paul's command silences and casts out the source. Reinforces the divination-prohibition cluster.

echoes.text: “‘The person that turns to those who are mediums, and to the wizards, to play the prostitute after them, I will even set my face against that person, and will cut him off from among his people.
echoes.note: The penalty against souls turning after mediums and familiar spirits; the pericope dramatizes the divine verdict on a profit-driven mantic spirit. Thematic recurrence within the Holiness Code's ban on spiritism.

echoes.text: Then Saul said to his servants, “Seek me a woman who has a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and inquire of her.” His servants said to him, “Behold, there is a woman who has a familiar spirit at Endor.” Saul disguised himself, and put on other clothing, and went, he and two men with him, and they came to the woman by night: and he said, “Please divine to me by the familiar spirit, and bring me up whomever I shall name to you.” The woman said to him, […]
echoes.note: The medium of Endor as the canonical narrative instance of a woman trafficking in a familiar/divining spirit; the Philippian slave girl is its degraded Greco-Roman counterpart, here exposed and dispossessed. Narrative-typological resonance.

echoes.text: Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine: and he was priest of God Most High. He blessed him, and said, “Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth: and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.” Abram gave him a tenth of all.
echoes.note: The spirit's cry that these are servants of 'the Most High God' (El Elyon) uses the divine title introduced by Melchizedek, God Most High, maker of heaven and earth; a Gentile-context title for the one true God now proclaimed (ironically) by a pagan spirit. Lexical-theological link to the El Elyon title-tradition.

echoes.text: Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace: he spoke and said, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, you servants of the Most High God, come out, and come here. Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out of the midst of the fire.
echoes.note: 'Servants of the Most High God' is the Septuagintal acclamation applied to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego by a pagan king; the slave girl's confession echoes this Gentile recognition of servants of God Most High. Verbal parallel to the title.

echoes.text: Then Pashhur struck Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the upper gate of Benjamin, which was in Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: The prophet Jeremiah is beaten and put in the stocks for proclaiming God's word; Paul and Silas, beaten with rods and fastened in stocks in the inner prison, replay the persecuted-prophet-in-stocks pattern. Strong situational coherence (beating + stocks for the word).

echoes.text: Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, the place where the king’s prisoners were bound, and he was there in custody.
echoes.note: Joseph, falsely accused, is cast into the prison where the king's prisoners are bound, yet the LORD is with him; the righteous servant unjustly imprisoned and divinely vindicated prefigures Paul and Silas. Typological resonance setting up the deliverance.

echoes.text: It shall be, if the wicked man is worthy to be beaten, that the judge shall cause him to lie down, and to be beaten before his face, according to his wickedness, by number. He may sentence him to no more than forty stripes. He shall not give more; lest, if he should give more, and beat him more than that many stripes, then your brother will be degraded in your sight.
echoes.note: The Mosaic regulation of judicial beating by a fixed number of stripes ('many stripes' laid on them) supplies the legal-cultural backdrop for the flogging, though here the Roman magistrates' beating is lawless. Conceptual link to the stripes motif.

echoes.text: You also put my feet in the stocks, and mark all my paths. You set a bound to the soles of my feet,
echoes.note: 'Thou puttest my feet in the stocks' as the poetic image of constraint by an adversary; the securing of Paul and Silas's feet in the stocks resonates with this Joban idiom of the afflicted righteous (cf. Job 33:11). Lexical (feet in stocks).

pericopes.text: But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them. Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened. The jailer, being roused out of sleep and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, “Don’t harm yourself, for we are all here!” He called for lights, sprang in, fell down trembling before Paul and Silas, brought them out, and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.” They spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to all who were in his house. He took them the same hour of the night, and washed their stripes, and was immediately baptized, he and all his household. He brought them up into his house, and set food before them, and rejoiced greatly, with all his household, having believed in God.

echoes.text: He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke away their chains. Let them praise Yahweh for his loving kindness, for his wonderful works to the children of men! For he has broken the gates of brass, and cut through bars of iron.
echoes.note: God 'brought them out of darkness... and brake their bands in sunder,' for 'he hath broken the gates of brass, and cut the bars of iron in sunder.' The midnight earthquake that opens all the prison doors and looses everyone's bonds is the narrative enactment of this thanksgiving for the imprisoned whom God frees. Strong volume and thematic coherence; the controlling subtext for the deliverance.

echoes.text: who executes justice for the oppressed; who gives food to the hungry. Yahweh frees the prisoners.
echoes.note: 'The LORD looseth the prisoners' as a signature of God's saving character; the loosing of every prisoner's bonds dramatizes this divine attribute. Direct thematic match.

echoes.text: At midnight I will rise to give thanks to you, because of your righteous ordinances.
echoes.note: 'At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee.' Paul and Silas praying and singing hymns to God 'about midnight' closely matches the psalmist's nocturnal praise of the righteous sufferer who blesses God at the very hour of distress.

echoes.text: But no one says, ‘Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night,
echoes.note: 'God my maker, who giveth songs in the night' as the wisdom theme of praise amid darkness; the midnight hymns of the prisoners embody songs given in the night. Conceptual parallel.

echoes.text: Then the earth shook and trembled. The foundations also of the mountains quaked and were shaken, because he was angry.
echoes.note: 'The earth shook and trembled; the foundations also of the hills moved and were shaken' in God's deliverance of his servant from enemies; the 'great earthquake' shaking 'the foundations of the prison' is the theophanic-rescue earthquake of the Davidic deliverance psalm. Lexical (foundations shaken) and thematic.

echoes.text: Mount Sinai, all it, smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked greatly.
echoes.note: The quaking of Sinai at God's descent supplies the theophany-as-earthquake background; the prison earthquake signals God's powerful presence. Thematic resonance, generic earthquake-theophany.

echoes.text: “I will go before you, and make the rough places smooth. I will break the doors of brass in pieces, and cut apart the bars of iron.
echoes.note: 'I will break in pieces the gates of brass, and cut in sunder the bars of iron' (to Cyrus); a second prophetic instance of God shattering prison/city barriers, reinforcing the Psalm 107 gate-breaking motif behind the opened doors. Recurrence of the broken-barriers theme.

echoes.text: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.
echoes.note: The Servant's commission 'to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house'; the liberation of the jailer's prisoners realizes this servant-mission imagery. Thematic.

echoes.text: You have turned my mourning into dancing for me. You have removed my sackcloth, and clothed me with gladness,
echoes.note: 'Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing'; the jailer who was about to kill himself ends 'rejoicing greatly with all his household,' the reversal-into-joy pattern of the deliverance psalms. Conceptual resonance for the turn from despair to rejoicing.

pericopes.text: But when it was day, the magistrates sent the sergeants, saying, “Let those men go.” The jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go; now therefore come out, and go in peace.” But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly, without a trial, men who are Romans, and have cast us into prison! Do they now release us secretly? No, most certainly, but let them come themselves and bring us out!” The sergeants reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans, and they came and begged them. When they had brought them out, they asked them to depart from the city. They went out of the prison, and entered into Lydia’s house. When they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them, and departed.

echoes.text: Then Eli answered, “Go in peace; and may the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of him.”
echoes.note: 'Go in peace' is the stock Hebrew dismissal-blessing (cf. Exodus 4:18; Judges 18:6); the jailer's 'go in peace' to the released prisoners carries this benedictory idiom. Lexical formula only.

echoes.text: The wicked flee when no one pursues; but the righteous are as bold as a lion.
echoes.note: 'The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.' The magistrates who were 'afraid when they heard that they were Romans' and came begging, while Paul stands boldly on his rights, illustrates this wisdom reversal of fear between the unjust and the vindicated righteous. Thematic.

echoes.text: Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon. He shaved himself, changed his clothing, and came in to Pharaoh.
echoes.note: Joseph brought out of the prison and publicly vindicated before the authorities; Paul's insistence that the magistrates themselves come and bring them out continues the unjustly-imprisoned-then-honorably-released pattern. Typological resonance closing the prison sequence.

echoes.text: Now in the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, on the thirteenth day of the month, when the king’s commandment and his decree drew near to be put in execution, on the day that the enemies of the Jews hoped to conquer them, (but it was turned out the opposite happened, that the Jews conquered those who hated them), the Jews gathered themselves together in their cities throughout all the provinces of the King Ahasuerus, to lay hands on those who wanted […]
echoes.note: The reversal in which fear of the formerly oppressed falls upon the officials and rulers who had moved against them; the Philippian magistrates' fear and capitulation echoes this peripeteia of vindication. Faint thematic link.

pericopes.text: Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue. Paul, as was his custom, went in to them, and for three Sabbath days reasoned with them from the Scriptures, explaining and demonstrating that the Christ had to suffer and rise again from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.” Some of them were persuaded, and joined Paul and Silas, of the devout Greeks a great multitude, and not a few of the chief women. But the unpersuaded Jews took along some wicked men from the marketplace, and gathering a crowd, set the city in an uproar. Assaulting the house of Jason, they sought to bring them out to the people. When they didn’t find them, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the rulers of the city, crying, “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also, whom Jason has received. These all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus!” The multitude and the rulers of the city were troubled when they heard these things. When they had taken security from Jason and the rest, they let them go.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we […]
echoes.note: Paul reasons 'from the Scriptures' that the Christ 'had to suffer'; the Suffering Servant is the natural scriptural ground for a suffering Messiah, a recurrent NT proof-text. Volume modest in the narrative summary itself but thematic coherence with the synagogue argument is strong.

echoes.text: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.
echoes.note: 'rise again from the dead' echoes the psalm's 'you will not abandon my soul to Sheol,' the standard apostolic resurrection proof from Scripture (cf. its explicit use in earlier Acts speeches). Recurrence high in Luke-Acts.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'rise again' may glance at 'on the third day he will raise us up'; verbal contact is thin and the third-day motif is not stated here, so the link is faint and contested.

echoes.text: Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing? The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,
echoes.note: The charge that Paul proclaims 'another king, Jesus' resonates with the psalm's rulers raging against the LORD and his Anointed; Luke elsewhere cites Psalm 2, so recurrence supports a faint background, though no quotation is made here.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'another king' set against Caesar's decrees may evoke the everlasting dominion given to the son of man, but verbal volume is negligible.

pericopes.text: The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea. When they arrived, they went into the Jewish synagogue. Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of the mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so. Many of them therefore believed; also of the prominent Greek women, and not a few men. But when the Jews of Thessalonica had knowledge that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Beroea also, they came there likewise, agitating the multitudes. Then the brothers immediately sent out Paul to go as far as to the sea, and Silas and Timothy still stayed there. But those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens. Receiving a commandment to Silas and Timothy that they should come to him very quickly, they departed.

echoes.text: but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.
echoes.note: The Beroeans 'examining the Scriptures daily' figurally images the blessed one who meditates on the law day and night; thematic coherence only, no verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: It shall be, when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write himself a copy of this law in a book, out of that which is before the priests the Levites. It shall be with him, and he shall read from it all the days of his life; that he may learn to fear Yahweh his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them;
echoes.note: Daily reading and searching of the written word loosely recalls the king's charge to read the law all his days; very faint.

pericopes.text: Now while Paul waited for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who met him. Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also were conversing with him. Some said, “What does this babbler want to say?” Others said, “He seems to be advocating foreign deities,” because he preached Jesus and the resurrection. They took hold of him, and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is, which is spoken by you? For you bring certain strange things to our ears. We want to know therefore what these things mean.” Now all the Athenians and the strangers living there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell or to hear some new thing.

echoes.text: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.
echoes.note: Paul's spirit 'provoked' (paroxynein) at a city full of idols echoes the LXX of Israel provoking God to anger with their idols, the same verb-field; thematic coherence between human and divine zeal against idolatry is strong.

echoes.text: Therefore also among the idols of the nations will there be a visitation, Because, though formed of things which God created, they were made an abomination, And stumbling blocks to the souls of men, And a snare to the feet of the foolish. For the devising of idols was the beginning of fornication, And the invention of them the corruption of life: For neither were they from the beginning, neither will they be forever; For by the vaingloriousness of men […]
echoes.note: A 'city full of idols' matches Wisdom's diatribe on the proliferation of cult images; deuterocanonical idol-polemic is the closest contemporary parallel and frames the whole Athens episode.

echoes.text: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they don’t speak. They have eyes, but they don’t see. They have ears, but they don’t hear. They have noses, but they don’t smell. They have hands, but they don’t feel. They have feet, but they don’t walk, neither do they speak through their throat. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.
echoes.note: The lifeless 'idols' that provoke Paul evoke the classic psalm of handmade gods of silver and gold that cannot see or hear; recurrence of this polemic across the Psalter is high.

echoes.text: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they can’t speak. They have eyes, but they can’t see. They have ears, but they can’t hear; neither is there any breath in their mouths. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.
echoes.note: Parallel idol-polemic to Psalm 115; included for completeness as a recurrent OT topos behind the scene.

echoes.text: Everyone who makes an engraved image is vain. The things that they delight in will not profit. Their own witnesses don’t see, nor know, that they may be disappointed. Who has fashioned a god, or molds an image that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all his fellows will be disappointed; and the workmen are mere men. Let them all be gathered together. Let them stand up. They will fear. They will be put to shame together. The blacksmith takes an ax, works […]
echoes.note: Isaiah's extended mockery of the craftsman who fashions a god stands behind both Paul's revulsion here and his later argument that the divine is not 'engraved by art'; sets up vv.29.

echoes.text: Hear the word which Yahweh speaks to you, house of Israel! Thus says Yahweh, “Don’t learn the way of the nations, and don’t be dismayed at the signs of the sky; for the nations are dismayed at them. For the customs of the peoples are vanity; for one cuts a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the workman with the ax. They deck it with silver and with gold; they fasten it with nails and with hammers, that it not move. They are like a palm tree, […]
echoes.note: Jeremiah's contrast of dead idols with the living Creator anticipates Paul's pivot from idols to the God who made all; thematic, not verbal.

pericopes.text: Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus, and said, “You men of Athens, I perceive that you are very religious in all things. For as I passed along, and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What therefore you worship in ignorance, this I announce to you. The God who made the world and all things in it, he, being Lord of heaven and earth, doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands, neither is he served by men’s hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he himself gives to all life and breath, and all things. He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons, and the boundaries of their dwellings, that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us. ‘For in him we live, and move, and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his offspring.’ Being then the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold, or silver, or stone, engraved by art and design of man. The times of ignorance therefore God overlooked. But now he commands that all people everywhere should repent, because he has appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has ordained; of which he has given assurance to all men, in that he has raised him from the dead.”

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: 'The God who made the world and all things in it' is creation-monotheism rooted in the opening of Genesis; high volume and thematic coherence, the foundation of the whole sermon.

echoes.text: Thus says God Yahweh, he who created the heavens and stretched them out, he who spread out the earth and that which comes out of it, he who gives breath to its people and spirit to those who walk in it.
echoes.note: Isaiah's God who 'created the heavens... gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who walk in it' tightly combines both of Paul's claims: maker of the world (v.24) and giver of life and breath (v.25). Strong verbal and conceptual overlap.

echoes.text: for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed the Sabbath day, and made it holy.
echoes.note: 'made the heaven and the earth, the sea and all that is in them' is echoed in 'made the world and all things in it... Lord of heaven and earth'; recurrent creation formula.

echoes.text: who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who keeps truth forever;
echoes.note: 'who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them' parallels v.24's creation summary; recurrence of the formula raises confidence.

echoes.text: You are Yahweh, even you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their army, the earth and all things that are on it, the seas and all that is in them, and you preserve them all. The army of heaven worships you.
echoes.note: 'You made heaven... the earth and all that is on it... and you give life to them all' parallels both creation and life-giving themes; included as a recurrent OT confession.

echoes.text: He blessed him, and said, “Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth:
echoes.note: 'Lord of heaven and earth' (v.24) echoes 'God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth'; faint title-level contact.

echoes.text: Behold, to Yahweh your God belongs heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth, with all that is therein.
echoes.note: 'heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth and all that is in it' supports 'Lord of heaven and earth'; recurrent title.

echoes.text: But will God in very deed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house that I have built!
echoes.note: Solomon's 'heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house I have built' directly grounds 'does not dwell in temples made with hands.' Strong thematic coherence at the dedication of the very institution Paul relativizes.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: what kind of house will you build to me? and what place shall be my rest? For all these things has my hand made, and so all these things came to be,” says Yahweh: “but to this man will I look, even to him who is poor and of a contrite spirit, and who trembles at my word.
echoes.note: 'Heaven is my throne and the earth my footstool; what house will you build for me?' is the prophetic charter for 'does not dwell in temples made with hands' and for needing nothing from human hands; quoted by Stephen in Acts 7, so recurrence in Acts is high.

echoes.text: “But will God indeed dwell with men on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house which I have built!
echoes.note: Parallel to 1 Kings 8:27, the same temple-cannot-contain-God confession behind v.24.

echoes.text: I don’t rebuke you for your sacrifices. Your burnt offerings are continually before me. I have no need for a bull from your stall, nor male goats from your pens. For every animal of the forest is mine, and the livestock on a thousand hills. I know all the birds of the mountains. The wild animals of the field are mine. If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is mine, and all that is in it. Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of […]
echoes.note: 'If I were hungry I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine' grounds v.25, that God is not 'served by human hands as though he needed anything'; strong thematic coherence with sacrificial critique.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: 'He himself gives to all life and breath' echoes God breathing the breath of life into the man; foundational creation text for the life-giver claim.

echoes.text: in whose hand is the life of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind?
echoes.note: 'In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind' closely matches 'gives to all life and breath.'

echoes.text: The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.
echoes.note: 'The breath of the Almighty gives me life' parallels v.25's life and breath; recurrent wisdom motif.

echoes.text: They fell on their faces, and said, “God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?”
echoes.note: 'God of the spirits of all flesh' supports the universal life-giver theme of v.25.

echoes.text: For thus says the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite. For I will not contend forever, neither will I be always angry; for the spirit would faint before me, and the souls who I have made.
echoes.note: The high and lofty One who nonetheless gives breath ('the breath that I have made') touches v.25; faint.

echoes.text: When the Most High gave to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the children of men, he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel.
echoes.note: 'When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance... he fixed the boundaries of the peoples' is the key text behind v.26, God making every nation and 'fixing the boundaries of their dwellings.' Strong verbal and conceptual coherence.

echoes.text: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them. God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
echoes.note: 'Made from one... every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth' draws on the creation and filling of the earth from the one human pair.

echoes.text: These are the families of the sons of Noah, by their generations, according to their nations. The nations divided from these in the earth after the flood.
echoes.note: The Table of Nations, all peoples spreading 'from one' after the flood, underlies the unity-of-nations claim in v.26.

echoes.text: God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of sky to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs to mark seasons, days, and years;
echoes.note: 'Determined appointed seasons' may glance at the luminaries set 'for seasons'; faint, since the sense here is more likely the epochs of nations.

echoes.text: He increases the nations, and he destroys them. He enlarges the nations, and he leads them captive.
echoes.note: 'He makes nations great, and destroys them; he enlarges nations, and leads them away' parallels v.26's sovereign setting of appointed times and boundaries for peoples.

echoes.text: You have set all the boundaries of the earth. You have made summer and winter.
echoes.note: 'You have fixed all the boundaries of the earth' directly supports 'the boundaries of their dwellings' in v.26.

echoes.text: But from there you shall seek Yahweh your God, and you shall find him, when you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul.
echoes.note: 'You will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search with all your heart' underlies v.27, that the nations 'should seek the Lord... and find him.'

echoes.text: Seek Yahweh while he may be found; call you on him while he is near:
echoes.note: 'Seek the LORD while he may be found' parallels v.27's seek-and-find; recurrent prophetic summons.

echoes.text: You shall seek me, and find me, when you shall search for me with all your heart.
echoes.note: 'You will seek me and find me, when you seek with all your heart' parallels v.27; recurrent seek-and-find formula.

echoes.text: Yahweh is near to all those who call on him, to all who call on him in truth.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is near to all who call on him' grounds 'he is not far from each one of us' (v.27).

echoes.text: Am I a God at hand, says Yahweh, and not a God afar off? Can any hide himself in secret places so that I shall not see him? says Yahweh. Don’t I fill heaven and earth? says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Am I a God near at hand... and not a God far off? Do I not fill heaven and earth?' closely supports 'not far from each one of us' and the immanence of vv.27-28.

echoes.text: For what great nation is there, that has a god so near to them, as Yahweh our God is whenever we call on him?
echoes.note: 'What nation has a god so near to it as the LORD?' supports the nearness theme of v.27; faint.

echoes.text: To whom then will you liken God? Or what likeness will you compare to him? A workman has cast an image, and the goldsmith overlays it with gold, and casts silver chains for it. He who is too impoverished for such an offering chooses a tree that will not rot. He seeks a skillful workman to set up an engraved image for him that will not be moved.
echoes.note: 'To whom will you liken God?... a craftsman casts an idol, a goldsmith overlays it with gold' directly grounds v.29, that the Divine Nature is not 'like gold, or silver, or stone, engraved by art.'

echoes.text: Everyone who makes an engraved image is vain. The things that they delight in will not profit. Their own witnesses don’t see, nor know, that they may be disappointed. Who has fashioned a god, or molds an image that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all his fellows will be disappointed; and the workmen are mere men. Let them all be gathered together. Let them stand up. They will fear. They will be put to shame together. The blacksmith takes an ax, works […]
echoes.note: The craftsman who fashions a god from wood/metal stands behind v.29's rejection of images 'engraved by art and design of man.'

echoes.text: There you shall serve gods, the work of men’s hands, wood and stone, which neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.
echoes.note: Idols 'the work of human hands, wood and stone, which neither see nor hear' parallels v.29's gold, silver, and stone made by human craft.

echoes.text: “To whom will you liken me, and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be like? Some pour out gold from the bag, and weigh silver in the balance. They hire a goldsmith, and he makes it a god. They fall down—yes, they worship. They bear it on the shoulder, they carry it, and set it in its place, and it stands, from its place it shall not move: yes, one may cry to it, yet it can not answer, nor save him out of his trouble.
echoes.note: 'To whom will you liken me?... they hire a goldsmith who makes it into a god' parallels v.29; recurrent Isaianic idol-polemic.

echoes.text: For verily all men by nature were but vain who had no perception of God, And from the good things that are seen they gained not power to know him that is, Neither by giving heed to the works did they recognize the architect; But either fire, or wind, or swift air, Or circling stars, or raging water, or luminaries of heaven, They thought to be gods that rule the world. And if it was through delight in their beauty that they took them to be gods, Let them […]
echoes.note: Wisdom's critique that people who admired the world's beauty failed to find its Maker, yet are 'not to be excused' because they could seek and find, closely tracks vv.24-29 (knowing the Creator from creation, seeking and finding). The deuterocanonical natural-theology bridge is the nearest analogue to the whole Areopagus argument.

echoes.text: But miserable were they, and in dead things were their hopes, Who called them gods which are works of men’s hands, Gold and silver, wrought with careful are, and likenesses of animals, Or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand.
echoes.note: 'Miserable... who called gods the works of human hands, gold and silver fashioned with skill, and likenesses of animals, or useless stone' is verbally very close to v.29's gold, silver, and stone shaped by human art.

echoes.text: But you have mercy on all men, because you have power to do all things, And you overlookest the sins of men to the end they may repent.
echoes.note: 'You overlook the sins of men, that they may repent' parallels v.30, God 'overlooked' the times of ignorance and now commands repentance.

echoes.text: Remember the commandments, and be not angry with your neighbor; And remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.
echoes.note: Faint contact with the call to overlook ignorance and turn; weak link to v.30.

echoes.text: before Yahweh; for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, the peoples with his truth.
echoes.note: 'He comes to judge the earth; he will judge the world in righteousness' is almost verbatim with v.31, that God 'will judge the world in righteousness.' High volume.

echoes.text: He will judge the world in righteousness. He will administer judgment to the peoples in uprightness.
echoes.note: 'He will judge the world in righteousness' is a near-exact verbal parallel to v.31; recurrence of this formula across the Psalter strengthens the link.

echoes.text: Let them sing before Yahweh, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity.
echoes.note: 'He comes to judge the earth; he will judge the world with righteousness' is the third near-identical parallel to v.31, confirming a fixed liturgical formula behind Paul's words.

echoes.text: Say among the nations, “Yahweh reigns.” The world is also established. It can’t be moved. He will judge the peoples with equity.
echoes.note: 'He will judge the peoples with equity' reinforces the universal-righteous-judgment theme of v.31.

echoes.text: “Yet I have set my King on my holy hill of Zion.” I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father. Ask of me, and I will give the nations for your inheritance, the uttermost parts of the earth for your possession. You shall break them with a rod of iron. You shall dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel.”
echoes.note: Judgment 'by the man whom he has ordained' evokes the installed/anointed son to whom the nations are given; coherent with the appointed agent of v.31.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: Judgment of the world entrusted to 'the man' (anthropos) recalls the son of man given everlasting dominion and judgment; supports the human appointed judge of v.31.

echoes.text: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.
echoes.note: 'God will bring every deed into judgment' supports the coming-judgment theme of v.31; faint, no verbal contact.

pericopes.text: Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others said, “We want to hear you again concerning this.” Thus Paul went out from among them. But certain men joined with him, and believed, among whom also was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The Athenians' reaction to 'the resurrection of the dead' brushes the OT bodily-resurrection hope of those who 'sleep in the dust' awakening; thematic background only, no verbal borrowing in the narrative response.

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'Your dead shall live... the earth will give birth to the dead' is the prophetic resurrection hope behind the doctrine the philosophers mock; faint.

pericopes.text: After these things Paul departed from Athens, and came to Corinth. He found a certain Jew named Aquila, a man of Pontus by race, who had recently come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome. He came to them, and because he practiced the same trade, he lived with them and worked, for by trade they were tent makers. He reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and persuaded Jews and Greeks.

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
echoes.note: Paul reasons in the synagogue 'every Sabbath' (v.4); the rhythm of weekly Sabbath gathering presupposes the Decalogue's Sabbath command. Faint and institutional rather than verbal, but the Sabbath frame is the OT scaffolding for the scene.

echoes.text: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
echoes.note: Paul stays with Aquila and Priscilla and works as a tentmaker (vv.2-3), earning bread by the labor of his own hands. A faint resonance with the Edenic decree of toil/sweat; the motif of apostolic self-support by manual labor draws on the dignity-and-burden-of-work theme rooted here.

pericopes.text: But when Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul was compelled by the Spirit, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ. When they opposed him and blasphemed, he shook out his clothing and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean. From now on, I will go to the Gentiles!”

echoes.text: Also I shook out my lap, and said, “So may God shake out every man from his house, and from his labor, that doesn’t perform this promise; even thus be he shaken out, and emptied.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh. The people did according to this promise.
echoes.note: Paul 'shook out his clothing' (garment) as a prophetic sign-act against those who oppose him — directly mirroring Nehemiah shaking out the fold of his robe as a curse-gesture: 'So may God shake out everyone... who does not perform this promise.' A symbolic disavowal handing the consequences back on the offenders.

echoes.text: then whoever hears the sound of the trumpet, and doesn’t take warning, if the sword come, and take him away, his blood shall be on his own head.
echoes.note: 'Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean' transposes the watchman oracle: the warned who ignore the trumpet bear their own blood, while the faithful watchman has delivered his soul. Paul casts himself as the discharged watchman, his hearers as the warned-but-unheeding.

echoes.text: Nevertheless, if you warn the wicked of his way to turn from it, and he doesn’t turn from his way; he shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul.
echoes.note: The watchman who warns the wicked and is not heeded 'has delivered his soul' — exactly Paul's claim 'I am clean.' Recurrence with Ezekiel 33:4 strengthens the watchman frame.

echoes.text: When I tell the wicked, You shall surely die; and you give him no warning, nor speak to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life; the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at your hand.
echoes.note: The original commissioning of the watchman: if he warns and the wicked does not turn, 'you will have delivered your soul.' Paul's 'I am clean / your blood on your heads' draws on this earlier statement of the same principle.

echoes.text: David said to him, “Your blood be on your head; for your mouth has testified against you, saying, ‘I have slain Yahweh’s anointed.’”
echoes.note: 'Your blood be on your own head' is David's verdict on the Amalekite — the same idiom of self-incurred bloodguilt that Paul pronounces over the resisting synagogue.

echoes.text: “‘For everyone who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death: he has cursed his father or his mother; his blood shall be upon him.
echoes.note: The recurring legal formula 'his blood shall be upon him' (cf. vv.11-13,16,27) is the juridical source of the 'blood on your own head' idiom of self-responsibility that Paul invokes.

echoes.text: It shall be that whoever goes out of the doors of your house into the street, his blood will be on his head, and we will be guiltless. Whoever is with you in the house, his blood shall be on our head, if any hand is on him.
echoes.note: Rahab's covenant: anyone who goes out of the house, 'his blood shall be on his own head,' while the household is held guiltless — the same shifting-of-bloodguilt formula behind Paul's declaration.

echoes.text: has lent on interest, and has taken increase; shall he then live? he shall not live: he has done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be on him.
echoes.note: 'His blood shall be upon himself' in the chapter on individual responsibility reinforces the bloodguilt idiom underlying Paul's words.

pericopes.text: He departed there, and went into the house of a certain man named Justus, one who worshiped God, whose house was next door to the synagogue. Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with all his house. Many of the Corinthians, when they heard, believed and were baptized. The Lord said to Paul in the night by a vision, “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent; for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.” He lived there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.

echoes.text: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.
echoes.note: The night-vision reassurance 'Do not be afraid... for I am with you' is the classic divine-encouragement formula, of which Isaiah 41:10 ('Fear not, for I am with you... I will strengthen you') is the paradigm. Paul stands in the line of those summoned and steadied by God's presence.

echoes.text: Don’t be afraid because of them; for I am with you to deliver you,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's prophetic call: 'Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you.' Paul's commission to keep speaking despite opposition echoes the prophet's reassurance against hostile hearers.

echoes.text: They will fight against you; but they will not prevail against you; for I am with you”, says Yahweh, “to deliver you.”
echoes.note: 'They will fight against you but will not prevail, for I am with you' closely matches 'no one will attack you to harm you, for I am with you' — the same promise of protected speech in a hostile city.

echoes.text: He said, “Certainly I will be with you. This will be the token to you, that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain.”
echoes.note: 'I will be with you' grounds Moses' sending; the same assurance underwrites Paul's mission in Corinth. The call-narrative pattern (objection met by promise of presence) shapes the vision.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him the same night, and said, “I am the God of Abraham your father. Don’t be afraid, for I am with you, and will bless you, and multiply your seed for my servant Abraham’s sake.”
echoes.note: Closest single parallel: the LORD appears to Isaac by night and says, 'Do not be afraid, for I am with you... I will multiply your offspring.' Night theophany + 'fear not' + 'I am with you' + promise of a great people maps almost point-for-point onto vv.9-10, including 'I have many people in this city.'

echoes.text: Haven’t I commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid, neither be dismayed: for Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.”
echoes.note: 'Do not be frightened... for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go' — the commissioning encouragement to a leader facing a daunting task, reused for Paul.

echoes.text: Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid or scared of them; for Yahweh your God himself is who goes with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you.”
echoes.note: 'Do not fear... for the LORD your God goes with you; he will not leave you' belongs to the same 'fear not / I am with you' tradition behind the vision.

echoes.text: Don’t be afraid; for I am with you. I will bring your seed from the east, and gather you from the west.
echoes.note: 'Fear not, for I am with you' paired with gathering a people resonates with both the reassurance and the promise of 'many people in this city.'

pericopes.text: But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews with one accord rose up against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat, saying, “This man persuades men to worship God contrary to the law.” But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If indeed it were a matter of wrong or of wicked crime, you Jews, it would be reasonable that I should bear with you; but if they are questions about words and names and your own law, look to it yourselves. For I don’t want to be a judge of these matters.” He drove them from the judgment seat. Then all the Greeks laid hold on Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. Gallio didn’t care about any of these things.

echoes.text: Unrighteous witnesses rise up. They ask me about things that I don’t know about.
echoes.note: Paul is haled before the tribunal by accusers who 'rose up' with malicious charges — the lament motif of malicious witnesses rising against the righteous sufferer ('Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things I do not know').

echoes.text: “You shall not spread a false report. Don’t join your hand with the wicked to be a malicious witness.
echoes.note: The concerted false accusation 'with one accord' before the judgment seat faintly recalls the law against joining a multitude to bring a malicious/false charge.

pericopes.text: Paul, having stayed after this many more days, took his leave of the brothers, and sailed from there for Syria, together with Priscilla and Aquila. He shaved his head in Cenchreae, for he had a vow. He came to Ephesus, and he left them there; but he himself entered into the synagogue, and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay with them a longer time, he declined; but taking his leave of them, and saying, “I must by all means keep this coming feast in Jerusalem, but I will return again to you if God wills,” he set sail from Ephesus. When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the assembly, and went down to Antioch. Having spent some time there, he departed, and went through the region of Galatia, and Phrygia, in order, establishing all the disciples.

echoes.text: The Nazirite shall shave the head of his separation at the door of the Tent of Meeting, and shall take the hair of the head of his separation, and put it on the fire which is under the sacrifice of peace offerings.
echoes.note: Paul 'shaved his head in Cenchreae, for he had a vow' — the Nazirite practice of shaving the head at the completion/discharge of a vow. Numbers 6:18 specifies shaving the consecrated head; the detail marks Paul's continued observance of Torah piety.

echoes.text: “‘All the days of his vow of separation no razor shall come on his head, until the days are fulfilled, in which he separates himself to Yahweh. He shall be holy. He shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow long.
echoes.note: The Nazirite law that no razor touch the head during the vow's duration (the hair grown then shaved) underlies the haircut-as-vow-completion in v.18. Recurrence with Numbers 6:18 anchors the Nazirite frame.

echoes.text: Three times in a year all of your shall males appear before Yahweh your God in the place which he chooses: in the feast of unleavened bread, in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tents. They shall not appear before Yahweh empty.
echoes.note: Paul's resolve to 'keep this coming feast in Jerusalem' (v.21) reflects the pilgrimage-feast obligation to appear before the LORD at the appointed feasts in Jerusalem.

echoes.text: Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord Yahweh.
echoes.note: The thrice-yearly command to appear before the Lord undergirds Paul's intention to keep the feast in Jerusalem; faint and institutional.

pericopes.text: Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus. He was mighty in the Scriptures. This man had been instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he knew only the baptism of John. He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately. When he had determined to pass over into Achaia, the brothers encouraged him, and wrote to the disciples to receive him. When he had come, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace; for he powerfully refuted the Jews, publicly showing by the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ.

echoes.text: I will also speak of your statutes before kings, and will not be disappointed.
echoes.note: Apollos, 'mighty in the Scriptures,' speaks boldly in the synagogue and publicly refutes opponents from Scripture — resonating with the psalmist's resolve to 'speak of your testimonies before kings and not be put to shame.' Faint thematic, no verbal borrowing.

pericopes.text: While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper country, came to Ephesus, and found certain disciples. He said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They said to him, “No, we haven’t even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” He said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.” Paul said, “John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying to the people that they should believe in the one who would come after him, that is, in Jesus.” When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. When Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they spoke with other languages and prophesied. They were about twelve men in all.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: The Spirit comes upon the twelve disciples and they prophesy and speak in other tongues. Joel's promise of the outpoured Spirit producing prophecy (Volume: shared Spirit-prophecy idiom; Recurrence: this is Luke's programmatic Pentecost text from Acts 2, re-applied here to a 'second Pentecost' at Ephesus; Thematic Coherence: strong, the Spirit poured on believers issuing in prophetic speech). Satisfaction: the Ephesian episode reads as a deliberate echo of the Joel fulfillment Luke announced in Acts 2.

echoes.text: Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more. But two men remained in the camp. The name of one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the Spirit rested on them; and they were of those who were written, but had not gone out to the Tent; and they prophesied in the camp. A young man ran, and told […]
echoes.note: When the Spirit rests on the seventy elders they prophesy; here the Spirit comes and the twelve prophesy. The corporate, derivative bestowal of the Spirit producing immediate prophecy is a close conceptual match (Volume: moderate; Recurrence: Luke elsewhere draws on Numbers 11 Moses/spirit motifs; Coherence: high). Moses' wish that all the Lord's people were prophets stands behind Luke's spreading-Spirit theology.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and commission him in their sight. You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before Yahweh. At his word they shall go out, and at his […]
echoes.note: Paul lays his hands on the disciples and the Spirit comes; Moses lays hands on Joshua, a man in whom is the Spirit, transferring authority. The laying-on-of-hands-to-convey-Spirit gesture has its primary OT root here (with Deut 34:9). Low volume, contested as it may simply be a fixed cultic gesture.

echoes.text: Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands on him. The children of Israel listened to him, and did as Yahweh commanded Moses.
