echoes.note: Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him; here laying on of hands conveys the Spirit. Reinforces the Mosaic hand-laying/Spirit-transfer pattern. Low volume, contested.

echoes.text: and the Spirit of Yahweh will come mightily on you, and you shall prophesy with them, and shall be turned into another man.
echoes.note: The Spirit of the Lord rushes upon Saul and he prophesies, turned into another man; here the Spirit comes and the disciples prophesy. A stock OT pattern of Spirit-onset producing ecstatic prophecy. Contested, faint verbal contact.

echoes.text: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God.
echoes.note: Paul explains John's baptism as preparatory, pointing to the Coming One. John's whole ministry is grounded in the Isaian voice preparing the way; this verse explicitly recalls the forerunner role. Faint here since the verbal weight is minimal in this pericope.

pericopes.text: He entered into the synagogue, and spoke boldly for a period of three months, reasoning and persuading about the things concerning the Kingdom of God. But when some were hardened and disobedient, speaking evil of the Way before the multitude, he departed from them, and separated the disciples, reasoning daily in the school of Tyrannus. This continued for two years, so that all those who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks.

echoes.text: But the house of Israel will not listen to you; for they will not listen to me: for all the house of Israel are obstinate and hard-hearted.
echoes.note: Paul preaches boldly in the synagogue until some are hardened and disobedient, speaking evil of the Way; Ezekiel is told the house of Israel will not listen because they are hard of forehead and stubborn of heart. The hardened-hearer motif of the prophet's rejected word is strongly coherent (Volume: shared hardening/refusal language; Recurrence: Luke uses Israel-hardening as a structuring theme in Acts; Coherence: high).

echoes.text: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: The hardening of those who hear the word, leading the messenger to turn elsewhere, echoes Isaiah's commission to a people whose heart is made fat and will not understand. Luke cites this text explicitly in Acts 28 as the climactic interpretation of Jewish unbelief, making it a recurring lens here. Coherence high; verbal contact in this pericope is allusive.

echoes.text: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.
echoes.note: Paul reasons and persuades about the Kingdom of God for three months. Daniel's God of heaven who sets up an everlasting kingdom is a chief OT source of the kingdom-of-God language. Faint, since the phrase is summary. Contested.

echoes.text: so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
echoes.note: Over two years all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord; Isaiah's word that goes out and does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose underlies Luke's repeated 'the word spread/grew' refrain. Faint here, fuller at 19:20. Contested.

pericopes.text: God worked special miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons were carried away from his body to the sick, and the evil spirits went out.

echoes.text: As they were burying a man, behold, they saw a band of raiders; and they threw the man into Elisha’s tomb. As soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.
echoes.note: Cloths that had touched Paul's body heal the sick and expel spirits; mere contact with Elisha's bones revives a dead man. The motif of healing power mediated through physical contact with a holy person (even at a remove) is a strong conceptual parallel to the Elisha cycle (Volume: shared contact-healing logic; Recurrence: Luke models Paul/Peter on Elijah-Elisha; Coherence: high).

echoes.text: Then he said to Gehazi, “Tuck your cloak into your belt, take my staff in your hand, and go your way. If you meet any man, don’t greet him; and if anyone greets you, don’t answer him again. Then lay my staff on the face of the child.” The mother of the child said, “As Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” He arose, and followed her. Gehazi passed on before them, and laid the staff on the face of the child; but there was neither […]
echoes.note: Elisha sends his staff (an extension of himself) ahead to heal, then heals by bodily contact; here objects from Paul's body carry healing virtue. The mediating-object pattern links the two. Low volume, contested.

echoes.text: Elijah took his mantle, and wrapped it together, and struck the waters, and they were divided here and there, so that they two went over on dry ground.
echoes.note: Elijah's mantle, a garment of the holy man, works miracle when applied; Paul's handkerchiefs and aprons function similarly as charged garments. Faint, contested.

pericopes.text: But some of the itinerant Jews, exorcists, took on themselves to invoke over those who had the evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, “We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.” There were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, who did this. The evil spirit answered, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?” The man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overpowered them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. This became known to all, both Jews and Greeks, who lived at Ephesus. Fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.

echoes.text: “You shall not take the name of Yahweh your God in vain, for Yahweh will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.
echoes.note: Jewish exorcists invoke the name of the Lord Jesus illegitimately and are violently humiliated; the prohibition against taking the divine name in vain stands behind the danger of wielding a holy name without authorization. Conceptual, low verbal contact. Contested.

echoes.text: Oh magnify Yahweh with me. Let us exalt his name together.
echoes.note: The outcome is that the name of the Lord Jesus is magnified; the psalmist's call to magnify the Lord and exalt his name supplies the idiom. Faint, formulaic. Contested.

echoes.text: Now the Philistines had taken the ark of God, and they brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod. The Philistines took the ark of God, and brought it into the house of Dagon, and set it by Dagon. When they of Ashdod arose early on the next day, behold, Dagon was fallen on his face to the ground before Yahweh’s ark. They took Dagon, and set him in his place again. When they arose early on the next day morning, behold, Dagon was fallen on his face to the ground […]
echoes.note: The evil spirit overpowers the would-be exorcists who flee naked and wounded, exposing the impotence of those who presume on holy power; compare the humiliation of Dagon falling before the ark when the holy is mishandled by outsiders. Figural parallel of the sacred overpowering presumptuous handlers. Faint, contested.

echoes.text: For from the rising of the sun even to the going down of the same, my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering: for my name is great among the nations,” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: Fear falls and the name of the Lord is magnified among Jews and Greeks alike; Malachi's vision of the Lord's name being great among the nations resonates with the name being exalted across ethnic lines at Ephesus. Faint, contested.

pericopes.text: Many also of those who had believed came, confessing, and declaring their deeds. Many of those who practiced magical arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. They counted their price, and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty.

echoes.text: There shall not be found with you anyone who makes his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, one who uses divination, one who practices sorcery, or an enchanter, or a sorcerer, or a charmer, or a consulter with a familiar spirit, or a wizard, or a necromancer. For whoever does these things is an abomination to Yahweh. Because of these abominations, Yahweh your God drives them out from before you.
echoes.note: Magicians publicly renounce and burn their books of magical arts; Deuteronomy names sorcery, divination, and the practice of magic as detestable abominations to be purged from Israel. The repudiation of magic is the precise behavior the law demands (Volume: strong thematic match of magic-renunciation; Recurrence: Luke repeatedly opposes the gospel to magic, Simon in ch.8, Bar-Jesus in ch.13; Coherence: high). The book-burning enacts the Deuteronomic purge.

echoes.text: “You shall not allow a sorceress to live.
echoes.note: The destruction of magical practice at Ephesus enacts the law's severe stance against sorcery, you shall not permit a sorceress to live. The Ephesians do not kill but burn the apparatus, yet the abolition of magic from the believing community is the same impulse. Coherence high; allusive.

echoes.text: “‘Don’t turn to those who are mediums, nor to the wizards. Don’t seek them out, to be defiled by them. I am Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: Believers turn from magical arts; Leviticus forbids turning to mediums and wizards lest one be defiled. The conversion-from-occult theme coheres strongly. Contested in that no single phrase is quoted.

echoes.text: but these two things shall come to you in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood; in their full measure shall they come on you, in the multitude of your sorceries, and the great abundance of your enchantments. For you have trusted in your wickedness; you have said, No one sees me; your wisdom and your knowledge, it has perverted you, and you have said in your heart, I am, and there is no one else besides me. Therefore evil will come on […]
echoes.note: Babylon's abundance of sorceries and enchantments cannot save her and will be burned like stubble; here the magicians' costly books (50,000 pieces of silver) are burned, the impotence of magic exposed before the word. A pointed figural parallel of magic consumed by fire. Contested.

echoes.text: I will destroy witchcraft from your hand; and you shall have no soothsayers.
echoes.note: I will cut off sorceries from your hand, and you shall have no more soothsayers; the eschatological cleansing of magic from God's people is enacted at Ephesus. Faint, contested.

echoes.text: He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.
echoes.note: Believers come confessing and declaring their deeds; whoever confesses and forsakes his sins obtains mercy. The open confession-and-renunciation pattern coheres. Faint, contested.

echoes.text: so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
echoes.note: So the word of the Lord grew mightily and prevailed; Isaiah's effectual word that accomplishes God's purpose underlies Luke's growth refrain. Faint, formulaic. Contested.

pericopes.text: Now after these things had ended, Paul determined in the spirit, when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.” Having sent into Macedonia two of those who served him, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.

echoes.text: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.
echoes.note: Paul resolves in the spirit on a journey culminating at Jerusalem and Rome, the imperial center; Daniel's vision of God's kingdom set up in the days of the Gentile empires gives a backdrop to the gospel's march toward Rome. Very faint, contested.

pericopes.text: About that time there arose no small stir concerning the Way. For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen, whom he gathered together, with the workmen of like occupation, and said, “Sirs, you know that by this business we have our wealth. You see and hear, that not at Ephesus alone, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul has persuaded and turned away many people, saying that they are no gods, that are made with hands. Not only is there danger that this our trade come into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing, and her majesty destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worships.”

echoes.text: Everyone who makes an engraved image is vain. The things that they delight in will not profit. Their own witnesses don’t see, nor know, that they may be disappointed. Who has fashioned a god, or molds an image that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all his fellows will be disappointed; and the workmen are mere men. Let them all be gathered together. Let them stand up. They will fear. They will be put to shame together. The blacksmith takes an ax, works […]
echoes.note: Demetrius's silversmiths make shrines of Artemis, and Paul has taught that gods made with hands are no gods; Isaiah's great satire on the craftsman who fashions an idol with his own hands and then worships it is the controlling OT polemic (Volume: strong, the made-with-hands idol-craftsman is the shared center; Recurrence: idol-polemic recurs across Isaiah and the Psalms which Luke knows; Coherence: very high, the economic self-interest of the idol-trade mirrors Isaiah's irony). Plausibility and satisfaction: this is the classic prophetic mockery of manufactured deity.

echoes.text: Hear the word which Yahweh speaks to you, house of Israel! Thus says Yahweh, “Don’t learn the way of the nations, and don’t be dismayed at the signs of the sky; for the nations are dismayed at them. For the customs of the peoples are vanity; for one cuts a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the workman with the ax. They deck it with silver and with gold; they fasten it with nails and with hammers, that it not move. They are like a palm tree, […]
echoes.note: Idols are the work of the craftsman's hands, silver and gold, decked and unable to act; the silversmith is put to shame by his idols. Demetrius the silver craftsman and his guild embody exactly this trade. Strong thematic and lexical coherence (silver, craftsman, the work of human hands). Plausible and satisfying as the source of Paul's 'no gods made with hands.'

echoes.text: Shall a man make to himself gods, which yet are no gods?
echoes.note: Can man make gods for himself? Such are no gods. Paul's words that they are no gods which are made with hands stand remarkably close to Jeremiah's rhetorical denial. Volume high for the specific phrase; contested only because it is a stock prophetic commonplace.

echoes.text: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they don’t speak. They have eyes, but they don’t see. They have ears, but they don’t hear. They have noses, but they don’t smell. They have hands, but they don’t feel. They have feet, but they don’t walk, neither do they speak through their throat. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.
echoes.note: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands; those who make them become like them. The silver-shrine trade and the made-with-hands charge directly invoke this psalm's idol-satire. Strong coherence and recurrence (paired with Ps 135).

echoes.text: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they can’t speak. They have eyes, but they can’t see. They have ears, but they can’t hear; neither is there any breath in their mouths. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.
echoes.note: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men's hands, mouths that cannot speak; a near-twin of Ps 115 reinforcing the made-with-hands polemic against the silver Artemis shrines. Coherence high.

echoes.text: But miserable were they, and in dead things were their hopes, Who called them gods which are works of men’s hands, Gold and silver, wrought with careful are, and likenesses of animals, Or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand. Yes and if some woodcutter, having sawn down a tree that is easily moved, Skilfully strippeth away all its bark, And fashioning it in comely form makes a vessel useful for the service of life; And burning the refuse of his […]
echoes.note: Deuterocanonical satire on the artisan who shapes a worthless image and prays to it for his livelihood; Demetrius openly admits the cult is his source of wealth (v.25). Wisdom's link between idol-craft and economic dependence on dead images is the closest ancient parallel to the silversmiths' protest. Strong coherence; Luke and Paul plausibly stand in this Hellenistic-Jewish idol-polemic tradition.

echoes.text: But the idol made with hands is accursed, itself and he that made it; Because his was the working, and the corruptible thing was named a god:
echoes.note: Cursed is the idol and the one who made it; the made object and its maker condemned together. Coheres with the indictment of the manufactured Artemis. Contested.

echoes.text: For a potter, kneading soft earth, Laboriously mouldeth each several vessel for our service: Nay, out of the same clay does he fashion Both the vessels that minister to clean uses, and those of a contrary sort, All in like manner; But what shall be the use of each vessel of either sort, The craftsman himself is the judge. And also, laboring to an evil end, he mouldeth a vain god out of the same clay, He who, having but a little before been made of earth, […]
echoes.note: The potter/craftsman who molds gods for gain, knowing he sins, caring only for profit; Demetrius's frank appeal to profit from the shrine-trade matches Wisdom's portrait of the mercenary idol-maker. Strong thematic coherence; contested as one of several overlapping idol texts.

echoes.text: Some pour out gold from the bag, and weigh silver in the balance. They hire a goldsmith, and he makes it a god. They fall down—yes, they worship. They bear it on the shoulder, they carry it, and set it in its place, and it stands, from its place it shall not move: yes, one may cry to it, yet it can not answer, nor save him out of his trouble.
echoes.note: They lavish gold and weigh out silver, hire a goldsmith to make a god, then bow down; it cannot move or save. The silversmith hiring out his craft to make a deity matches Demetrius's guild. Coherence high; contested among the cluster.

echoes.text: “What value does the engraved image have, that its maker has engraved it; the molten image, even the teacher of lies, that he who fashions its form trusts in it, to make mute idols? Woe to him who says to the wood, ‘Awake!’ or to the mute stone, ‘Arise!’ Shall this teach? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in its midst.
echoes.note: What profit is an idol when its maker has shaped it, a teacher of lies, woe to him who says to wood Awake; the futility of the crafted image the maker trusts. Coheres with the made-with-hands theme. Contested.

echoes.text: There you shall serve gods, the work of men’s hands, wood and stone, which neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.
echoes.note: There you will serve gods, the work of men's hands, wood and stone, which neither see nor hear; the made-with-hands formula. Faint, contested, part of the cluster.

pericopes.text: When they heard this they were filled with anger, and cried out, saying, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” The whole city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul’s companions in travel. When Paul wanted to enter in to the people, the disciples didn’t allow him. Certain also of the Asiarchs, being his friends, sent to him and begged him not to venture into the theater. Some therefore cried one thing, and some another, for the assembly was in confusion. Most of them didn’t know why they had come together. They brought Alexander out of the multitude, the Jews putting him forward. Alexander beckoned with his hand, and would have made a defense to the people. But when they perceived that he was a Jew, all with one voice for a time of about two hours cried out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

echoes.text: They took the bull which was given them, and they dressed it, and called on the name of Baal from morning even until noon, saying, “Baal, hear us!” But there was no voice, nor any who answered. They leaped about the altar which was made. At noon, Elijah mocked them, and said, “Cry aloud; for he is a god. Either he is musing, or he has gone aside, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he sleeps and must be awakened.” They cried aloud, and cut themselves in […]
echoes.note: The crowd cries Great is Artemis of the Ephesians with one voice for about two hours; the prophets of Baal call on their god from morning until noon, O Baal hear us, raving in vain while no one answers. The prolonged, frenzied, futile invocation of a powerless deity is a striking figural parallel exposing the impotence of the idol (Volume: shared marathon-cry of pagan devotees; Coherence: high). Satisfaction: Luke's reader hears the Carmel irony behind the Ephesian shouting.

echoes.text: Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing?
echoes.note: The whole city is thrown into uproar and rushes together in confusion; why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain. The raging Gentile mob set against the Lord's work fits the psalm's tumult of the nations. Faint, contested.

echoes.text: When Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said to Moses, “There is the noise of war in the camp.” He said, “It isn’t the voice of those who shout for victory, neither is it the voice of those who cry for being overcome; but the noise of those who sing that I hear.” As soon as he came near to the camp, he saw the calf and the dancing. Then Moses’ anger grew hot, and he threw the tablets out of his hands, and broke them beneath the […]
echoes.note: A confused mass shouting and surging in devotion to a false god recalls the noise of the camp at the golden calf, a tumult of idolatrous celebration. Figural and faint. Contested.

pericopes.text: When the town clerk had quieted the multitude, he said, “You men of Ephesus, what man is there who doesn’t know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great goddess Artemis, and of the image which fell down from Zeus? Seeing then that these things can’t be denied, you ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rash. For you have brought these men here, who are neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers of your goddess. If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen who are with him have a matter against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them press charges against one another. But if you seek anything about other matters, it will be settled in the regular assembly. For indeed we are in danger of being accused concerning this day’s riot, there being no cause. Concerning it, we wouldn’t be able to give an account of this commotion.” When he had thus spoken, he dismissed the assembly.

echoes.text: Everyone who makes an engraved image is vain. The things that they delight in will not profit. Their own witnesses don’t see, nor know, that they may be disappointed. Who has fashioned a god, or molds an image that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all his fellows will be disappointed; and the workmen are mere men. Let them all be gathered together. Let them stand up. They will fear. They will be put to shame together. The blacksmith takes an ax, works […]
echoes.note: The town clerk appeals to the image of Artemis that fell from heaven (Diopetes); Isaiah's satire that the idol is in truth a manufactured object stands in tension with the civic claim of a heaven-fallen image, underscoring the irony Luke wants the reader to feel. Faint here, fuller at 19:23-27. Contested.

echoes.text: who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves, and the turmoil of the nations.
echoes.note: The town clerk quiets and stills the roaring multitude; only God stills the roaring of the seas and the tumult of the peoples. A faint figural touch on the stilling of crowd-tumult. Contested.

echoes.text: A fool vents all of his anger, but a wise man brings himself under control.
echoes.note: The clerk urges them to be quiet and do nothing rash; a wise man holds back the fool's outburst of anger. Faint sapiential resonance. Contested.

pericopes.text: After the uproar had ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, took leave of them, and departed to go into Macedonia. When he had gone through those parts, and had encouraged them with many words, he came into Greece. When he had spent three months there, and a plot was made against him by Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he determined to return through Macedonia. These accompanied him as far as Asia: Sopater of Beroea; Aristarchus and Secundus of the Thessalonians; Gaius of Derbe; Timothy; and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia. But these had gone ahead, and were waiting for us at Troas. We sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and came to them at Troas in five days, where we stayed seven days.

echoes.text: “‘Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; even the first day you shall put away yeast out of your houses, for whoever eats leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel. In the first day there shall be to you a holy convocation, and in the seventh day a holy convocation; no kind of work shall be done in them, except that which every man must eat, that only may be done by you. You shall observe the feast […]
echoes.note: Luke dates the Troas voyage 'after the days of Unleavened Bread,' invoking the Passover/Massot calendar prescribed here. The festival reference is precise and structural (it anchors the chronology), though it functions as a time-marker rather than an interpretive citation; volume is moderate, recurrence in Luke-Acts of festal dating is real (cf. Pentecost in v.16).

echoes.text: You shall eat no leavened bread with it. You shall eat unleavened bread with it seven days, even the bread of affliction; for you came out of the land of Egypt in haste; that you may remember the day when you came out of the land of Egypt all the days of your life. No yeast shall be seen with you in all your borders seven days; neither shall any of the flesh, which you sacrifice the first day at evening, remain all night until the morning.
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's restatement of the seven days of unleavened bread underlies the same festal marker; an alternative locus for the calendar allusion behind 'days of Unleavened Bread.'

echoes.text: For I have heard the slander of many, terror on every side, while they conspire together against me, they plot to take away my life.
echoes.note: The recurring 'plot made against him by Jews' (v.3, cf. v.19) resonates faintly with the lament topos of the righteous sufferer surrounded by those who scheme to take his life; thematic coherence with Paul-as-persecuted-servant, but no verbal borrowing.

pericopes.text: On the first day of the week, when the disciples were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and continued his speech until midnight. There were many lights in the upper room where we were gathered together. A certain young man named Eutychus sat in the window, weighed down with deep sleep. As Paul spoke still longer, being weighed down by his sleep, he fell down from the third story, and was taken up dead. Paul went down, and fell upon him, and embracing him said, “Don’t be troubled, for his life is in him.” When he had gone up, and had broken bread, and eaten, and had talked with them a long while, even until break of day, he departed. They brought the boy in alive, and were greatly comforted.

echoes.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]
echoes.note: The raising of Eutychus is a deliberate Elijah typology: a man of God descends to a dead youth, throws himself upon the body, and the boy's life returns. Elijah 'stretched himself upon the child' (LXX) and the child's life came back to him; Paul 'fell upon him, embracing him' and declares 'his life is in him.' Volume is high (the bodily prostration on the corpse), recurrence strong (Luke pairs his apostles with Elijah/Elisha resurrections elsewhere), thematic coherence excellent.

echoes.text: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]
echoes.note: The Elisha raising of the Shunammite's son is the closest structural twin: prophet enters where the dead child lies, stretches/lies upon him, life returns, and the living child is restored to the household 'greatly comforted.' The deliverance of the boy 'alive' (v.12) mirrors the son given back. Two resurrection narratives converge here, reinforcing the Elijah/Elisha pattern.

echoes.text: When the child was grown, one day he went out to his father to the reapers. He said to his father, “My head! My head!” He said to his servant, “Carry him to his mother.” When he had taken him, and brought him to his mother, he sat on her knees until noon, and then died.
echoes.note: The Shunammite boy's collapse and death by midday provides the death-of-the-youth setup that the raising narrative answers; included as the antecedent scene to the 2 Kings 4:32-37 type.

pericopes.text: But we who went ahead to the ship set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for he had so arranged, intending himself to go by land. When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard, and came to Mitylene. Sailing from there, we came the following day opposite Chios. The next day we touched at Samos and stayed at Trogyllium, and the day after we came to Miletus. For Paul had determined to sail past Ephesus, that he might not have to spend time in Asia; for he was hastening, if it were possible for him, to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.

echoes.text: “‘You shall count from the next day after the Sabbath, from the day that you brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven Sabbaths shall be completed: even to the next day after the seventh Sabbath you shall number fifty days; and you shall offer a new meal offering to Yahweh. You shall bring out of your habitations two loaves of bread for a wave offering made of two tenth parts of an ephah of fine flour. They shall be baked with yeast, for first fruits […]
echoes.note: Paul hastens 'to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost' (v.16); the Feast of Weeks counted fifty days from the Massot offering is legislated here, naming and grounding the festival Luke invokes. The reference is precise but functions chronologically rather than as exegetical citation.

echoes.text: You shall count for yourselves seven weeks. From the time you begin to put the sickle to the standing grain you shall begin to number seven weeks. You shall keep the feast of weeks to Yahweh your God with a tribute of a freewill offering of your hand, which you shall give, according as Yahweh your God blesses you. You shall rejoice before Yahweh your God: you, your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, the Levite who is within your […]
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's command to keep the Feast of Weeks at the place the Lord chooses (Jerusalem) underlies Paul's urgency to be there for Pentecost; an alternative locus for the festal allusion.

pericopes.text: From Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called to himself the elders of the assembly. When they had come to him, he said to them, “You yourselves know, from the first day that I set foot in Asia, how I was with you all the time, serving the Lord with all humility, with many tears, and with trials which happened to me by the plots of the Jews; how I didn’t shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, teaching you publicly and from house to house, testifying both to Jews and to Greeks repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus. Now, behold, I go bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there; except that the Holy Spirit testifies in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions wait for me. But these things don’t count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to fully testify to the Good News of the grace of God.

echoes.text: Son of man, I have made you a watchman to the house of Israel: therefore hear the word from my mouth, and give them warning from me. When I tell the wicked, You shall surely die; and you give him no warning, nor speak to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life; the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at your hand. Yet if you warn the wicked, and he doesn’t turn from his wickedness, nor from his wicked way, […]
echoes.note: Paul's self-description as one who 'didn't shrink from declaring anything profitable' (v.20) and testified repentance (v.21) begins the watchman motif that crests in v.26-27; the prophet appointed watchman who must declare the whole message anticipates Paul's accounting. Verbal overlap is light here, fuller in the next pericope.

echoes.text: If I say, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name, then there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with forbearing, and I can’t.
echoes.note: 'I go bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem' (v.22) and the Spirit's testimony that 'bonds and afflictions wait for me' (v.23) resonate with the prophetic compulsion to a costly word one cannot withhold; thematic coherence with Jeremiah's constrained, suffering vocation, no verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: Yahweh, the God of their fathers, sent to them by his messengers, rising up early and sending, because he had compassion on his people, and on his dwelling place: but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the wrath of Yahweh arose against his people, until there was no remedy.
echoes.note: Paul's ministry 'with many tears' amid 'plots of the Jews' (v.19) and his journey toward inevitable suffering echoes the deuteronomistic pattern of the persistently rejected prophets/messengers; faint thematic link.

pericopes.text: “Now, behold, I know that you all, among whom I went about preaching the Kingdom of God, will see my face no more. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am clean from the blood of all men, for I didn’t shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. Take heed, therefore, to yourselves, and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and God which he purchased with his own blood. For I know that after my departure, vicious wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock. Men will arise from among your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them. Therefore watch, remembering that for a period of three years I didn’t cease to admonish everyone night and day with tears.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, speak to the children of your people, and tell them, When I bring the sword on a land, and the people of the land take a man from among them, and set him for their watchman; if, when he sees the sword come on the land, he blow the trumpet, and warn the people; then whoever hears the sound of the trumpet, and doesn’t take warning, if the sword come, and take him away, his blood shall be on his own head. He […]
echoes.note: Paul's 'I am clean from the blood of all men' (v.26) directly takes up the watchman oracle: the watchman who warns is innocent of the blood of those who perish, while the negligent watchman bears their blood. The blood-guilt formula is distinctive and the watchman-over-the-people role frames the whole farewell. High volume and thematic coherence.

echoes.text: Son of man, I have made you a watchman to the house of Israel: therefore hear the word from my mouth, and give them warning from me. When I tell the wicked, You shall surely die; and you give him no warning, nor speak to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life; the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at your hand. Yet if you warn the wicked, and he doesn’t turn from his wickedness, nor from his wicked way, […]
echoes.note: The first watchman commission, where the prophet who fails to warn has the sinner's blood 'required at your hand' but the faithful one 'delivers his soul,' is the twin source of Paul's blood-innocence claim (v.26) tied to declaring 'the whole counsel of God' (v.27). Recurs with Ezek 33; together a strong watchman intertext.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and tell them, even to the shepherds, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat, and you clothe yourself with the wool, you kill the fatlings; but you don’t feed the sheep. You haven’t strengthened the diseased, neither have you healed that which was sick, neither […]
echoes.note: The charge to 'shepherd the assembly of the Lord' and guard 'all the flock' over which they are made overseers (v.28), against shepherds who exploit and fail to protect, draws on Ezekiel's oracle against the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves and let the flock be scattered and devoured. The overseer-shepherd-flock cluster is dense and coherent.

echoes.text: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.
echoes.note: The tender shepherd who gathers and feeds the flock informs the pastoral 'shepherd the assembly' charge (v.28); the positive shepherd image complements the Ezekiel 34 indictment.

echoes.text: Her princes in its midst are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, that they may get dishonest gain.
echoes.note: 'Vicious wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock' (v.29) takes up Ezekiel's image of the princes 'like wolves tearing the prey, shedding blood, destroying souls' for gain. The wolves-versus-flock predation maps closely onto the corrupt leaders devouring the people.

echoes.text: Her princes in the midst of her are roaring lions. Her judges are evening wolves. They leave nothing until the next day.
echoes.note: Zephaniah's officials as 'evening wolves that leave nothing for the morning' is a strong alternative locus for the savage-wolves-not-sparing image (v.29); reinforces the prophetic wolf-leader topos.

echoes.text: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered.
echoes.note: The flock scattered and become food for 'every beast of the field' because there was no shepherd undergirds the warning that wolves will ravage the flock after Paul's departure (v.29); ties the wolf threat back into the Ezekiel 34 shepherd oracle.

echoes.text: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul. […]
echoes.note: 'Men will arise from among your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them' (v.30) echoes the Deuteronomic warning against prophets who arise from within Israel to lead the people astray after them, who must be purged; thematic and structural coherence (internal seducers drawing the people away).

echoes.text: Yahweh said to me, “Take for yourself yet again the equipment of a foolish shepherd. For, behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land, who will not visit those who are cut off, neither will seek those who are scattered, nor heal that which is broken, nor feed that which is sound; but he will eat the flesh of the fat sheep, and will tear their hoofs in pieces. Woe to the worthless shepherd who leaves the flock! The sword will be on his arm, and on his […]
echoes.note: The worthless shepherd who abandons and devours the flock provides a further wolf/false-shepherd resonance for the predatory leaders foreseen in v.29-30.

echoes.text: “Let Yahweh, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: Moses' prayer for a successor 'that the congregation of the Lord be not as sheep without a shepherd' faintly underlies Paul's succession-anxiety farewell, handing the flock to the elders before his departure (v.28-31).

pericopes.text: Now, brothers, I entrust you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build up, and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. I coveted no one’s silver, or gold, or clothing. You yourselves know that these hands served my necessities, and those who were with me. In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’” When he had spoken these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. They all wept a lot, and fell on Paul’s neck and kissed him, sorrowing most of all because of the word which he had spoken, that they should see his face no more. And they accompanied him to the ship.

echoes.text: Yes, he loves the people. All his saints are in your hand. They sat down at your feet. Each receives your words. Moses commanded us a law, an inheritance for the assembly of Jacob.
echoes.note: 'The inheritance among all those who are sanctified' (v.32) echoes Moses' blessing where the holy ones are in God's hand and Moses commands the law as 'an inheritance' for the assembly; the sanctified-ones-plus-inheritance pairing is distinctive.

echoes.text: How was he counted among sons of God? And how is his lot among saints?
echoes.note: 'His lot is among the saints' (the righteous numbered among the holy ones / sons of God) is a close deuterocanonical parallel to 'the inheritance among all those who are sanctified' (v.32); strong conceptual and lexical fit for the eschatological inheritance among the holy.

echoes.text: Here I am. Witness against me before Yahweh, and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? Of whose hand have I taken a ransom to blind my eyes therewith? I will restore it to you.” They said, “You have not defrauded us, nor oppressed us, neither have you taken anything of any man’s hand.” He said to them, “Yahweh is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that […]
echoes.note: Paul's farewell protest 'I coveted no one's silver, or gold, or clothing' (v.33-34) closely mirrors Samuel's farewell self-vindication: 'Whose ox have I taken? ... from whose hand have I taken a bribe?' with the people as witnesses. Both are leaders' departure speeches asserting financial blamelessness; high structural and thematic coherence.

echoes.text: Moses was very angry, and said to Yahweh, “Don’t respect their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them, neither have I hurt one of them.”
echoes.note: Moses' protest 'I have not taken one donkey from them, neither have I hurt one of them' is a second leader's disavowal of taking from the people, reinforcing Paul's 'I coveted no one's silver or gold' (v.33).

echoes.text: There is one who scatters, and increases yet more. There is one who withholds more than is appropriate, but gains poverty. The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.
echoes.note: 'It is more blessed to give than to receive' (v.35) coheres with the wisdom maxim that the one who scatters increases while the one who withholds comes to want, and the generous soul is enriched; OT sapiential ground for the generosity logion.

echoes.text: My son, deprive not the poor of his living, And make not the needy eyes to wait long. Make not a hungry soul sorrowful; Neither provoke a man in his distress. To a heart that is provoked add not more trouble; And defer not to give to him that is in need. Reject not a suppliant in his affliction; And turn not away your face from a poor man. Turn not away your eye from one that asks of you, And give none occasion to a man to curse you: For if he curse you […]
echoes.note: Sirach's exhortation to give to the poor and help the weak/needy is a deuterocanonical parallel to laboring 'to help the weak' and the blessedness of giving (v.35).

echoes.text: He fell on his brother Benjamin’s neck, and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck. He kissed all his brothers, and wept on them. After that his brothers talked with him.
echoes.note: 'They all wept a lot, and fell on Paul's neck and kissed him' (v.37) reproduces the Joseph reunion idiom: falling on the neck, weeping, and kissing. The verbal cluster (neck + weeping + kiss) is distinctive Septuagintal language for emotional parting/reunion.

echoes.text: Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept.
echoes.note: Esau 'fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept' is a second close parallel for the falling-on-the-neck, weeping, kissing farewell of v.37.

echoes.text: Yahweh grant you that you may find rest, each of you in the house of her husband.” Then she kissed them, and they lifted up their voice, and wept. They said to her, “No, but we will return with you to your people.” Naomi said, “Go back, my daughters. Why do you want to go with me? Do I still have sons in my womb, that they may be your husbands? Go back, my daughters, go your way; for I am too old to have a husband. If I should say, ‘I have hope,’ if I […]
echoes.note: Naomi's parting from her daughters-in-law, who 'lifted up their voices and wept' and 'kissed' at separation, offers a further departure-with-weeping-and-kissing resonance for v.37.

pericopes.text: When we had departed from them and had set sail, we came with a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. Having found a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we went aboard, and set sail. When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left hand, we sailed to Syria, and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload her cargo. Having found disciples, we stayed there seven days. These said to Paul through the Spirit, that he should not go up to Jerusalem. When those days were over, we departed and went on our journey. They all, with wives and children, brought us on our way until we were out of the city. Kneeling down on the beach, we prayed. After saying goodbye to each other, we went on board the ship, and they returned home again.

echoes.text: It was so, that when Solomon had made an end of praying all this prayer and supplication to Yahweh, he arose from before the altar of Yahweh, from kneeling on his knees with his hands spread out toward heaven.
echoes.note: Paul and the Tyrian disciples kneel on the beach to pray as Solomon kneels at the dedication of the temple; the gesture of kneeling for solemn prayer recalls the OT posture of supplication. Verbal volume is low (a common gesture), but the deliberate corporate kneeling at a moment of parting and danger gives the scene a liturgical coloring; thematically coherent with Israel's prayer postures.

echoes.text: When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.
echoes.note: Kneeling for prayer as a marked act of piety before adversity echoes Daniel kneeling three times a day; the connection is gestural rather than verbal, low volume, but coheres with the motif of prayer in the face of coming persecution.

echoes.text: Surely the Lord Yahweh will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.
echoes.note: The disciples warn Paul 'through the Spirit' not to go up to Jerusalem, reflecting the prophetic principle that the Lord reveals coming events to his servants; faint thematic resonance with prophetic foreknowledge rather than a verbal borrowing.

pericopes.text: When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais. We greeted the brothers, and stayed with them one day. On the next day, we, who were Paul’s companions, departed, and came to Caesarea. We entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him. Now this man had four virgin daughters who prophesied.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: Philip's four virgin daughters 'who prophesied' enact Joel's promise that in the last days sons and daughters shall prophesy — the prophecy Peter cited programmatically at Pentecost (Acts 2). Strong thematic coherence and recurrence within Acts make this a deliberate narrative demonstration of the Joel oracle's fulfillment; verbal volume rests on the shared key term 'prophesy' applied specifically to daughters.

echoes.text: Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand; and all the women went out after her with tambourines and with dances.
echoes.note: Female prophets are a recognized OT category — Miriam 'the prophetess' leads Israel; Philip's prophesying daughters stand in this line of Spirit-gifted women. Thematic coherence is good though there is no verbal borrowing of the Miriam scene specifically.

echoes.text: So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asaiah, went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe (now she lived in Jerusalem in the second quarter); and they talked with her.
echoes.note: Huldah the prophetess, consulted as an authoritative oracle, is part of the OT pattern of recognized women prophets that Luke evokes by noting the daughters' prophetic activity; recurrence of the female-prophet motif (cf. also Isaiah 8:3, Nehemiah 6:14) supports the link, though purely thematic.

pericopes.text: As we stayed there some days, a certain prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. Coming to us, and taking Paul’s belt, he bound his own feet and hands, and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit: ‘So will the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man who owns this belt, and will deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’” When we heard these things, both we and they of that place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem. Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” When he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, “The Lord’s will be done.”

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh to me, Go, and buy yourself a linen belt, and put it on your waist, and don’t put it in water. So I bought a belt according to Yahweh’s word, and put it on my waist. Yahweh’s word came to me the second time, saying, Take the belt that you have bought, which is on your waist, and arise, go to the Euphrates, and hide it there in a cleft of the rock. So I went, and hid it by the Euphrates, as Yahweh commanded me. After many days, Yahweh said […]
echoes.note: Agabus takes Paul's belt and binds his own feet and hands as an enacted oracle ('Thus says the Holy Spirit'), the classic prophetic sign-act. Jeremiah's linen loincloth/belt sign is the closest parallel both in the use of a belt/girdle as the symbolic object and in the dramatized word; high thematic coherence and notable verbal overlap in the belt as the medium of the sign.

echoes.text: You also, son of man, take a tile, and lay it before yourself, and portray on it a city, even Jerusalem: and lay siege against it, and build forts against it, and cast up a mound against it; set camps also against it, and plant battering rams against it all around. Take for yourself an iron pan, and set it for a wall of iron between you and the city: and set your face toward it, and it shall be besieged, and you shall lay siege against it. This shall be a […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel is bound with cords and lies bound to bear Israel's siege as a sign-act; Agabus's self-binding to portray Paul's coming bondage belongs to the same genre of embodied prophecy. Strong thematic coherence with the bound-prophet enacting another's fate; the binding motif gives solid volume.

echoes.text: at that time Yahweh spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, “Go, and loosen the sackcloth from off your waist, and take your shoes from off your feet.” He did so, walking naked and barefoot. Yahweh said, “As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign and a wonder concerning Egypt and concerning Ethiopia, so the king of Assyria will lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Ethiopia, young and old, naked and barefoot, […]
echoes.note: Isaiah walks naked and barefoot as a sign of coming captivity 'into the hands' of a foreign power, just as Agabus's sign foretells Paul being delivered 'into the hands of the Gentiles.' Same sign-act genre with a captivity-to-foreigners content; high coherence, the verbal volume carried by the handed-over-to-Gentiles outcome.

echoes.text: At that time, when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him on the way; now Ahijah had clad himself with a new garment; and they two were alone in the field. Ahijah laid hold of the new garment that was on him, and tore it in twelve pieces. He said to Jeroboam, “Take ten pieces; for thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, ‘Behold, I will tear the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to you
echoes.note: Ahijah tears his new garment into pieces as a prophetic sign of the kingdom's division — another instance of an enacted oracle using a garment/cloth object, supporting the sign-act background of Agabus, though less verbally specific than Jeremiah or Isaiah.

echoes.text: Then Hananiah the prophet took the bar from off the prophet Jeremiah’s neck, and broke it. Hananiah spoke in the presence of all the people, saying, Thus says Yahweh: Even so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon within two full years from off the neck of all the nations. The prophet Jeremiah went his way.
echoes.note: The yoke/bond sign-acts of Jeremiah (and Hananiah's counter-sign) belong to the same prophetic-symbol tradition of binding to dramatize coming subjugation; recurrence of the bondage-sign motif reinforces the genre Agabus invokes.

echoes.text: Samuel told him every bit, and hid nothing from him. He said, “It is Yahweh. Let him do what seems good to him.”
echoes.note: The companions' resigned 'The Lord's will be done' closely matches Eli's 'It is the LORD; let him do what seems good to him' upon hearing an oracle of doom — submission to a revealed and unwelcome divine word. Strong thematic coherence and a near-formulaic verbal parallel of pious resignation.

echoes.text: Samuel told him every bit, and hid nothing from him. He said, “It is Yahweh. Let him do what seems good to him.”
echoes.note: Repeated to flag the wider OT formula of submission to divine will (cf. 2 Samuel 15:26, David: 'let him do to me as seems good to him'); the recurrence of this stock phrase of acceptance strengthens the figural reading of the disciples' words.

echoes.text: Surely the Lord Yahweh will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.
echoes.note: The prophetic-disclosure formula 'Thus says the Holy Spirit' adapts the standard messenger formula 'Thus says the LORD' (pervasive in the prophets), grounding Agabus in OT prophetic speech; high recurrence of the formula across the prophets, low verbal specificity to any single text.

pericopes.text: After these days we took up our baggage and went up to Jerusalem. Some of the disciples from Caesarea also went with us, bringing one Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we would stay. When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. The day following, Paul went in with us to James; and all the elders were present. When he had greeted them, he reported one by one the things which God had worked among the Gentiles through his ministry. They, when they heard it, glorified God. They said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law. They have been informed about you, that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children neither to walk after the customs. What then? The assembly must certainly meet, for they will hear that you have come. Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who have taken a vow. Take them, and purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses for them, that they may shave their heads. Then all will know that there is no truth in the things that they have been informed about you, but that you yourself also walk keeping the law. But concerning the Gentiles who believe, we have written our decision that they should observe no such thing, except that they should keep themselves from food offered to idols, from blood, from strangled things, and from sexual immorality.” Then Paul took the men, and the next day, purified himself and went with them into the temple, declaring the fulfillment of the days of purification, until the offering was offered for every one of them.

echoes.text: “‘This is the law of the Nazirite: when the days of his separation are fulfilled, he shall be brought to the door of the Tent of Meeting, and he shall offer his offering to Yahweh, one male lamb a year old without defect for a burnt offering, and one ewe lamb a year old without defect for a sin offering, and one ram without defect for peace offerings, and a basket of unleavened bread, cakes of fine flour mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with […]
echoes.note: The four men under a vow whom Paul joins, purifying himself, paying their expenses, and completing the days of purification 'until the offering was offered,' enacts the Nazirite completion rite: shaving the head and presenting offerings at the end of the vow. High thematic coherence and strong verbal volume on shaving, purification days, and the concluding offering.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them: ‘When either man or woman shall make a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to Yahweh, he shall separate himself from wine and strong drink. He shall drink no vinegar of wine, or vinegar of fermented drink, neither shall he drink any juice of grapes, nor eat fresh grapes or dried. All the days of his separation he shall eat nothing that is made of the […]
echoes.note: The opening Nazirite legislation defines the vow and its requirements that the four men have taken; Paul's sponsorship presupposes the whole statute, making the broader chapter directly in view alongside the completion subsection.

echoes.text: “‘If any man dies very suddenly beside him, and he defiles the head of his separation; then he shall shave his head in the day of his cleansing. On the seventh day he shall shave it. On the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest, to the door of the Tent of Meeting. The priest shall offer one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering, and make atonement for him, because he sinned by reason of the dead, and […]
echoes.note: The provision for purification when a vow is interrupted/defiled underlies the act of 'purifying' oneself with the men; thematically coherent with Paul's ritual purification before entering the temple, though the text emphasizes completion more than defilement.

echoes.text: God said to Abraham, “As for you, you will keep my covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations. This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you. He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he […]
echoes.note: The charge that Paul teaches Jews 'not to circumcise their children' invokes the Abrahamic covenant of circumcision; the dispute over Mosaic customs and circumcision presupposes this foundational statute. Strong thematic coherence; verbal volume on circumcision of children/offspring.

echoes.text: “Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, has turned my wrath away from the children of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I didn’t consume the children of Israel in my jealousy. Therefore say, ‘Behold, I give to him my covenant of peace. It shall be to him, and to his seed after him, the covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because he was jealous for his God, and made atonement for the children of […]
echoes.note: The thousands 'zealous for the law' echo the OT ideal of zeal for the LORD's commandments embodied by Phinehas, whose zeal won a covenant of priesthood; the language of zeal for the law (cf. 1 Kings 19:10, Elijah) frames the Jerusalem believers' concern. Thematic coherence with the zeal motif, no direct quotation.

echoes.text: “‘Any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who eats any kind of blood, I will set my face against that soul who eats blood, and will cut him off from among his people. For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life. Therefore I have said to the children of Israel, “No person […]
echoes.note: James's restated decree that Gentile believers abstain from blood and from things strangled rests on the Holiness Code's prohibition of eating blood, applied to resident aliens as well as Israel. Strong thematic coherence with the apostolic council's grounding in Leviticus 17-18; verbal volume on blood.

echoes.text: “You shall say to them, ‘Any man there is of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice, and doesn’t bring it to the door of the Tent of Meeting, to sacrifice it to Yahweh; that man shall be cut off from his people.
echoes.note: The prohibition against idol-food in the decree ('keep themselves from food offered to idols') draws on Leviticus 17's strictures on sacrifices and on the sojourner, the resident-alien legislation widely seen as the source pool for the apostolic decree; coherent though the idol-food element also rests on broader Pentateuchal idolatry law.

echoes.text: “‘None of you shall approach anyone who are his close relatives, to uncover their nakedness: I am Yahweh. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father, nor the nakedness of your mother: she is your mother. You shall not uncover her nakedness. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife. It is your father’s nakedness. “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, the daughter of your father, or the daughter of your mother, […]
echoes.note: The decree's prohibition of sexual immorality (porneia) corresponds to the Holiness Code's catalogue of forbidden unions, the fourth item commonly traced to Leviticus 18, especially as binding on the resident alien (Lev 18:26). Thematic coherence with the council's Levitical basis.

pericopes.text: When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, when they saw him in the temple, stirred up all the multitude and laid hands on him, crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches all men everywhere against the people, and the law, and this place. Moreover, he also brought Greeks into the temple, and has defiled this holy place!” For they had seen Trophimus, the Ephesian, with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. All the city was moved, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple. Immediately the doors were shut. As they were trying to kill him, news came up to the commanding officer of the regiment that all Jerusalem was in an uproar. Immediately he took soldiers and centurions, and ran down to them. They, when they saw the chief captain and the soldiers, stopped beating Paul. Then the commanding officer came near, arrested him, commanded him to be bound with two chains, and inquired who he was and what he had done. Some shouted one thing, and some another, among the crowd. When he couldn’t find out the truth because of the noise, he commanded him to be brought into the barracks. When he came to the stairs, he was carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd; for the multitude of the people followed after, crying out, “Away with him!”

echoes.text: in that you have brought in foreigners, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in my sanctuary, to profane it, even my house, when you offer my bread, the fat and the blood, and they have broken my covenant, to add to all your abominations. You have not performed the duty of my holy things; but you have set performers of my duty in my sanctuary for yourselves. Thus says the Lord Yahweh, No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and […]
echoes.note: The charge that Paul 'brought Greeks into the temple, and has defiled this holy place' directly engages Ezekiel's denunciation of admitting uncircumcised foreigners into the sanctuary, profaning God's house. Strong thematic coherence with the temple-defilement-by-Gentiles accusation; this is the conceptual basis of the soreg barrier the crowd believes was breached.

echoes.text: When the tabernacle is to move, the Levites shall take it down; and when the tabernacle is to be set up, the Levites shall set it up. The stranger who comes near shall be put to death.
echoes.note: The lethal seriousness of the crowd ('trying to kill him') over an outsider entering sacred precincts reflects the Pentateuchal death sanction against the unauthorized approaching the sanctuary; thematic background to the temple's exclusion zones, low verbal volume.

echoes.text: The Lord has cast off his altar, he has abhorred his sanctuary; He has given up into the hand of the enemy the walls of her palaces: They have made a noise in Yahweh’s house, as in the day of a solemn assembly.
echoes.note: The tumult in the temple courts, seizing and dragging Paul out, and the doors immediately shut faintly evoke the OT scenes of the sanctuary overrun and its gates violated; atmospheric resonance only, no verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: When Ahab saw Elijah, Ahab said to him, “Is that you, you troubler of Israel?” He answered, “I have not troubled Israel; but you, and your father’s house, in that you have forsaken the commandments of Yahweh, and you have followed the Baals.
echoes.note: The crowd brands Paul the man who teaches 'against the people, and the law, and this place,' casting him as a troubler of Israel — the same accusation Ahab levels at Elijah ('troubler of Israel'). Faint thematic parallel of the faithful prophet charged with subverting the nation.

pericopes.text: As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he asked the commanding officer, “May I speak to you?” He said, “Do you know Greek? Aren’t you then the Egyptian, who before these days stirred up to sedition and led out into the wilderness the four thousand men of the Assassins?” But Paul said, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people.” When he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the stairs, beckoned with his hand to the people. When there was a great silence, he spoke to them in the Hebrew language, saying,

echoes.text: Moses said to Yahweh, “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.”
echoes.note: Paul's request to address the hostile crowd, beckoning for silence before a defense, faintly recalls the OT pattern of the divinely commissioned spokesman who must speak to a resistant people; the connection is typological and weak, with no verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: and their children spoke half in the speech of Ashdod, and could not speak in the Jews’ language, but according to the language of each people.
echoes.note: Paul's speaking 'in the Hebrew language' to the people signals covenant identity and the language of Israel; Nehemiah's concern over loss of the language of Judah supplies a faint thematic backdrop to Hebrew speech as a marker of belonging, though no quotation is involved.

pericopes.text: “Brothers and fathers, listen to the defense which I now make to you.” When they heard that he spoke to them in the Hebrew language, they were even more quiet. He said, “I am indeed a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, instructed according to the strict tradition of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God, even as you all are this day. I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women. As also the high priest and all the council of the elders testify, from whom also I received letters to the brothers, and traveled to Damascus to bring them also who were there to Jerusalem in bonds to be punished.

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Paul's self-description as 'zealous for God' (v3) echoes Elijah's signature self-defense, 'I have been very zealous for the LORD' — the OT idiom of cultic zeal that justified violence against deviants, which Paul applies to his persecuting career. Coherent with the chapter's portrait of misdirected zeal; verbal contact via 'zealous.'

echoes.text: “Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, has turned my wrath away from the children of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I didn’t consume the children of Israel in my jealousy. Therefore say, ‘Behold, I give to him my covenant of peace. It shall be to him, and to his seed after him, the covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because he was jealous for his God, and made atonement for the children of […]
echoes.note: Phinehas' zeal that turned away wrath is the paradigm of violent piety standing behind 'zealous for God, even as you all are' — the very zealotry that drove Paul to bind men and women. Thematic only, no verbal borrowing; contested as background rather than allusion.

echoes.text: God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.
echoes.note: 'the law of our fathers' (v3), anticipating 'the God of our fathers' in v14, draws on the patriarchal-covenant formula whose anchor is Exodus 3:15. Faint here; the formula lands more fully in the Ananias speech.

echoes.text: Moses commanded us a law, an inheritance for the assembly of Jacob.
echoes.note: 'instructed according to the strict tradition of the law of our fathers' rests on the Mosaic law as the ancestral inheritance of Israel; Deut 33:4 ('the law Moses commanded, the inheritance of the assembly of Jacob') supplies the conception. Background, contested.

pericopes.text: As I made my journey, and came close to Damascus, about noon, suddenly a great light shone around me from the sky. I fell to the ground, and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ He said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you persecute.’ “Those who were with me indeed saw the light and were afraid, but they didn’t understand the voice of him who spoke to me. I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ The Lord said to me, ‘Arise, and go into Damascus. There you will be told about all things which are appointed for you to do.’ When I couldn’t see for the glory of that light, being led by the hand of those who were with me, I came into Damascus.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s angel called to him out of the sky, and said, “Abraham, Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.”
echoes.note: The doubled vocative 'Saul, Saul' (v7) follows the OT pattern of urgent divine address by repeated name — 'Abraham, Abraham' at the binding of Isaac. The form signals a theophanic call/redirection. Recurs across the OT call narratives below.

echoes.text: When Yahweh saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the midst of the bush, and said, “Moses! Moses!” He said, “Here I am.”
echoes.note: 'Moses, Moses' from the burning bush is the closest formal parallel: a doubled-name call out of blinding/luminous divine presence that commissions the hearer. Strong thematic and formal coherence with Paul's vocation-by-theophany.

echoes.text: Yahweh came, and stood, and called as at other times, “Samuel! Samuel!” Then Samuel said, “Speak; for your servant hears.”
echoes.note: 'Samuel, Samuel' — doubled-name nocturnal call of the prophet who must learn the LORD's identity ('Speak, for your servant hears') just as Paul asks 'Who are you, Lord?' Reinforces the recurrence of the call-form.

echoes.text: As the appearance of the rainbow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of Yahweh’s glory. When I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard a voice of one that spoke.
echoes.note: The overwhelming light/glory before which Paul 'fell to the ground' (v7) reproduces Ezekiel's response to 'the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD' — 'I fell on my face.' Theophanic glory + prostration is the shared structure inaugurating prophetic commission.

echoes.text: So I was left alone, and saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me; for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength. Yet heard I the voice of his words; and when I heard the voice of his words, then was I fallen into a deep sleep on my face, with my face toward the ground.
echoes.note: Daniel's vision: he alone sees it, his companions flee in terror, his strength fails, he falls to the ground at the voice — closely matching v7-9 where the light fells Paul, his companions see the light and are afraid but do not grasp the voice. Notable volume.

echoes.text: Yahweh will strike you with madness, with blindness, and with astonishment of heart. You will grope at noonday, as the blind gropes in darkness, and you shall not prosper in your ways. You will only be oppressed and robbed always, and there will be no one to save you.
echoes.note: Covenant-curse blindness ('the LORD will strike you with blindness... you shall grope at noonday') resonates with Paul struck sightless 'about noon' (v6, 11), led by the hand. Ironic inversion — judgment-blindness becomes the threshold of conversion. Contested verbal link via 'noon'/'blindness.'

pericopes.text: One Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well reported of by all the Jews who lived in Damascus, came to me, and standing by me said to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight!’ In that very hour I looked up at him. He said, ‘The God of our fathers has appointed you to know his will, and to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his mouth. For you will be a witness for him to all men of what you have seen and heard. Now why do you wait? Arise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord.’

echoes.text: God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.
echoes.note: Ananias' 'The God of our fathers has appointed you' (v14) deploys the patriarchal covenant title fixed at the burning bush ('the God of your fathers... my name forever'), grounding Paul's commission in Israel's God. Verbal formula and thematic coherence.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.
echoes.note: 'to see the Righteous One' (v14) draws on the Servant who 'shall make many to be accounted righteous,' titled the righteous one; the Suffering Servant title is applied christologically to the one Paul is to witness. Coheres with the chapter's commissioning frame.

echoes.text: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.
